data.question: Elucidating the mechanism for task-dependent switching of the role of neural circuitry in working memory.
data.context: This remains an unresolved issue in understanding working memory models based on RC.

data.question: Physical implementation of a quantum reservoir system.
data.context: This is a challenge for realizing quantum RC.

data.question: Optimizing each physical reservoir by selecting the best-suited material or substrate and tuning hyper-parameters (e.g., shape, size).
data.context: Necessary for maximizing the computational power and performance of physical RC systems.

data.question: Ensuring scalability in single reservoirs as well as in combined multiple reservoirs.
data.context: Important for expanding the computational capacity of physical RC systems.

data.question: Suitably choosing a training algorithm compatible with the physical property of RC.
data.context: Crucial for efficient real-time information processing, especially when the readout speed limits total computation speed.

data.question: Further investigation is required for full-scale development of physical RC, covering performance evaluations in practical applications, implementation technology, and theoretical understanding of dynamics and computational function.
data.context: These are necessary for advancing physical RC beyond its early stage.

data.question: Expand the practical applications and develop next-generation machine learning systems using physical RC.
Develop energy-efficient machine learning hardware devices and chips based on physical RC.
Explore natural computing based on novel substrates using physical RC.
Explore efficient implementation methods for each type of reservoir.
Exploit novel physical phenomena for RC.
Combine physical RC with other machine learning algorithms/hardware.
Conduct mathematical modeling and analysis of physical reservoirs under physical constraints and practical conditions to systematically determine reservoir settings.
Evaluate computational performance, processing speed, memory, power efficiency, and scalability of physical RC systems for comparison with current digital computers.
Develop a physically realized readout to overcome the limitation of training speed in the readout.
Studies on biological reservoirs are expected to provide new insights into the mechanism of real-time information processing in various brain regions.
Examination of RC from the neuroscience viewpoint is expected to be useful for its applications in brain machine interfacing, disease care, and robot control.
Explore skyrmion fabrics as potentially attractive options for implementing a reservoir.

The simplicity of single-node reservoirs with delayed feedback is advantageous for physical implementation compared with network-based reservoirs, yet designing and implementing an appropriate delayed feedback loop is not a straightforward task.
data.context: Architectural simplicity and implementation complexity.

data.question: Physical implementation of reservoirs is amenable to various physical systems because adaptive training is not necessary, yet physical constraints make it difficult to optimize reservoir conditions for efficient operation.
data.context: Ease of hardware realization (due to fixed reservoir weights) and difficulty of performance optimization (due to physical constraints).

data.caption: Memory hierarchies in brains and computers. In brains, (a) Neurons and synapses are the fundamental elements of both neural computation and memory formation. Multiple excitatory and inhibitory neurons, embedded in recurrent canonical microcircuits, form basic computational primitives that can carry out state-dependent sensory processing and computation. Multiple clusters of recurrent networks are coupled together via long-distant connections to implement sensory fusion, inference, and symbolic manipulation. In computers, (b) Central Processing Units containing multiple cores are connected to both main memory and peripheral memory blocks. Each core comprises a micro-processor and local memory (e.g., local registers and Level-1 cache). All cores typically share access to another block of fast memory integrated on the same chip (e.g., Level-2 cache). The main memory block is the primary storage area, typically larger than the memory blocks inside the CPU, but requiring longer access times. The peripheral memory block requires even longer access rates, but can store significantly larger amounts of data.
data.description: This figure presents two diagrams illustrating memory hierarchies: (a) for brains and (b) for computers. Diagram (a) shows a brain with interconnected neurons and synapses, highlighting their role in neural computation and memory formation within recurrent canonical microcircuits and coupled networks. Diagram (b) depicts a computer architecture with a Central Processing Unit (CPU) containing multiple cores, each with local registers and cache. These cores are connected to main memory and peripheral memory, with a shared Level-2 cache.
data.significance: This figure visually contrasts the distributed memory and processing in biological brains with the separated memory and processing units in conventional von Neumann computer architectures, setting the stage for the paper's discussion on neuromorphic systems.

data.caption: Multi-layer neural networks. (a) Hierarchical convolu-tional network with feed-forward connections; (b) Deep neural network with all-to-all connections. Converging connections are only shown for two representative neurons (i.e., with large fan-in) in the bottom two layers, while an example of a neuron projecting to multiple targets (i.e., a neuron with large fan-out) is shown only in the second-to-last layer. Connections in (b) can be both feed-forward and feed-back.
data.description: This figure displays two types of multi-layer neural networks: (a) a hierarchical convolutional network with feed-forward connections, showing layers of neurons where connections converge from previous layers to subsequent ones; and (b) a deep neural network with all-to-all connections between layers, indicating both feed-forward and feed-back connections. Both diagrams use circles to represent neurons and lines to represent connections, illustrating fan-in and fan-out concepts.
data.significance: This figure illustrates the fundamental architectures of deep neural networks, specifically convolutional and all-to-all connected networks, which are key targets for implementation in neuromorphic hardware.

data.caption: Example architecture of a convolutional multi-layered network.
data.description: This figure shows a block diagram of a convolutional multi-layered network architecture. It consists of a "Visualsensor" input, followed by two layers of "Featuremaps" (L1 and L2), and finally a "Classifier" output. Arrows indicate the feed-forward data flow between these stages.
data.significance: This figure provides a high-level overview of a convolutional network's architecture, which is a common model implemented in neuromorphic systems for tasks like visual processing.

data.caption: Simplified architecture of the Minitaur system. Each core has 2048 B of state cache, 8192 B of weight cache, and 2 DSPs: one for multiplying the decay, one for summation of the input current. The darker gray blocks indicate use of BRAMS. Events can be streamed from the computer via the input buffer and added to the event queue which also holds the events from the output neurons in the Minitaur Core. These events are then streamed out through the output buffer or to the neurons in the Core using the Connection Manager block. Adapted from [43].
data.description: This figure presents a simplified block diagram of the Minitaur system's architecture, showing a single core replicated 32 times (x32). Key components include a DDR2 Memory Interface, Parallel Distributor, Connection Manager and Rule Lookup, Event Queue, Command and Control, Output Buffer, Input Buffer, and the Minitaur Core. The Minitaur Core itself contains State Cache (2048 B), Weight Cache (8192 B), Exp Decay Mem, State Manager, Neuron Membrane Decay Manager, Input Summation DSP, Weight Manager, Spiking DSP, and Rule Lookup. Darker gray blocks indicate BRAMS usage.
data.key_data: State cache: 2048 B; Weight cache: 8192 B; DSPs per core: 2; Cores: 32
data.significance: This figure details the internal architecture of the Minitaur neuromorphic system, highlighting its memory organization (caches, BRAMs) and processing elements (DSPs) within a multi-core design, which is crucial for understanding its performance and scalability for deep neural networks.

data.caption: NeuroCore chip block diagram (adapted from [25]). The chip comprises a 256×256 array of neuron elements, an asynchronous digital transmitter for sending the events generated by the neurons, a receiver block for accepting events from other sources, a router block for communicating packets among chips, and a memory blocks for supporting different network configurations. The neuron block comprises four different types of synapse analog circuits that integrate the incoming digital events into analog currents over time, four analog gating variable circuits that model the ion channel population dynamics, a soma circuit that generates the neuron output spikes, and a dendritic circuit that integrates the synaptic currents over space, from neighboring neurons.
data.description: This figure shows a block diagram of the NeuroCore chip. It includes RAM and Router blocks, a "NeuroCore" block containing a "Receiver" and "Transmitter", and a detailed "Neuron" block. The Neuron block is further broken down into four instances of "Synapse Gating Variable", "Dendrite", and "Soma". Arrows indicate data flow between these components.
data.key_data: Neuron elements array size: 256x256; Synapse analog circuits types: 4; Analog gating variable circuits types: 4
data.significance: This figure illustrates the mixed-signal analog/digital architecture of the NeuroGrid's NeuroCore chip, emphasizing the co-localization of neuron and synapse circuits and their biologically plausible dynamics, which is a key feature of this neuromorphic approach.

data.caption: Soft Winner-Take-All network behaviors: linear (top row) and non-linear (bottom row). The horizontal axis of each trace represents the spatial location of the neurons in the network, while the vertical axis represents the neurons response amplitude. Figure adapted from [101].
data.description: This figure presents six line charts illustrating different behaviors of a Soft Winner-Take-All (sWTA) network. The top row shows linear behaviors: "Analog gain", "Locus invariance", and "Gain control by common mode input". The bottom row shows non-linear behaviors: "Selective amplification", "Signal restoration", and "Multi-stability". The x-axis for all plots is "spatial location of the neurons in the network", and the y-axis is "neurons response amplitude".
data.significance: This figure demonstrates the diverse computational capabilities of soft Winner-Take-All networks, ranging from linear processing to complex non-linear functions like selective amplification and signal restoration, supporting their role as powerful computational primitives in neuromorphic systems.

data.caption: ROLLS neuromorphic processor: micrograph of a neu-romorphic processor chip that allocates most of its area to non-linear synapse circuits for memory storage and distributed massively parallel computing.
data.description: This figure shows a micrograph of the ROLLS neuromorphic processor chip. The layout highlights several blocks including four large arrays of "STP Synapses (128x128)" and four large arrays of "LTP Synapses (128x128)", along with "AER Input", "AER Output", "Linear synapses + I&F neurons", "Test Structures", and "Bias Generator ADC" blocks. The majority of the chip area is visibly dedicated to the synapse arrays.
data.key_data: STP Synapses array size: 128x128; LTP Synapses array size: 128x128
data.significance: This micrograph visually confirms the paper's claim that the ROLLS processor dedicates most of its area to synapse circuits, underscoring the co-localization of memory and computation, and its focus on implementing non-linear synaptic dynamics and plasticity.

data.caption: Forming stable attractors in the ROLLS neuromorphic processor (a) State of the bi-stable LTP synapses at the beginning, during, and at the end of the experiment; (b) Raster plots representing the response of the neurons, both during input stimulus presentation (for one second at t=0s, 2s, 4s, 6s), and after stimulus is removed; (c) Example of a measured neuron membrane potential at the beginning, during, and at the end of the training sessions, during stimulus presentation.
data.description: This figure illustrates the formation of stable attractors in the ROLLS neuromorphic processor through three sets of plots: (a) Four heatmaps show the state of bi-stable LTP synapses (Neuron ID vs. Neuron ID) at different stages (beginning, during, and end) of the experiment, indicating attractor formation through darker blocks. (b) Four raster plots show neuron spiking activity (Neuron ID vs. Time in seconds, 0-9s) during input stimulus presentation and after stimulus removal, demonstrating sustained activity in specific neuron groups. (c) Three line charts show the measured membrane potential (0.2-1.4) of a neuron over time (0-1.0s) at the beginning, during, and end of training, showing increasing and sustained depolarization.
data.key_data: Time (s) in raster plots: 0-9; Membrane potential: 0.2-1.4; Time (s) in membrane potential plots: 0-1.0
data.significance: This figure provides experimental evidence of the ROLLS processor's ability to form associative memories through spike-timing dependent plasticity, demonstrating the emergence of stable attractor states in a neuromorphic system, which is crucial for cognitive functions.

data.caption: Memory structures in computers versus memory structures in brains and neuromorphic systems.
data.description: This table compares memory structures across three categories: "Relative time scale", "Computers", and "Brains and Neuromorphic Systems". The "Relative time scale" column includes Short, Medium, and Long. The "Computers" column lists examples like registers, cache, dynamic RAM, and hard-disks. The "Brains and Neuromorphic Systems" column lists examples such as synapse and neural dynamics (short-term plasticity), spike-based plasticity (STDP), working memory circuits, structural plasticity, and axonal growth.
data.key_data: Relative time scale; Computers; Brains and Neuromorphic Systems; Short; Fast local memory (e.g., registers and cache memory banks inside the CPU); Synapse and neural dynamics at the single neuron level (short-term plasticity, spike-frequency adaptation, leak, etc.); Medium; Main memory (e.g., dynamic RAM); Spike-based plasticity (STDP, Hebbian learning, etc.) Formation of working memory circuits (e.g., recurrent networks, attractors, etc.); Long; Peripheral memory (e.g., hard-disks); Structural plasticity, axonal growth, long-term changes in neural path-ways.
data.significance: This table systematically compares the temporal scales and types of memory mechanisms in conventional computers versus biological brains and neuromorphic systems, highlighting the distributed and dynamic nature of memory in the latter, which is central to the paper's argument for alternative computing paradigms.

data.caption: Properties of Engineered Living Materials. ELMs leverage the adaptive responses, self-replicating potential, and robustness of biological systems for the programmed assembly and modulation of novel materials. The material can be engineered by genetic, spatial patterning, or chemical means, and can be designed for a wide variety of functions. These ELMs could be employed as micro to large-scale structural materials, as a kind of biohybrid device that integrates synthetic materials with living systems, or for specialty applications such as biocatalysis or toxin sequestration.
data.description: A central circular diagram depicts a bacterium cell within a network, labeled 'Engineered Living Materials'. Surrounding this central image are four bulleted lists of properties and functions. On the left, 'Genetic Modification', 'Mechanical Control of Bulk Structure', 'Chemical Functionalization', and 'Biotemplating' are listed under 'Engineered'. On the right, 'Structural Materials', 'Biohybrid Devices', 'Biocatalytic Materials', and 'Biosorptive Materials' are listed under 'Materials'. Below the central image, 'Cell as a Biofactory', 'Self-healing Materials', 'Dynamic Response', and 'Self-growing Materials' are listed under 'Living'.
data.significance: This figure visually defines Engineered Living Materials (ELMs) by outlining their core properties, engineering strategies, and diverse functional applications, establishing the conceptual framework for the paper.

data.caption: ELMs as Bioinspired Materials Engineering. A single seed contains all the essential information needed to create a tree, and it does so by genetically encoding the metabolic functions required for acquiring energy (photosynthesis) and mechanisms for utilizing local resources (carbon dioxide and water). It also contains the information necessary for successful multi-scale hierarchical morphogensis based on principles of cellular self-organization and molecular self-assembly. These living structures are capable of dynamically responding to the environment and can maintain and renew themselves over time. Synthetic ELMs attempt to replicate these characteristics, by using synthetic biology to engineer cells to fabricate, assemble, and maintain autonomously
data.description: A schematic comparing 'Natural Living Macroscale Structure' (a tree) with 'Engineered Living Macroscale Structure' (a stylized column). Both originate from a 'Seed' or 'Single Engineered Cell', respectively, drawing 'Water, Energy Sources, Nutrients, & Carbon Sources'. The natural tree shows 'Crystalline cellulose', 'Hemicellulose', 'Lignin', 'Wood macrofibers', and 'Wood cells' as components. The engineered structure shows 'Self-assembled biopolymers', 'ECM production', and 'Engineered cells'. Both pathways involve 'Maintenance & Renewal', 'Self Organization & Self Assembly', and 'Morphogenesis'.
data.significance: This figure illustrates the bioinspiration for ELMs by drawing parallels between the natural growth and self-assembly of a tree from a seed and the engineered creation of complex materials from single cells, highlighting the desired characteristics of ELMs.

data.caption: Engineering Bacterial Polysaccharides. (a) Strategy for in vivo generation of modified polysaccharides by metabolic pathway engineering. (b) Generation of polysaccharides containing fucose analogs and their modifications located at C-6 position of fucose. Both images are from Yi, et al.[18]
data.description: Panel (a) shows a schematic of metabolic pathway engineering, where a 'Pathway disruption' leads to the use of an 'Exogenous pathway' and 'Unnatural substrate' to generate modified polysaccharides. Panel (b) illustrates the chemical structures involved in the generation of polysaccharides containing fucose analogs. It shows a series of fucose derivatives with different R groups (OH, N3, H2N, H, O) at the C-6 position, originating from 'E. coli O86:B7Δgmd-fcl harboring pET15b-fkp' via a 'Salvage pathway (Fkp)'. The structures are numbered 1 through 10.
data.significance: This figure demonstrates a key strategy for engineering ELMs by metabolically modifying bacterial polysaccharides, showcasing how genetic manipulation can alter the chemical composition of building blocks for novel material properties.

data.caption: Engineered Polysaccharide-Based ECMs for Functional Biofilms. (a) Bacterial polymer biosynthesis pathways from intermediates of central metabolism (polysaccharides shown in green).[173] Cellulose (b-d). (b) Engineering the thickness and piezoelectricity of bacterial cellulose.[26] (c) Engineering of spatial and temporal patterned and functionalized cellulose materials on a macroscale.[25] (d) In vivo curdlan and cellulose bionanocomposite synthesis to modulate cellulose properties.[28]
data.description: Panel (a) is a metabolic pathway diagram showing the biosynthesis of various polysaccharides (Alginate, Xanthan, K30 antigen, Gellan, Curdlan, Cellulose, Dextran) from carbon sources and intermediates like Glucose-6-P and Acetyl-CoA. Panel (b) displays SEM micrographs of bacterial cellulose films (WT, PA, PAB, PABCD) and a table comparing their thickness, crystallinity index, and stress at break. Panel (c) illustrates spatial and temporal patterning of cellulose production in E. coli, showing 'A Spatial patterning' with different colored regions and 'B Temporal patterning' with pellicles grown under various induction conditions over time. Panel (d) shows a schematic of 'curdlan/cellulose bionanocomposites' synthesis in Gluconacetobacter xylinus via 'Gene Transformation' of 'Curdlan synthase', along with a micrograph of the composite material.
data.key_data: WT film thickness: 4.8 ± 0.8 µm; WT crystallinity index: 92 ± 4 %; WT stress at break: 47.9 MPa; PA film thickness: 7.4 ± 0.3 µm; PA crystallinity index: 97 ± 10 %; PA stress at break: 40.7 MPa; PAB film thickness: 6.2 ± 0.3 µm; PAB crystallinity index: 91 ± 6 %; PAB stress at break: 48.5 MPa; PABCD film thickness: 10.3 ± 0.6 µm; PABCD crystallinity index: 89 ± 3 %; PABCD stress at break: 48.5 MPa
data.significance: This figure highlights successful engineering efforts to control the production and properties of bacterial polysaccharides, demonstrating how genetic and metabolic manipulation can create functional biofilms with tunable mechanical and structural characteristics for ELMs.

data.caption: Engineered Protein-Based ECMs for Functional Biofilms. S-layer proteins (a-b). (a) Schematic of S-layer proteins in gram positive and negative bacteria.[30] (b) Scheme of S-layer protein on bacterial cell surface and SEM image of cell surface of Thermoanaerobacter thermohydrosulfuricus L111 showing a hexagonal (p6) surface lattice.[30] (c) The construction of the three paradigmatic systems involved the division of the production and organization of the enzymes and scaffold proteins into different strains of L. plantarum.[35] (d) Scheme of genetic programming and modularity of the BIND system.[39] (e) Catalytic-BIND: biofilm functionalization with enzymes through
data.description: Panel (a) illustrates the S-layer protein arrangement on Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria. Panel (b) shows a schematic of native and recombinantly produced S-layer proteins on a bacterial cell surface, accompanied by an SEM image of Thermoanaerobacter thermohydrosulfuricus L111 with a hexagonal surface lattice. Panel (c) depicts the 'Designer cellulosomes' concept, showing how secreted and anchored enzymes can be combined with scaffoldin from different bacterial cells. Panel (d) presents the 'Biofilm-Integrated Nanofiber Display (BIND)' system, where E. coli is engineered to secrete CsgA-peptide fusions that self-assemble into nanofibers on the cell surface. Panel (e) shows the 'Catalytic-BIND' system, where enzymes are immobilized onto E. coli biofilms using conjugation strategies. Panel (f) displays SEM/EDS and TEM images of environmentally switchable conductive biofilms. Panel (g) conceptually depicts a 'Mercury-Triggered Curli Production' circuit leading to a 'Mercury-Remediating Biofilm Sponge'.
data.significance: This figure showcases various strategies for engineering protein-based extracellular matrices (ECMs) in bacteria, demonstrating how S-layer proteins, functional amyloids, and genetic circuits can be leveraged to create functional biofilms for diverse applications like biocatalysis and bioremediation.

data.caption: Engineering Bacteria to Control Biofilm Pattern Formation. (a) Effect of indole (500 µM) on the biofilm formation and motility of wild-type and engineered E. coli.[48] (b) µBE metabolic circuit with the two E. coli cell types communicate by using the LasI / LasR QS module of P. aeruginosa (top) and dispersal of dual-species biofilms using arabinose (bottom).[47] (c) Toluene degradation pathway from P. putida F1 and partial pathways carried out by mutant strains PpF4 and PpF10732 (top). Spatial patterns arising from the consortium of mutants (bottom).[52] (d) Schematic representation of the engineered plasmid conferring constitutive metal uptake and inducible adhesion (top).
data.description: Panel (a) is a bar chart showing the motility (in cm) of wild-type and engineered E. coli strains (W/T, trpE, tnaC, tnaA, sdiA) in the presence and absence of 500 µM indole. Panel (b) illustrates a µBE metabolic circuit for biofilm dispersal, showing 'Disperser cell' and 'Initial colonizer cell' communication via QS molecules (3OC12HSL) and subsequent biofilm dispersal triggered by arabinose. Time-lapse images (10h, 15h, 21h, 29h, 33h, 37h, 43h, 47h) show biofilm formation and dispersal. Panel (c) shows the toluene degradation pathway and spatial patterns formed by P. putida F1 mutant strains (PpF4, PpF10732) on agar plates over time (72h, 120h, 120h no toluene). Panel (d) presents a schematic of an engineered plasmid for metal uptake and adhesion, along with SEM images showing biofilm thickness (53±2 µm, 71±5 µm, 67±5 µm) for S61 strain under different metal ion concentrations (No metal, 1 µM Co2+, 1 µM Ni2+).
data.key_data: W/T motility (no indole): ~3.5 cm; W/T motility (500 µM indole): ~1.5 cm; trpE motility (no indole): ~3.5 cm; trpE motility (500 µM indole): ~3.5 cm; tnaC motility (no indole): ~3.5 cm; tnaC motility (500 µM indole): ~3.5 cm; tnaA motility (no indole): ~3.5 cm; tnaA motility (500 µM indole): ~3.5 cm; sdiA motility (no indole): ~3.5 cm; sdiA motility (500 µM indole): ~3.5 cm; S61 biofilm thickness (No metal): 53±2 µm; S61 biofilm thickness (1 µM Co2+): 71±5 µm; S61 biofilm thickness (1 µM Ni2+): 67±5 µm
data.significance: This figure demonstrates the ability to engineer bacterial systems for controlled biofilm formation, dispersal, and patterning, showcasing how synthetic biology can be used to create ELMs with dynamic and responsive behaviors for applications like bioremediation.

data.caption: Living soft robots' motion relies on the patterning of cardiac muscle cells. (a) Muscular thin films exploit the anisotropy of cardiomyocytes seeded onto different fibronectin-patterned PDMS surfaces to generate complex actuation patterns. Left. A strip with anisotropically organized cadiomyocytes coils and uncoils, middle. A rectangular strip with discrete arrayed muscle fibers spontaneously adopts an helical conformation, right. Cardiomyocytes aligned length-wise along a strip form a “gripper” device.[70] (b) The locomotion of a jellyfish was replicated using electrically-stimulated muscle sheets to form a medusoid. [71] (c) An artifical ray robot was fabricated with genetically engineered cardiomyocytes that can respond to optical stimuli. Different frequencies were used for stimulating muscle contraction and for maneuvering.[72]
data.description: Panel (a) shows micrographs of muscular thin films. The left image shows a strip coiling and uncoiling with 0.29 mm displacement. The middle image shows a rectangular strip adopting a helical conformation. The right image shows cardiomyocytes forming a 'gripper' device. Panel (b) illustrates the 'Jellyfish stroke cycle and functions' with key factors like thrust, recoil, and feeding current, and shows a 'medusoid' replicating jellyfish swimming. Panel (c) depicts an 'ARTIFICIAL RAY' robot with layers (3D elastomer body, golden skeleton, interstitial elastomer, muscle) and shows its 'undulatory gait' and 'maneuvering' capabilities, with a scale bar of 5 mm.
data.key_data: Displacement: 0.29 mm; Artificial ray robot scale bar: 5 mm
data.significance: This figure illustrates the development of living soft robots by patterning cardiac muscle cells on polymeric substrates, demonstrating how biological actuation can be harnessed to create complex, responsive, and locomotive ELMs.

data.caption: Living cells have been integrated with polymers to create smart functional living polymeric composites with added functionalities. Penicillin-producing fungi cells were used to create (a) living antibiotic-releasing surfaces that can sustain release over time because of their in situ production[62] and (b) smart self-cleaning surfaces that can metabolize food spills.[63]
data.description: Panel (a) compares a 'Classic non-living material' with 'Function loaded' to a 'Living surface' with 'Seeded with appropriate microorganisms'. The living surface consumes 'Nutrients' and performs 'On-site production and release'. Panel (b) illustrates a 'Self-cleaning living surface' where 'Food spill' triggers 'Growing fungi in living layer', which then facilitates 'Transport of food, gas, and secondary metabolites through membrane'.
data.significance: This figure demonstrates the concept of 'smart living surfaces' by showing how fungi-polymer composites can be engineered to continuously produce and release antibiotics or metabolize food spills, highlighting the self-sustaining and responsive functionalities of ELMs.

data.caption: Microorganisms for the production of or the directed assembly of organic polymers. (a) Several key genes and operons are involved in the synthesis of biopolymers produced by bacteria.[173] (b) Bacterial synthesis of polyhydroxyalkanoates through fermentation is part of the carbon life cycle of these biodegradable polymers.[75] (c) Through their redox metabolism, bacteria can induce polymerization in monomer-catalyst suspensions, resulting in surface-bound polymers.[82]
data.description: Panel (a) lists various bacterial gene operons involved in the synthesis of biopolymers, categorized by their function (e.g., polymer synthesis enzymes, precursor biosynthesis enzymes, transcriptional regulators). Panel (b) illustrates the carbon life cycle of polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHAs), showing how 'Carbon sources' are converted by 'Bacteria' through 'Fermentation' into 'PHAs', which can be extracted, purified, molded into 'Bioplastic products', and undergo 'Recycling' or 'Composting'. Panel (c) depicts how bacteria can induce atom transfer radical polymerization (ATRP) through 'Cu reduction', leading to the formation of 'Templated' (surface-bound) and 'Non-templated' polymers from 'Monomer-catalyst suspensions'.
data.significance: This figure illustrates the diverse capabilities of microorganisms in producing and assembling organic polymers, showcasing the potential of bacterial metabolic pathways and redox processes for creating biodegradable plastics and surface-bound functional materials as ELMs.

data.caption: Living composites with carbon materials. Integrating ELMs with inroganic materials serve for the fabrication of various devices. (a) Bionic composites made of yeast cells fermented with graphene nanoplatelets (GNPs) (top) or carbon nanotubes (CNTs) (bottom).[85, 86] (b) Biomemory device fabricated through the self-assembly of Shewanella oneidensis bacteria with graphene oxide (left. SEM image of the composite, right. Write/erase function of the biomemory device).[87]
data.description: Panel (a) shows two schematics of bionic composites. The top schematic illustrates yeast cells fermenting 'Sucrose + H2O' to produce 'GNPs' and form a composite. The bottom schematic shows fermented cells encapsulating 'CNTs' after drawing 'Sucrose + H2O'. Panel (b) displays an SEM image (left) of a composite formed by Shewanella oneidensis bacteria and graphene, with a scale bar of 1 µm. The right side of panel (b) is a line chart showing the 'Current (mA)' over 'Time (Sec)' for a biomemory device, comparing 'Abiotic carbon cloth', 'Abiotic graphene', 'S. oneidensis biofilm', and 'Graphene-S. oneidensis' materials, demonstrating write/erase functionality.
data.key_data: SEM image scale bar: 1 µm; Current (mA) range: -40 to 40 mA; Time (Sec) range: 0.0 to 3.5 Sec
data.significance: This figure demonstrates the integration of living microorganisms with carbon nanomaterials to create bionic composites with enhanced mechanical, electrical, and self-healing properties, showcasing their utility in advanced applications like biomemory devices.

data.caption: Silica-based ELMs from Diatom Engineering. (a) Scanning electron microscopy images of cell walls from different diatom species. Images in top and middle rows show overviews of single silica cell walls, and images in bottom row show details of diatom silica cell walls.[174] (b) Images obtained by confocal fluorescence microscopy of T. pseudonana transformants expressing silaffin fusion protein tpSil3-GFP. The four images in the left half (“cell”) were taken from live cells, the images in the right half ("cell wall") were taken from isolated biosilica. Each micrograph is an overlay of two images recorded in the “green channel” (excitation: 488 nm, emission: 505/550 nm bandpass filter) and the "red channel” (excitation: 543 nm, emission: 585 nm long-pass filter). The green color is indicative of GFP, the red color is caused by chloroplast autofluorescence. Scale bar: 2 µm (identical scale for all micrographs).[99] (c) HabB activity in T. pseudonana
data.description: Panel (a) presents SEM images of diatom cell walls, showing various intricate patterns and structures at different magnifications (500nm scale bars). Panel (b) shows confocal fluorescence microscopy images of T. pseudonana cells and cell walls expressing GFP-fused silaffin protein, with a scale bar of 2 µm. Panel (c) includes a line graph showing the kinetics of 2-aminophenol formation over time (t/h) for WT and transformant biosilica (C1, C2, C3), and a bar graph comparing the half-life of soluble HabB, immobilized HabB in biosilica, and R5 peptide-immobilized silica under various conditions (55°C, 50% MeOH, pH 6, pH 5, 50% CH3CN). Panel (d) illustrates the hypothetical pathway for intracellular transport of silaffin-enzyme fusion proteins to the silica deposition vesicle (SDV). Panel (e) depicts genetically engineered diatom biosilica (green) containing liposome-encapsulated drug molecules (yellow) targeting neuroblastoma (red) and lymphocyte (purple) cells.
data.key_data: SEM scale bars: 500nm; Confocal microscopy scale bar: 2 µm; 2-aminophenol concentration range: 0.0 to 40.0 µmol L-1; Time (t/h) range: 0 to 5 h; Half-life (min) range: 0 to 300 min
data.significance: This figure demonstrates the advanced engineering of diatoms to create silica-based ELMs with intricate structures and functional capabilities, including enzyme immobilization and targeted drug delivery, showcasing the potential for highly sophisticated bio-inorganic hybrid materials.

data.caption: Self-healing Biological Concrete. (a) Schematic of crack-healing by concrete-immobilized bacteria. Bacteria on fresh crack surfaces become activated due to water ingression, start to multiply and precipitate minerals such as calcite (CaCO3), which eventually seal the crack[103] (b) Self-healing admixture composed of expanded clay particles (left) loaded with bacterial spores and organic bio-mineral precursor compound (calcium lactate). When embedded in the concrete matrix (right) the clay particles serve as internal reservoirs containing the two-component healing agent consisting of bacterial spores and a suitable bio-mineral precursor compound.[102]
data.description: Panel (a) is a four-step schematic illustrating crack-healing in bioconcrete: 1. Bioconcrete contains dormant bacteria. 2. Upon damage, the interior is exposed to the environment. 3. Water ingress activates the dormant bacteria. 4. Bacterially induced mineralization fills the fracture. Panel (b) shows photographs of concrete specimens: 'A: Control specimen before healing' and 'after healing', and 'B: Bacterial specimen before healing' and 'after healing'. Panel (c) displays SEM micrographs of CaCO3 precipitation in silica gel (100x and 1000x magnification) and PU foam (100x and 1000x magnification), with 100µm and 10µm scale bars. Panel (d) is a photograph of the bioMASON machine for producing biobricks.
data.key_data: CaCO3 in silica gel (100x) scale bar: 100µm; CaCO3 in silica gel (1000x) scale bar: 10µm; CaCO3 in PU foam (100x) scale bar: 100µm; CaCO3 in PU foam (1000x) scale bar: 10µm
data.significance: This figure illustrates the development of self-healing concrete and biologically fabricated bricks, demonstrating how bacteria can be engineered to precipitate calcium carbonate to repair cracks and form building materials, offering sustainable alternatives in construction.

data.caption: Engineered ELMs from Mutualistic Microbial Consortia. A collection of microorganisms with mutualistic or complementary functions can be assembled to produce functional materials. (a) Living soft matter was produced in situ by growing cellulose-producing bacteria and photosynthetic microalgae.[110] (b) The resulting material consists of a moldable gel of entrapped microalgae in a cellulose matrix.
data.description: Panel (a) is a schematic showing the mutualistic growth of microalgae and acetobacter in 'TAP+GY growth media' under 'Air' conditions, leading to a 'symbiotic biomaterial'. Panel (b) shows a photograph of a green, moldable gel (5 cm scale) and an SEM micrograph of the material at 10 µm scale, revealing the entrapped microalgae within a cellulose matrix.
data.key_data: Photograph scale: 5 cm; SEM micrograph scale: 10 µm
data.significance: This figure highlights the potential of mutualistic microbial consortia to produce ELMs, demonstrating how co-culturing different microorganisms can lead to the in situ fabrication of functional, moldable biomaterials like cellulose-microalgae gels.

data.caption: Lignocellulosic Living Organisms as ELMs. (a-c) Tree shaping allows for the mechanical manipulation of living tree tissues into a growing structure. (d) One version of this architectural design system is known as Baubontanik and incorporates modern design materials with tree shaping, as shown in the construction of a tower. Over time, the trees are able to fuse around temporary metal scaffolding. (e) Tree shaping takes advantage of inosculation, or proximity grafting, the ability of tree tissues in trunks, branches, or roots to fuse together when in close proximity. Shown are cross-sections of inosculated branches. All photos for (a-e) copyright Ferdinand
data.description: Panels (a), (b), and (c) show photographs of a tree-shaped tower structure at different stages of growth, demonstrating 'tree shaping'. Panel (d) provides close-up photographs of tree branches growing around metal scaffolding, illustrating the Baubotanik architectural design system. Panel (e) displays cross-sections of inosculated (fused) branches, numbered 2, 3, 5, and 6, with a scale bar of 2 cm. Panel (f) is a concept design of a tree-based habitat shaped using CNC scaffolds.
data.key_data: Cross-sections scale bar: 2 cm
data.significance: This figure showcases tree shaping as an example of large-scale ELM fabrication, where living lignocellulosic organisms are physically manipulated to create functional architectural structures, demonstrating the potential for growing complex, self-maintaining materials.

data.caption: Mycelium-based ELM materials. (a) A 'mycotecture' concept structure composed of mycelium, Mycotectural Alpha, on exhibit at Kunsthalle Düsseldorf in 2009. Photograph copyright Philip Ross. (b) Mycelium-based bricks for construction. (c) When the bricks are placed together, the mycelium grow into each other, organically fusing the bricks together. (d) The mycelial material can also be shaped into functional structures such as furniture. (e) In addition, flexible materials such as tough leather-like fabrics can be made from mycelium. (f) A photograph of Mycoworks mycelium material shows the wood chip feedstock and the growing mycelial hyphae. Photos (a-f) are all copyright MycoWorks. (g) A flowchart of the process for preparation of mycelial materials. Mycelium-based foam technology from Ecovative Design used for ecologically-friendly packaging (h) and building insulation (i). (j) SEM image of the mycelium from the Ecovative materials. Photos (h-j) copyright Ecovative Design.
data.description: Panel (a) shows a 'mycotecture' concept structure made of mycelium. Panel (b) displays mycelium-based bricks. Panel (c) illustrates mycelium fusing bricks together. Panel (d) shows furniture made from mycelial material. Panel (e) presents leather-like fabrics from mycelium. Panel (f) is a photograph of Mycoworks mycelium material with wood chip feedstock. Panel (g) is a flowchart for mycelial material preparation: 'Fungal Culture' -> 'Wood Feedstock' -> 'Inoculation and Growth' -> 'Denaturing to Kill Fungal Cells' -> 'Moisture Content Reduction'. Panel (h) shows Ecovative packaging, panel (i) shows building insulation, and panel (j) is an SEM image of mycelium from Ecovative materials with a scale bar of 100 µm.
data.key_data: SEM image scale bar: 100µm
data.significance: This figure highlights mycelium-based materials as a commercially successful example of large-scale ELMs, demonstrating their versatility in creating structures, furniture, fabrics, and insulation, and showcasing their potential for sustainable manufacturing.

data.caption: Large-scale production of bacterial cellulose materials. (a) Harvested bacterial cellulose material. Photo copyright Scobytec. (b) Skin dressing made from microbial cellulose materials. Photo copyright www.fzmb.de. (c) As a structural material, modular geometric objects can be created from molded bacterial cellulose. Photo copyright Jannis Hülsen. (d) An example of architectural materials made of bacterial cellulose grown on a support scaffold of jute wires. Photo copyright Institute for Advanced Architecture of Catalonia. (e) Bacterial cellulose can also be used as a large-scale textile material, here used to create various garments. Photo copyright Suzanne Lee.
data.description: Panel (a) shows a harvested bacterial cellulose material. Panel (b) displays a skin dressing made from microbial cellulose. Panel (c) presents modular geometric objects created from molded bacterial cellulose. Panel (d) illustrates architectural materials made of bacterial cellulose grown on a jute wire scaffold. Panel (e) shows various garments (jackets, tops) made from bacterial cellulose as a textile material.
data.significance: This figure illustrates the diverse applications and large-scale production potential of bacterial cellulose as an ELM, ranging from biomedical uses like skin dressings to structural materials, architectural components, and textiles.

data.caption: Large-scale Bioproduction Technologies for ELMs. (a) Basic bioreactor architectures. In contrast to CSTR reactors, which are efficient for production of planktonic cells, PBR and MBBRs contain packing materials that allow for the growth of interfacial biomass and are more suited for maximizing biofilm growth. (b) Preparatory-scale ELMs can be separated from the cellular components after growth, using chemical treatments and vacuum-assisted filtration. Right images are SEM micrographs showing isolated layered ELM amyloid mat materials. (c) On an industrial level, high-throughput separation of solids from liquids can be applied to ELMs grown in liquid
data.description: Panel (a) illustrates three bioreactor architectures: 'CSTR' (Continuous Stirred Tank Reactor), 'PBR' (Packed Bed Reactor) with 'Bed Material / Biocarrier', and 'MBBR' (Moving-Bed Bioreactor) also with 'Bed Material / Biocarrier', all showing 'Biofilm Growth'. Panel (b) depicts the process of separating 'Curli nanofiber aggregates' from 'Bacteria, debris, DNA, RNA...' using chemical treatments (Guanidine HCl, DNAse, RNAse, Sodium dodecyl sulfate) and filtration. SEM micrographs show the 'Top surface' (100 nm scale) and 'Cross-section' (20 nm scale) of isolated layered ELM amyloid mat materials. Panel (c) shows an industrial-scale 'Dewetting Solids' process using rollers to separate solids from liquids, starting from 'Feedstock Wet Material'.
data.key_data: SEM micrograph scale bar (top surface): 100 nm; SEM micrograph scale bar (cross-section): 20 nm
data.significance: This figure outlines scalable bioproduction and processing technologies for ELMs, demonstrating how bioreactor designs and separation methods can be adapted for efficient, large-scale manufacturing of biofilm-based materials.

data.caption: Electrospun living polymer fibers. (a) Yeast cells were embedded in a water-soluble polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP) core matrix, and enveloped with a poly vinylidene fluoride-cohexafluoropropylene shell. In the middle panel, encapsulated yeast cells are shown in purple.[146] (b) Electrospun living bacteria composite fibers were prepared using a poly-(vinyl alcohol) (PVA) core subsequently coated with a hydrophobic poly(p-xylylene) (PPX) shell via chemical vapor deposition (left). The fibers were mounted onto a wire frame (5 cm wide) that could be used for decontamination (right).[147]
data.description: Panel (a) illustrates the fabrication of electrospun fibers with yeast cells. It shows 'C. tropicalis' cells embedded in a 'PVP' core, enveloped by a 'PVDF' shell, leading to 'Fabrication' and 'Application'. A micrograph shows encapsulated yeast cells in purple. Panel (b) depicts electrospun living bacteria composite fibers. The left schematic shows 'Bacteria' embedded in a 'PVA' core, coated with a 'PPX' shell via 'CVD'. The right image shows these fibers mounted on a wire frame (5 cm wide) for decontamination.
data.key_data: Wire frame width: 5 cm
data.significance: This figure demonstrates electrospinning as a versatile method for fabricating ELMs by encapsulating living cells within polymer fibers, enabling the creation of functional composites for applications like decontamination.

data.caption: 3D Printing for Spatial Patterning of ELMs. (a) Top: Confocal laser scanning microscopy (CLSM) reconstruction of bacteria (green) within spheroid “rooms” created from photocrosslinked gelatin that are connected by channels (red). Scale bar, 20 µm. Bottom: Light microscopy top view of encapsulated P. aeruginosa cells growing within the microfabricated structure over time. Scale bar, 20 µm. (b) This method can be used to construct complex structures containing different bacterial species, as demonstrated from nested structures where the inner chamber contains S. aureus bacteria surrounded by P. aeruginosa bacteria in the outer chamber. Left: Model and light
data.description: Panel (a) shows CLSM reconstruction of bacteria (green) in gelatin spheroid 'rooms' connected by channels (red), with a 20 µm scale bar. Below, light microscopy images show P. aeruginosa growth over time (10, 215, 1000 min) in microfabricated structures, also with a 20 µm scale bar. Panel (b) illustrates nested bacterial structures with S. aureus in the inner chamber and P. aeruginosa in the outer chamber, shown as a model and light microscopy image (left), and CLSM reconstruction (right) with 10 µm scale bars. Panel (c) shows an inexpensive bacterial 3D printer (left) and CLSM reconstructions of 3D-printed E. coli populations (top right) and rhamnose-induced RFP expression (bottom right) over time (0h, 8h, 24h, 48h), with a 200 µm scale bar. Panel (d) depicts the 3D tissue-printing process for kidney nephron tubules: (i) print silicone gasket, (ii) cast pluronic gelatin-fibrinogen, (iii) evacuate, (iv) add cells, perfuse. Phase contrast images show cells in 3D-printed tubule after 6 weeks (500 µm and 250 µm scale bars), and TEM cross-section after 5 weeks (5 µm scale bar).
data.key_data: CLSM reconstruction scale bar (a, top): 20 µm; Light microscopy scale bar (a, bottom): 20 µm; CLSM reconstruction scale bars (b): 10 µm; RFP expression time points: 0h, 8h, 24h, 48h; CLSM reconstruction scale bar (c): 200 µm; Phase contrast image scale bars (d): 500 µm, 250 µm; TEM cross-section scale bar (d): 5 µm
data.significance: This figure demonstrates the power of 3D printing technologies in creating spatially patterned ELMs, enabling precise control over cellular organization and the fabrication of complex, anisotropic living composites for various applications, including synthetic tissue engineering.

data.caption: Synthetic Morphogenesis for Engineering Hierarchically Defined Multicellular Structures. (a) Use of AHL production and sensing elements to generate a band detector circuit for genetically programmed morphogenesis. Right, top image shows a bullseye pattern formed by the sender cells in the middle expressing CFP surrounded by two cell types with different band detectors, expressing GFP and DsRed. Right, bottom image shows designed shapes can be generated by defined placement of the sender cells (here expressing DsRed); the GFP cells containing the band detector circuit only grow at a defined AHL range and thus form a heart shape.[161] (b) By combining a genetic dark sensor with an AHL-gradient response circuit, only cells directly adjacent to the dark zones (edges) are turned on by the synthetic circuit, creating an edge-detection device. Bottom images: left shows the photomask used in the experiment, center is a photo of a bacterial lawn containing the edge detector circuit, and right shows the mathematically modeled prediction.[162] (c) Generation of striped patterns from growing populations of bacterial cells using an AHL-generation circuit that stops
data.description: Panel (a) illustrates AHL-based band detector circuits for morphogenesis. The left side shows schematics of 'Sender' and 'Band detector' cells with genetic components (TetR, LuxR, LacI). The right side shows a bullseye pattern (top) with CFP, GFP, and DsRed expressing cells, and a heart shape (bottom) formed by GFP cells in a defined AHL range. Panel (b) depicts an edge-detection device combining a 'Dark Sensor' and an 'AHL' gradient response circuit. It shows a photomask (left), an in vivo result (center) of a bacterial lawn with the edge detector circuit, and an in silico prediction (right), with a 1.4cm scale bar and a color gradient from 10 to 35. Panel (c) shows the generation of striped patterns from bacterial cells using an AHL-generation circuit, with images at 300 min, 706 min, 900 min, 1960 min, and 1900 min. Panel (d) shows complex patterns formed by bacterial populations. Panel (e) displays a confocal microscopy image of B. subtilis biofilm populations self-organizing into fractal patterns.
data.key_data: Edge-detection device scale bar: 1.4cm; Color gradient range: 10 to 35; Striped pattern time points: 300 min, 706 min, 900 min, 1960 min, 1900 min
data.significance: This figure demonstrates the application of synthetic morphogenesis to engineer hierarchically defined multicellular structures, showcasing how genetic circuits and intercellular communication can be programmed to create complex patterns and dynamic behaviors in ELMs.

data.caption: Fig. 1. RC frameworks where the reservoir is fixed and only the readout weights Wout are trained. (a) A conventional RC system with an RNN-based reservoir as in ESNs and LSMs. (b) A physical RC system in which the reservoir is realized using a physical system or device.
data.description: Two diagrams illustrating Reservoir Computing (RC) frameworks. Both show 'Input' feeding into a 'Reservoir' and then to a 'Readout' which produces 'Output'. The reservoir has internal weights 'W' and input weights 'Win', while the readout has weights 'Wout'. (a) 'Conventional RC' shows the reservoir as an abstract box. (b) 'Physical RC' shows the reservoir as 'Physical systems / devices'.
data.significance: This figure introduces the fundamental concept of Reservoir Computing, distinguishing between conventional RNN-based reservoirs and physical system-based reservoirs, which is the focus of the review.

data.caption: Fig. 2. A fluidic RC where the reservoir is the water in a bucket (Fernando & Sojakka, 2003). Figure reproduced with permission from Springer Nature.
data.description: A photograph showing a physical setup for fluidic Reservoir Computing. It depicts a bucket filled with water, with several small electric motors submerged, creating ripples on the water surface. The setup includes a camera above the bucket to record the water surface.
data.significance: This figure illustrates an early and unconventional example of physical Reservoir Computing, demonstrating that complex physical systems can serve as reservoirs for computation.

data.caption: Fig. 3. RC using a single nonlinear node reservoir with time-delayed feedback (Appeltant et al., 2011).
data.description: A schematic diagram of a single nonlinear node reservoir with time-delayed feedback. An 'Input' signal is masked and fed into a 'Nonlinear node'. The output of the nonlinear node is fed back through a delay line (represented by a loop with delay 'θ') and also serves as the 'Virtual nodes' for the 'Readout' layer, which produces the 'Output'. The virtual nodes are sampled at different points along the delay line.
data.significance: This figure presents a hardware-friendly architecture for RC using a single nonlinear node and time-delayed feedback, which is a common approach for physical implementations due to its simplicity.

data.caption: Fig. 4. RC using cellular automata (Yilmaz, 2015b).
data.description: A diagram illustrating a Reservoir Computing system based on cellular automata. An 'Input' is fed into a 'Reservoir' which is depicted as a grid of cells, representing the cellular automaton. The state of the cells evolves over 'Time' from an 'Initial condition'. The 'Space' dimension is also shown. The states of the reservoir cells are then fed to a 'Readout' layer with weights 'Wout' to produce an 'Output'.
data.significance: This figure shows how cellular automata, with their simple rules and complex emergent behavior, can be utilized as physical reservoirs for RC, offering advantages for parallel hardware implementation.

data.caption: Fig. 5. RC using coupled oscillators. (a) A mechanical reservoir with coupled nonlinear oscillators (Coulombe, York, & Sylvestre, 2017). (b) A DNA reservoir with coupled chemical oscillators (Goudarzi, Lakin, & Stefanovic, 2013). (c) A synchronization-based RC with coupled phase oscillators (Yamane, Katayama, Nakane, Tanaka, & Nakano, 2015).
data.description: Three sub-diagrams illustrating different types of coupled oscillator reservoirs for RC. (a) 'A mechanical reservoir with coupled nonlinear oscillators' shows a chain of masses connected by springs, with external 'Forcing' and 'Amplitude modulation input', producing 'Mass position output'. (b) 'A DNA reservoir with coupled chemical oscillators' shows a microfluidic reactor with 'Influx' and 'Efflux' and three interacting 'DNA species' (labeled 1, 2, 3). (c) 'A synchronization-based RC with coupled phase oscillators' shows an 'Input' affecting multiple 'Phase oscillator' nodes, which then produce a 'Phase difference output'.
data.significance: This figure highlights the diversity of physical systems that can act as RC reservoirs, specifically showcasing mechanical, chemical (DNA-based), and phase-coupled oscillators as examples of coupled nonlinear dynamical systems.

data.caption: Fig. 6. (a) Electronically implemented RC system using a single-node reservoir based on the Mackey-Glass equation with delay (Soriano, Ortín and Keuninckx et al., 2015). Figure reproduced and modified with permission from Springer Nature. (b) Architecture of an FPGA-based LSM system for speech recognition (Schrauwen, D' Haene, Verstraeten, & Van Campenhout, 2008). Figure reproduced with permission from Elsevier.
data.description: Two sub-diagrams illustrating electronic RC implementations. (a) 'Electronically implemented RC system using a single-node reservoir based on the Mackey-Glass equation with delay'. It shows an 'Input' undergoing 'pre-processing' (mask, input bias, gain), then fed to a 'Reservoir' (Mackey-Glass equation with delay, implemented with analog components like summation, nonlinearity, amplifiers, and filters), and finally 'post-processing' (ADC, trained weights) to produce 'Output'. Analog components include LM358, BC548B, resistors (1k, 10k, 3.3k), and capacitors (2.7nF). Digital components include DAC and ADC. (b) 'Architecture of an FPGA-based LSM system for speech recognition'. It shows 'Input' going through 'Audio codec', 'Lyon's cochlear model', 'Spiking Neural Networks Circuits' (labeled 1 and 2), 'Double buffer' (labeled 1 and 2), 'Filtering & Weighted sum', and 'Microblaze soft processor' to produce 'Output'.
data.key_data: {'Resistors': '1k, 10k, 3.3k'}; {'Capacitor': '2.7nF'}; {'AD/DA converters': '12-bits resolution'}
data.significance: This figure provides concrete examples of electronic RC implementations, showcasing both analog single-node delayed feedback systems and FPGA-based spiking neural network architectures for practical applications like speech recognition.

data.caption: Fig. 7. (a) Schematic illustration of an RC system based on a memristor-based reservoir. (b) A fabricated memristor array where several cells are selected to work as a reservoir on the whole (Du et al., 2017). The inset shows tungsten oxide (WOx) memristor with a metal-insulator-metal structure. Figure reproduced from Du et al. (2017), licensed under CC-BY 4.0. (c) An atomic switch network device composed of self-assembled silver nanowires (Stieg et al., 2014). Figure reproduced with permission from Springer Nature.
data.description: Three sub-figures illustrating memristor-based RC. (a) 'Schematic illustration of an RC system based on a memristor-based reservoir'. It shows an 'Input voltage signal' fed into a bridge-like circuit composed of four memristors, producing 'Output current signals'. (b) 'A fabricated memristor array where several cells are selected to work as a reservoir'. A micrograph of a chip with a grid of memristor cells. The inset shows a cross-section of a WOx memristor with Pd/Au, W, SiOx, and Si Substrate layers. (c) 'An atomic switch network device composed of self-assembled silver nanowires'. Two micrographs, 'TOP-DOWN' and 'BOTTOM-UP', showing a dense network of nanowires.
data.significance: This figure demonstrates the physical realization of memristive reservoirs, highlighting their potential for energy-efficient and compact RC systems using novel materials and nanoscale devices.

data.caption: Fig. 8. A 4 x 4 node array optical reservoir with a swirl connection pattern (Vandoorne et al., 2011).
data.description: A schematic diagram of a 4x4 node array optical reservoir. It shows 16 interconnected 'Semiconductor optical amplifier (SOA)' nodes arranged in a grid. Each node has 'in' and 'out' ports, and connections follow a swirl pattern, with 'Optical power input' and 'Light signal output' indicated.
data.key_data: {'Array size': '4x4 nodes'}
data.significance: This figure illustrates a chip-integrated photonic reservoir design using an array of SOAs, showcasing a spatially distributed optical reservoir architecture.

data.caption: Fig. 9. Time-delay reservoir configuration examples. Blue and gray lines represent optical and electronic signals, respectively. (a) Opto-electronic feedback loop. (b) All-optical feedback loop with gain. (c) Passive optical feedback and opto-electronic node with gain. (d) Feedback into a laser cavity by a partially reflecting mirror. (For interpretation of the references to color in this figure legend, the reader is referred to the web version of this article.)
data.description: Four sub-diagrams illustrating different time-delay reservoir configurations, distinguishing between optical and electronic signal paths (blue and gray lines). (a) 'Opto-electronic feedback loop': 'Optical source' -> 'Modulator' -> 'Fiber' -> 'Photodiode' -> 'Combinator' (electronic feedback loop) -> 'Modulator'. 'Masked staircase signal input' and 'Output for off-line processing' are shown. (b) 'All-optical feedback loop with gain': 'Optical source' -> 'Modulator' -> 'Fiber' -> 'Optical gain' (all-optical feedback loop) -> 'Modulator'. 'Modulated signal input' and 'Output for off-line processing' are shown. (c) 'Passive optical feedback and opto-electronic node with gain': 'Input' -> 'PD NL Amp' -> 'VCSEL' -> 'Output'. A passive optical feedback loop is shown from VCSEL output back to PD NL Amp. (d) 'Feedback into a laser cavity by a partially reflecting mirror': 'Drive Laser' -> 'Reservoir Laser' (with internal 'Mirror' feedback) -> 'Output'. 'Modulated signal input' is fed into the Reservoir Laser.
data.significance: This figure provides a comprehensive overview of various time-delay reservoir configurations, which are crucial for photonic RC implementations due to their hardware efficiency and ability to generate high-dimensional states from a single nonlinear node.

data.caption: Fig. 10. (a) Schematic illustration of the spin torque oscillator (left) and the reservoir device structure with a bias current input and a voltage output (right) (Torrejon et al., 2017). (b) Schematic illustration of a spin-wave-based reservoir device (Nakane, Tanaka, & Hirose, 2018). Figure reproduced with permission from IEEE. (c) A possible structure of a skyrmion-based reservoir device (Prychynenko et al., 2018).
data.description: Three sub-diagrams illustrating spintronic RC devices. (a) 'Schematic illustration of the spin torque oscillator (left) and the reservoir device structure with a bias current input and a voltage output (right)'. Left shows 'Spin precession' in a 'Free layer', 'Insulator', 'Pinned layer' stack. Right shows 'Input signal i(t)' and 'DC bias Io' fed into a device with 'Input electrode' and 'Output electrode', producing 'Output V'. (b) 'Schematic illustration of a spin-wave-based reservoir device'. Shows a layered structure with 'magneto-electric coupling layer', 'garnet film', and 'conductive substrate'. Input electrodes are on the top layer, and output electrodes are on the bottom. (c) 'A possible structure of a skyrmion-based reservoir device'. Shows a 'Magnetic layer' with a 'Moving skyrmion'. 'Input I' is fed from 'Source' to 'Drain', producing 'Output V'.
data.significance: This figure introduces novel spintronic devices as potential physical reservoirs, leveraging spin dynamics (spin torque oscillators, spin waves, and skyrmions) for energy-efficient and nanoscale RC.

data.caption: Fig. 11. (a) A tensegrity structure-based reservoir (Caluwaerts et al., 2014). Figure reproduced with permission from NASA Ames Research Center. (b) A reservoir based on a soft octopus robot (Nakajima, Hauser, Li, & Pfeifer, 2015). Figure reproduced from (Nakajima et al., 2015), licensed under CC-BY 4.0.
data.description: Two photographs illustrating mechanical reservoirs for RC. (a) 'A tensegrity structure-based reservoir'. A physical robot structure composed of interconnected rods and cables, forming a compliant body. (b) 'A reservoir based on a soft octopus robot'. A soft robotic arm resembling an octopus tentacle, demonstrating a highly compliant body.
data.significance: This figure showcases mechanical systems, specifically tensegrity structures and soft robots, as physical reservoirs, demonstrating the concept of morphological computing where the body's complex dynamics are exploited for computation.

data.caption: Fig. 12. A possibility that some brain regions work as reservoirs.
data.description: A conceptual diagram illustrating the idea of brain regions acting as reservoirs. Various sensory 'Input' types (Visual, Auditory, Olfactory, Gustatory, Tactile) are fed into a 'Reservoir?' (represented by a stylized brain region). The output is shown as 'Neural response output' over 'Time' for different 'Index' (presumably different neurons or channels).
data.significance: This figure presents the hypothesis that certain brain regions might function as biological reservoirs, linking RC principles to neuroscience and offering a framework for understanding brain computation.

data.caption: Fig. 13. A reservoir of in-vitro cell cultures.
data.description: A schematic diagram illustrating a reservoir based on in-vitro cultured cells. It shows a petri dish containing 'Cultured cells' on a 'MEA' (Microelectrode Array). 'Electrode input' and 'Electrode output' are indicated, showing how electrical signals interact with the cell culture.
data.significance: This figure demonstrates the use of in-vitro biological components as physical reservoirs, providing a model system to investigate the computational capabilities of biological networks in a controlled laboratory setting.

data.claim: The 3D-MIND device can be fabricated with high yield using standard photolithography and origami-inspired assembly, allowing for precise distribution of electronic sensors and stimulators in three dimensions.
data.support: Detailed description of fabrication steps, including photolithography and physical folding, and characterization of sensor alignment precision (Fig. 1c-i, Supplementary Fig. 2, 3, 4, 5).

data.claim: The 3D-MIND provides a stable electrical interface for long-term recording of neural activity, with sensors exhibiting low impedance and noise levels suitable for action potential recording.
data.support: Characterization of electrical impedance and noise level across a frequency range (Fig. 1j, Supplementary Fig. 6a,b), demonstrating stable signal-to-noise ratio over the culture's lifetime (Fig. 2l).

data.claim: The 3D-MIND integrates non-invasively with 3D cultured neural networks, supporting extensive neurite growth in all 3D directions and preserving native neural network morphology.
data.support: Volumetric confocal fluorescence images showing neuron connections and neurite growth (Fig. 2a, Supplementary Fig. 1c-f), demonstration of device interpenetration with neural networks (Fig. 2b,c, Supplementary Video 1), and confirmation of unchanged neuronal density (Supplementary Fig. 7).

data.claim: The device enables stable, long-term tracking of extracellular action potentials and robust burst activities from 3D neural cultures for over 6 months, with burst characteristics resembling in vivo brain activity more closely than 2D cultures.
data.support: Electrical recordings showing APs for up to 191 DIV with no signal decay (Fig. 2f,g), analysis of burst characteristics over 6 months (Fig. 2h-k), and comparison of burst distributions to 2D cultures (Supplementary Fig. 8a,b,c).

data.claim: The 3D-MIND can be used for chronic monitoring of pharmacological modulations, with recorded signals demonstrating physiologically relevant responses to various drugs.
data.support: Monitoring of neural firing activity in response to bicuculline, TTX, and CNQX, showing expected changes and recovery after drug removal (Fig. 2m, Supplementary Fig. 9).

data.claim: The device allows for volumetric electrophysiology mapping and tracking of neuronal connectivity evolution in 3D neural networks over months.

Panel 'b' displays representative recording traces and perievent raster plots from three sensors (322, 114, 231) in response to electrical stimulation at sensor 231, with corresponding spike distribution histograms. data.claim: The complexity of human neurobiology, characterized by cell type diversity and genetic variations, is not adequately captured by most current neural organoid models.
data.support: Discussion of the inherent heterogeneity of human brain, the limited range of cell lines used in organoid research, and the underrepresentation of specific ethnicities in PSC repositories (e.g., CIRM, EBiSC, WiCell, RIKEN, Coriell data).

data.claim: Increasing genetic diversity in neural organoids can be achieved through approaches like cell pooling (cell villages), chimeroids, and mosaic organoids, which enable high-throughput screening across multiple genetic backgrounds.
data.support: Explanation of how cell pooling maximizes expression variance readout and uncovers cis-acting regulators, and how chimeroids (mixing multiple hiPSCs post neural induction) and mosaic organoids (CRISPR-Cas9 induced mutations) allow investigation of interindividual differences and disease-associated mutations.

data.claim: Building tissue complexity in neural organoids can be achieved through spontaneous self-assembly of multiple cell types from common progenitors or through enforced assembly of pre-differentiated region-specific organoids (assembloids) or seeding non-neural cell types.
data.support: Examples of self-assembled neuromusculoskeletal and intestinal organoids, discussion of seeding microglia-like cells or vascular endothelial cells onto brain organoids, and the concept of fusing distinct organoids to form assembloids (e.g., cortico-motor, somatosensory pathway, loop circuits).

data.claim: There is an inherent trade-off between tissue complexity and reproducibility in neural organoid models, where higher complexity often correlates with lower reproducibility.
data.support: Comparison of different model types (2D cultures, spheroids, single-region organoids, self-assembled multi-region organoids, assembloids) in terms of their relative genetic diversity, tissue complexity, and reproducibility (Fig. 4), including reported success rates for various assembloid assemblies.

data.claim: The choice of neural organoid model (reductionist vs. complex) should be tailored to the specific biological question, balancing cost-effectiveness, rigor, and the need for genetic diversity or tissue complexity.
data.support: Argument that reductionist models are sufficient for disease modeling, drug screening, and cytotoxicity assays, while complex models are needed for higher-order tissue interactions; recommendations for improving reproducibility in complex models (e.g., PSC quality control, axial patterning).

data.claim: Human neurobiology is fundamentally complex and heterogeneous, and these characteristics are important to model for accurate research.
Pluripotent stem cells (ESCs and iPSCs) are valid and effective starting materials for generating in vitro models of human brain development.
In vitro models, despite their limitations, can provide valuable insights into in vivo processes and disease mechanisms.
Genetic and ethnic diversity in research models is crucial for the generalizability and translational relevance of findings.
Reproducibility and standardization are essential for robust scientific conclusions in organoid research.
