data.caption: Genetic and tissue diversity in neural organoids. Pluripotent stem cells (PSCs), including embryonic stem cells (ESCs) and induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs), upon neural differentiation give rise to neural organoids with varying tissue identity, size, and morphology. This variation results in distinct cellular profiles across different cell lines. Studies on single cell line organoid restrict the genetic diversity represented across the population. Chimeroids address genetic diversity by incorporating multiple PSC lines within a single organoid. When donor cells are pooled at the neural stem cell (NSC) stage, homogeneous cell type representation can be achieved. Assembloids address tissue complexity by fusing region-specific organoids to model complex neural circuitry.
data.description: A schematic diagram illustrating different approaches to achieve genetic and tissue diversity in neural organoids. It begins with 'PSCs' (represented by multiple colored circles) differentiating into 'Organoids' with 'different morphology and tissue identity' (represented by varied shapes and colors). A UMAP plot shows distinct clusters for these organoids. The diagram then branches into two main strategies: 'Assembloids' (labeled 'tissue complexity') and 'Chimeroids' (labeled 'genetic diversity'). Assembloids are depicted as fused organoids, while Chimeroids show multiple PSCs contributing to a single organoid, with a UMAP plot showing mixed clusters.
data.significance: This figure visually explains the concepts of genetic and tissue diversity in neural organoids and introduces the main strategies (chimeroids and assembloids) used to achieve these complexities, setting the stage for the detailed discussion in the paper.

data.caption: Strategies to achieve tissue complexity in neural organoids. Tissue complexity can be achieved through spontaneous differentiation and self-assembly (right): pluripotent stem cells (PSCs) undergo spontaneous multi-lineage differentiation and organ self-assembly. 3D neuromusculoskeletal organoids, harbouring spinal cord identity together with skeleton and skeletal muscles, derive from neuromesoderm precursors obtained from PSCs [11]. Spontaneous development of diverse neural and non-neural tissue occurs in unguided brain organoids where ventral and dorsal forebrain coexist with choroid plexus (ChP), cortical hem, midbrain, hindbrain and mesoderm-like cells [61,62]. Enforced assembly of multiple tissue organoids (assembloids) (left): Fusion of distinct organoid types (e.g. cortical, spinal and skeletal muscle organoids) creates cortico-motor assembloids that mimic high-order tissue interactions [50]. In this case, organoid fusion is obtained on already-differentiated individual organoids. Cell seeding and extrinsic assembly (top): mesodermal cells derived from PSCs, such as microglia, are seeded on brain organoids to achieve neural-non neural cell interactions and increase the complexity of the tissue [14]. Guided differentiation to single identity tissue (bottom): PSCs are directed to single identity organoids through guided protocols [3,44,49,63-65]. This case represents the lowest tissue complexity achievable in 3D.
data.description: A detailed schematic illustrating various methods to generate neural organoids with increased tissue complexity. It shows two main pathways: 'Self-assembly' (right) and 'Enforced assembly' (left). Self-assembly from 'PSCs (single identity)' can lead to 'unguided organoid' (showing ventral/dorsal forebrain, ChP, cortical hem, midbrain, hindbrain, mesoderm-like cells) or 'guided organoids' (single identity, e.g., ventral forebrain, midbrain, dorsal forebrain). It also shows 'neuromusculoskeletal organoid' (with skeletal, muscular, neuro components) and 'brain organoid + microglia' (via cell seeding). Enforced assembly involves fusing distinct organoid types (e.g., 'cortico-motor organoid' from 'cortico-spinal assembloid' and 'muscle spheroid') or seeding 'non-neural cells' onto a 'brain organoid'.
data.significance: This figure provides a comprehensive overview of the experimental strategies for building tissue complexity in neural organoids, distinguishing between self-assembly and enforced assembly methods, and highlighting the different levels of complexity achievable.

data.caption: Flowchart for selecting an appropriate in vitro neural model based on research goals. A schematic flowchart guiding the choice of neural organoid models in accordance with the specific focus of investigation. Self-assembly of multi-tissue organoids differs from multi-tissue assembloids for the intrinsic self-differentiation and self-organisation of multiple cell and tissue types from the same pluripotent progenitor, often under the same culturing conditions. Refs: [4–8, 11, 12, 43, 47, 50, 61, 81–84].
data.description: A flowchart titled 'Investigation topic?' at the top, guiding the user through decisions to select an appropriate neural model. It branches from 'Investigation topic?' to 'Cell intrinsic questions' and 'Functional mechanistic studies'. 'Cell intrinsic questions' leads to '2D cultures, neural rosettes' or '3D neural cultures'. '3D neural cultures' further branches into 'Disease Modeling' (leading to 'Patient-derived organoids' with options like 'Single patient-derived SNPs', 'Multiple mutations of one cell line', or 'Pooled organoids of multiple cell lines') and 'Functional mechanistic studies' (leading to 'Organ development' or 'Organ development & tissue interaction', which further branches to 'Tissue transplantation' or 'Multi-region organoid culture (assembloids)').
data.significance: This flowchart serves as a practical guide for researchers to choose the most suitable neural organoid model based on their specific research questions, balancing the trade-offs between complexity and analytical clarity.

data.caption: Balancing complexity and reproducibility in neural models. Conceptual not-to-scale relative positioning of 2D cultures, spheroids, organoids, self-assembly, and multi-unit assembloids across genetic diversity, reproducibility and tissue complexity. Tissue complexity often comes at the cost of reproducibility. Assembloids, which model multi-tissue interactions, typically reduce experimental reproducibility-reproducibility decreases as more neural components are assembled. Single cell line organoids, spheroids and 2D cultures are limited in genetic diversity. In contrast, chimeroids, mosaic organoids, and multiplexed organoids support high-throughput screening across multiple PSC lines retaining an overall good reproducibility across experiments. These approaches enable the analysis of disease phenotypes in different genetic backgrounds, SNP-associated traits, thereby addressing genetic diversity. Organoids display different degrees of tissue complexity and reproducibility depending on the protocol. Self-organising organoids (#) from unguided protocols can achieve greater complexity than assembloids but less reproducibility [61,62]. Instead, single-tissue directed organoids (*) display lower complexity and high reproducibility [3,44,49,63-65], similar to spheroids [82]. 'Representative success rate of the assembly: 90% [4]. 2Representative success rate of the assembly: 86.3-93% [11]. 3Representative success rate of the assembly: 81% [50]. 4Representative success rate of the assembly: 60-87.7% [75,77].
data.description: A 2D scatter plot with 'relative genetic diversity' on the x-axis and 'relative reproducibility' on the y-axis, illustrating the trade-offs between these factors for various neural models. 'Relative tissue complexity' is also indicated, generally increasing from left to right. Models plotted include '2D cultures', 'spheroids', 'organoids*', 'multiplexed organoids', 'mosaic organoids', 'chimeroids', '2-unit assembloids¹', '3-unit self-assemblies²', '3-unit assembloids³', 'organoids#', '4-unit assembloids⁴', and 'in vivo'.
data.key_data: 2-unit assembloids: 90% success rate; 3-unit self-assemblies: 86.3-93% success rate; 3-unit assembloids: 81% success rate; 4-unit assembloids: 60-87.7% success rate
data.significance: This figure visually summarises the central trade-off in neural organoid research: increasing tissue complexity often comes at the cost of reproducibility, while genetic diversity can be achieved with varying levels of reproducibility depending on the model. It helps researchers understand the strengths and weaknesses of different models in terms of these key parameters.

data.name: Path Integration
data.description: The cognitive process by which an animal estimates movement from self-motion cues to maintain an up-to-date representation of position and orientation.

data.name: Medial Entorhinal Cortex
data.description: Entorhinal cortical region containing grid cells and targeted for superficial MEC recordings in this study.

data.name: Reference Frames
data.description: Coordinate systems in which grid-cell activity can be anchored, including room, arena, and lever-centred frames.

data.name: Local Reference Frames
data.description: Task-relevant coordinate frames used by grid cells during reference-frame switching.

data.name: Lever-Centred Reference Frame
data.description: Reference frame anchored to the task-relevant lever object in AutoPI homing.

data.name: Room Reference Frame
data.description: External room-centred frame to which grid modules anchor at the beginning of search and increasingly return in light trials.

data.name: Toroidal Manifold
data.description: Population-level grid-cell phase relationship represented in toroidal coordinates.

data.name: Grid-Cell Phase
data.description: Relative phase of grid-cell firing within the grid-cell population manifold.

data.name: Grid Orientation Drift
data.description: Accumulated drift in internal grid movement-direction representation during self-motion navigation.

data.name: Homing Behaviour
data.description: Return movement to a home base after lever pressing in the AutoPI task.

data.name: Self-Motion Cues
data.description: Vestibular, proprioceptive, motor, and optic-flow-independent cues used for path integration.

data.name: Head-Direction System
data.description: Directional neural system potentially related to grid orientation and angular path integration.

data.name: Hippocampal Place Cells
data.description: Hippocampal neurons with spatially localised firing fields, discussed in relation to object-anchored fields in AutoPI.

data.claim: Grid cells did not maintain a stable spatial grid pattern during AutoPI path integration-based navigation, despite showing periodic firing during random foraging.
data.support: Grid scores and map similarity were lower in AutoPI light and dark trials than in random foraging; controls argued against lever presence, reduced coverage, or biased head-direction sampling as sufficient explanations.

data.claim: Grid cells tracked movement in multiple reference frames within single trials.
data.support: During dark search, many firing fields aligned with arena Y-position; during dark homing, firing fields were predominantly determined by distance from the lever.

data.claim: Temporal firing associations and spatial offsets of grid-cell pairs remained largely preserved across behavioural conditions.
data.support: Pairwise instantaneous firing-rate correlations and spike-triggered cross-firing rate maps were significantly correlated across random foraging and AutoPI conditions.

data.claim: Co-modular grid-cell population activity encoded approximate movement vectors from self-motion cues during dark AutoPI.
data.support: A recurrent neural network trained on toroidal coordinates reconstructed movement paths; directional precision remained above chance in all analysed dark AutoPI sessions.

data.claim: Grid cells reanchored to the task-relevant lever by translation of the grid pattern rather than by rotation.
data.support: Lever positions decoded in toroidal space clustered near a stable location; orientation comparisons showed lever encounter did not introduce greater rotation drift than distance-matched search paths.

data.claim: Grid orientation drift accumulated with dark-trial search duration and path length.
data.support: Decoded directional precision decreased from beginning to end of long dark searches, and absolute decoded directional error increased with search duration.

data.claim: Grid orientation drift predicted homing heading direction.
data.support: Trial-level grid-field orientation around the lever and decoded trial drift during search, lever contact, and homing positively correlated with animal homing heading direction.

data.claim: Grid cells estimate position within multiple local reference frames rather than operating as a single global positioning system.
data.support: The authors integrate absent global grid maps, preserved toroidal population relationships, lever reanchoring, accumulated drift, and behavioural prediction to reject a rigid global-coordinate account.

data.definition: The cognitive process by which an animal estimates movement from self-motion cues to maintain an up-to-date representation of position and orientation.
The mean vector length of the decoded directional-error distribution.
The circular mean of the decoded directional-error distribution within a trial.
Mean concentration of a bivariate von Mises distribution fitted to inferred object or bridge positions in toroidal space.

data.question: Whether path integration is computed within the grid-cell network itself or inherited from upstream self-motion and head-direction circuits.
data.context: The Discussion links grid orientation drift to angular path integration and self-motion signals but does not resolve circuit locus.

data.question: Whether similar lever or object reanchoring occurs in larger grid modules.
data.context: The analysed sessions required enough simultaneously recorded same-module grid cells, leaving module-scale generality open.

data.question: Whether grid cells change their anchoring point in other tasks where hippocampal place cells switch reference frames.
data.context: The authors connect their findings to object-anchored hippocampal place fields in AutoPI and to cue-induced grid phase changes.

data.claim: FADE can adapt per-parameter weight decay rates online using meta-gradients derived from forward-mode differentiation.
data.support: Derivation for online linear regression (Algorithm 1, Section 2) using meta-gradient approximations similar to IDBD.

data.claim: FADE discovers distinct decay rates for relevant and irrelevant features in online linear tracking problems.
data.support: Figure 1 shows that weights associated with irrelevant features converge to a high decay rate (λ ≈ 0.9) for faster forgetting, while relevant features settle near a low decay rate (λ ≈ 0.02) for longer memory.

data.claim: FADE complements step-size adaptation (IDBD), with FADE+IDBD achieving the lowest error in linear tracking tasks, outperforming FADE and IDBD alone.
data.support: Table 1 shows FADE+IDBD achieves an MSE of 1.246 (σ_η=0) and 2.646 (σ_η=1.0), which is lower than IDBD (1.486, 2.937) and FADE (1.653, 3.044) individually.

data.claim: FADE, when applied to the final layer of neural networks, significantly improves performance over strong baselines like AdamW in non-linear teacher-student tracking problems.
data.support: Table 2 shows FADE+SGD (0.0073) and FADE+Adam (0.0087) achieve roughly half the MSE of AdamW (0.0138) over the final 500K steps.

data.claim: FADE's adaptation is effective across a wide range of non-stationarity rates (fast, slow, and stable outputs) in non-linear tracking.
data.support: Figure 2 shows per-group MSE improvements with FADE adaptation (θλ=2) compared to fixed decay (θλ=0). Figure 3 illustrates FADE increasing decay for fast-changing outputs and decreasing it for stable outputs.

data.claim: FADE is robust to the initialization of the decay rate, recovering strong performance even from poor initializations in non-linear tracking and streaming classification.
data.support: Table 3 and Table 4 show that with FADE (θλ > 0), the sensitivity gap to initial decay rate (γ0) narrows considerably, and performance recovers from poor initializations (e.g., γ0 = -2.3). Figure 5 demonstrates recovery from a poor initialization in EMNIST.

data.claim: FADE outperforms weight clipping, the best prior method, on streaming label-permuted EMNIST classification problems.
data.support: Table 5 shows FADE+SGD achieves an average online accuracy of 0.807 and FADE+Adam achieves 0.750, both outperforming SGD+WClip (0.612).

data.claim: Applying a suitable fixed non-zero decay rate only to the final layer can be a strong baseline, but FADE automates this adaptation at a per-parameter level, providing benefits in terms of improved MSE and robustness.
data.support: Tables 6 and 7 show that fixed weight decay on the head (θλ=0) can achieve high accuracy with optimal tuning (e.g., 0.801 for SGD at γ0=-6.9), but FADE consistently improves performance and robustness across initializations.

data.claim: Meta-gradients are approximated using forward-mode differentiation, assuming that changing a meta-parameter associated with weight 'i' primarily affects weight 'i' itself, with negligible effect on other weights.
The linear approximation for meta-gradients is sufficient for the final layer of neural networks, despite the overall non-linearity of the network.

The chosen online non-stationary problems (linear tracking, non-linear teacher-student tracking, streaming label-permuted EMNIST) are representative and sufficient for evaluating continual learning performance.
The evaluation metrics (MSE, online accuracy) are appropriate for assessing the effectiveness of forgetting mechanisms.

data.definition: A method that adapts per-parameter weight decay rates online via approximate meta-gradient descent.
Parameterized for each parameter w_i as λ_i = exp(γ_i), where γ_i is a meta-parameter updated by gradient descent on the prediction error.
A trace that tracks the sensitivity ∂w_i/∂γ_i, maintained online to mediate the effect of γ_i on the error through the weight update.
Approximately 1/λ_i, where λ_i is the per-parameter decay rate. Increasing λ_i shortens the horizon (faster forgetting), and decreasing it lengthens the horizon (more retention).
A hyperparameter used in the update rule for the meta-parameter γ_i.
Denotes max(·, 0), used for stability.
A phenomenon where neural networks fail to retain what was previously learned when data changes over time.
A failure mode where neural networks fail to adapt and learn new things.

Interpreted as a 'forgetting mechanism' in online non-stationary continual learning settings, controlling how much past information each weight retains to balance acquiring new knowledge with retaining old knowledge.

data.question: FADE's meta-gradient derivation is exact for SGD but only approximate for Adam.
data.context: FADE+SGD outperforms FADE+Adam in non-linear tracking, suggesting the approximation for Adam is less effective.

data.question: The linear meta-gradient approximation used in FADE is insufficient for hidden layers in deep neural networks.
data.context: A naive extension of FADE to all layers performs significantly worse than applying FADE only to the head, and is sensitive to initialization.

data.question: Scaling FADE to larger architectures.
data.context: FADE is derived for the online linear setting and applied to the final layer of neural networks. Extending it to all layers of deep, non-linear networks presents open challenges.

data.question: Formalize the interaction between the decay rates of the network head and those of the hidden layers, while accounting for nonlinearities between layers.
Design meta-gradient approximations that are invariant to the underlying architecture, making them easier to apply across different depths, nonlinearities, and layer types.
Extend FADE to each layer in a network and combine it with common architectural modifications, such as layer normalization.
Enable FADE's use in settings where non-stationarity arises naturally, such as reinforcement learning.
FADE's meta-gradient derivation holds exactly for SGD but only approximately for Adam, leading to performance differences between FADE+SGD and FADE+Adam.
data.context: The theoretical exactness of FADE's derivation for SGD and its approximate nature when combined with Adam.

data.caption: Evolution of FADE's average decay rates for relevant and irrelevant weight groups on the linear tracking problem with zero noise, starting from λ₀ ≈ 0.3(γ₀ = −1.2), with α = 0.1 and θλ = 0.01.
data.description: A line chart showing the average decay rate (λ) on the y-axis, ranging from 0.0 to 1.0, against the number of steps on the x-axis, ranging from 0 to 200,000. Two distinct lines represent 'Weight group Relevant' and 'Weight group Irrelevant'. The 'Relevant' group's decay rate stabilizes around 0.02, while the 'Irrelevant' group's decay rate stabilizes around 0.9.
data.key_data: Relevant weight group: starts around 0.3, stabilizes around 0.02 after ~50,000 steps.; Irrelevant weight group: starts around 0.3, stabilizes around 0.9 after ~50,000 steps.
data.significance: This figure demonstrates FADE's ability to automatically differentiate between relevant and irrelevant features by assigning them distinct, adaptive decay rates, thus supporting the claim of selective forgetting.

data.caption: MSE by group on nonlinear tracking problem. With γ₀ = −9.2(λ₀ ≈ 0.0001), comparing FADE+SGD (θλ = 2) with its fixed-decay counterpart FADE+SGD (θλ = 0).
data.description: Four line charts (a, b, c, d) displaying Mean Squared Error (MSE) on the y-axis against Time steps on the x-axis (up to 2 million steps). Each chart compares FADE+SGD with adaptive decay (θλ = 2) against fixed decay (θλ = 0) for different output groups: (a) Fast, (b) Stable, (c) Slow, and (d) Slow (zoomed in). FADE with adaptive decay consistently shows lower MSE across all groups, particularly after an initial learning phase.
data.key_data: (a) Fast: FADE (θλ=2) MSE stabilizes around 0.0175, FADE (θλ=0) MSE stabilizes around 0.025.; (b) Stable: FADE (θλ=2) MSE stabilizes around 0.002, FADE (θλ=0) MSE stabilizes around 0.004.; (c) Slow: FADE (θλ=2) MSE stabilizes around 0.007, FADE (θλ=0) MSE stabilizes around 0.012.; (d) Slow, zoomed in: Shows periodic spikes in MSE for both methods, with FADE (θλ=2) consistently lower.
data.significance: This figure illustrates that FADE's adaptive decay mechanism significantly improves performance (lower MSE) across different non-stationarity rates (fast, slow, stable) in a nonlinear tracking problem, highlighting its effectiveness beyond fixed decay.

data.caption: Evolution of FADE's average per-group decay rates on the nonlinear tracking problem starting from a shared initialization γ₀ ≈ 10⁻⁴ (dashed line), and θλ = 2.0.
data.description: A line chart showing the evolution of average decay rates (λ) on a logarithmic y-axis (from 5x10⁻⁵ to 5x10⁻³) against Time steps on the x-axis (up to 2 million steps). Separate lines represent the decay rates for 'Fast', 'Slow', and 'Stable' output groups, all starting from a shared initial λ₀ (dashed line). The 'Fast' group's decay rate increases, 'Slow' remains intermediate, and 'Stable' decreases.
data.key_data: Initial λ₀: ~10⁻⁴ (γ₀ ≈ -9.2); Fast group: λ increases to ~2x10⁻³; Slow group: λ remains around ~10⁻⁴; Stable group: λ decreases to ~5x10⁻⁵
data.significance: This figure demonstrates FADE's ability to adaptively learn distinct decay rates for different output groups based on their non-stationarity, increasing decay for fast-changing outputs and decreasing it for stable ones, which is crucial for effective continual learning.

data.caption: Online accuracy on label-permuted EMNIST. FADE+SGD and FADE+Adam apply FADE to the final layer.
data.description: A line chart showing online accuracy on the y-axis (from 0.1 to 0.9) against the number of tasks on the x-axis (from 0 to 2000). Multiple lines represent different methods: SGD, SGD + WD, Adam, AdamW, SGD + WClip, FADE + Adam, and FADE + SGD. FADE+SGD and FADE+Adam achieve the highest and most stable accuracy.
data.key_data: FADE + SGD: highest accuracy, stabilizes around 0.8.; FADE + Adam: second highest, stabilizes around 0.75.; SGD + WClip: stabilizes around 0.6.; Other methods (SGD, SGD+WD, Adam, AdamW): significantly lower accuracy, mostly below 0.4.
data.significance: This figure demonstrates FADE's superior performance in streaming classification with label permutations, achieving significantly higher online accuracy compared to strong baselines like AdamW and SGD + WClip.

data.caption: Online accuracy on label-permuted EMNIST with FADE + Adam, starting from γ₀ = −11.5 (λ₀ ≈ 10⁻⁵). Despite an initial drop, FADE with θλ > 0 recovers strongly, with a final accuracy of over 0.7.
data.description: A line chart showing online accuracy on the y-axis (from 0.1 to 0.7) against the number of tasks on the x-axis (from 0 to 2000). Multiple lines represent FADE + Adam with different meta-step-sizes (θλ = 0, 0.1, 0.5, 1.0), all starting from a very low initial decay rate (λ₀ ≈ 10⁻⁵). Adaptive FADE (θλ > 0) shows strong recovery and high final accuracy, while fixed decay (θλ = 0) performs poorly.
data.key_data: FADE (θλ=0): accuracy remains low, around 0.2-0.3.; FADE (θλ=0.1, 0.5, 1.0): accuracy drops initially but recovers to above 0.7.
data.significance: This figure highlights FADE's ability to recover from poor initializations of the decay rate, demonstrating its adaptivity and robustness in challenging continual learning scenarios.

data.caption: Online accuracy with partial label permutations.
data.description: A line chart showing online accuracy on the y-axis (from 0.2 to 0.9) against the number of tasks on the x-axis (from 0 to 2000). Multiple lines represent different methods: SGD, SGD + WD, Adam, AdamW, SGD + WClip, FADE + Adam, and FADE + SGD. FADE+SGD and FADE+Adam achieve the highest and most stable accuracy.
data.key_data: FADE + SGD: highest accuracy, stabilizes around 0.84.; FADE + Adam: second highest, stabilizes around 0.8.; SGD: stabilizes around 0.7.; SGD + WClip: stabilizes around 0.7.; SGD + WD: stabilizes around 0.68.; AdamW: stabilizes around 0.5.; Adam: stabilizes around 0.4.
data.significance: This figure visually confirms FADE's strong performance in streaming classification with partial label permutations, showing that FADE-based methods consistently achieve higher and more stable online accuracy compared to other baselines.

data.claim: A computation is defined as 'immortal' if it is a concatenation and combination of reference computations, and 'mortal' if it is not immortal.
data.support: Conceptual distinction based on the separability of software from hardware, inspired by Hinton (2022).

data.claim: If an immortal computation 'c' is realized by a system 'S', then 'S' must also be able to realize the reference computations ('Cref') from which 'c' is composed (Implication 1).
data.support: Logical deduction from the differential definition of immortal computation (Definition 1).

data.claim: Computations that can be coded with any existing programming language ('Prog') are a subclass of immortal computations ('CImm').
data.support: Programs are defined relative to Instruction Set Architectures (ISAs), ensuring hardware independence, which is the core characteristic of immortal computation (2.3).

data.claim: Turing computations ('CTM') are a subclass of programs ('Prog').
data.support: Turing-complete programming languages can implement any Turing computation, meaning a program can instantiate a Turing computation (5.1).

data.claim: Computational functionalism implies the existence of a specific computation 'c*' (representing consciousness) such that a system 'S' is capable of conscious experience if and only if 'S' can realize 'c*' (Implication 2).
data.support: Reformulation of Putnam's (1967) Condition 2 for computational functionalism.

data.claim: Consciousness ('c*') is not a program ('c* ∉ Prog').
data.support: Proof by contradiction (Lemma 1) using Assumption 1 (existence of a non-programmable conscious system), Implication 2 (consciousness is 'c*'), Implication 1 (immortal computation realization), and the claim that programs are immortal computations.

data.claim: Consciousness ('c*') is not a Turing computation ('c* ∉ CTM').
data.support: Follows directly from Lemma 1 (consciousness is not a program) and the claim that Turing computations are a subclass of programs (Lemma 2).

data.claim: Consciousness ('c*') is a mortal computation.
data.support: Follows from Lemma 2 (consciousness is not a Turing computation) and the premise that immortal computations are a subclass of Turing computations (2.1). If 'c*' is not a Turing computation, it cannot be an immortal computation ('c* ∉ CImm'), which by definition means 'c*' is mortal (Lemma 3).

data.claim: The results provide initial reason to believe that current or near-future AI cannot be conscious.
data.support: Deduction from the claims that consciousness is mortal and not Turing, combined with the observation that contemporary AI systems are Turing computations (and thus immortal).

data.claim: Computational functionalism is true, as defined by Putnam (1967) and rephrased in Implication 2.
There exists at least one system 'S' (e.g., non-human animals) that is capable of conscious experience but cannot be programmed (Assumption 1).
Immortal computations ('CImm') are a subclass of Turing computations ('CTM') (2.1).

The scientific study of consciousness, or consciousness science, already comprises a host of mathematical models, methods, and questions, building on mathematical tools from other sciences and the amenability of consciousness itself to mathematical description.
data.support: It builds on mathematical models and methods developed in other sciences (e.g., brain models, analysis techniques) and consciousness itself is amenable to mathematical description and representation.

data.claim: Mathematical consciousness science is the application and study of formal and mathematical methods as applied in, or relevant to, the scientific study of consciousness, encompassing experimental, theoretical, conceptual, and methodological questions.
data.support: Analogies to mathematical physics, mathematical biology, and mathematical neuroscience are drawn to define the field.

data.claim: The large number and variation among existing theories of consciousness are arguably due to a lack of noteworthy constraints in proposing theories and the absence of a thorough paradigm for theory-building.
data.support: Reference to T. S. Kuhn (1962) and an analogy to the development of Newtonian mechanics in physics.

data.claim: Mathematics can provide a more faithful representation of phenomenal character in theories of consciousness through the use of mathematical structures and spaces.
data.support: This allows for a more accurate representation of the target phenomenon and requires the use of formal theories of consciousness.

data.claim: Mathematics offers flexibility and precision in explicating ideas, experimental findings, or metaphysics, which is a significant advantage over non-formal language in constructing theories of consciousness.
data.support: Mathematical definitions are precise, free of multiple meanings, and require spelling out all relevant details.

data.claim: Theories of consciousness might need to engage with mathematical formalism because they address brain functions at high precision, operate on scales beyond the brain, or rely on principles not precisely expressible in natural language.
data.support: Predictive Processing Theory (PP) and Active Inference are cited as examples where neuroscience developments necessitate mathematical formulation.

data.claim: If the desideratum of universality for theories of consciousness (i.e., applicability to any conscious dynamical system regardless of origin) is endorsed, then such theories must be formulated mathematically.
data.support: Mathematics is presented as the only language capable of describing the vast range of systems (e.g., LLMs, hurricanes) required by universality.

data.claim: Mathematics could be required to unify the different theories of consciousness that exist to date.
data.support: The Conscious Turing Machine (CTM) model is given as an example of incorporating core formal ideas from various theories (GNWT, PP) into a single framework.

data.claim: Mathematical approaches can help overcome the confines of non-formal language, allowing for the construction of theories that rely on concepts difficult or impossible to express otherwise, especially for minimal phenomenal experiences or idealist/dual-aspect metaphysics.
data.support: Mathematics is not tied to classical logic and offers a unique starting point to transcend limitations of natural language, citing works on idealist/dual-aspect metaphysics.

data.claim: A theory of consciousness must explain why measures of consciousness (or C-tests) measure what they measure, otherwise, it cannot be empirically investigated.
data.support: This is presented as a constraint derived from (Kleiner & Hoel, 2021) and (Kleiner & Hartmann, 2023), with its violation implying theories are 'wrong or (...) outside the realm of science' as per Doerig et al. (2019).

data.claim: Virtually all theories of consciousness proposed to date fail to satisfy the constraint of explaining why measures measure what they measure, either by not modeling subjective report or by being too general.
data.support: Formal IIT is cited as an example of the former, and GNWT as an example of the latter, leading to 'substitutions' where experience changes but reports remain constant.

data.claim: The minimal condition for theories to meet the 'explain measures' constraint is 'dynamical relevance', requiring consciousness to make a difference to the time evolution of its reference theory's states.
data.support: Identified in (Kleiner & Hartmann, 2023) and refined in (Kleiner & Ludwig, 2023), emphasizing that this is not in conflict with physicalism but ensures consciousness has a proper role in cognitive architecture.

data.claim: Using mathematical structure and spaces in theories of consciousness leads to structural theories that are more explanatory and predictive than non-structural counterparts.
data.support: Structural theories represent phenomenal character more comprehensively, including qualities, properties, and relations, leading to more detailed and rigorous hypotheses.

data.claim: Mathematical consciousness science can improve and clarify existing theories, as exemplified by its contributions to Integrated Information Theory (IIT) and Predictive Processing (PP) with Active Inference.
data.support: For IIT, it involves explicating its mathematical object, exploring problems in its formal constructions, and defining its content with more apt mathematics (e.g., category theory). For PP, it involves categorical formulations and extensions using projective geometry.

data.claim: The 'unfolding argument' (Doerig et al., 2019) and other criticisms of IIT's formalism highlight a fundamental issue with testing IIT that also applies to other major theories of consciousness.
data.support: Kleiner and Hoel (2021) showed that this issue arises from IIT's mathematical formalism and the typical paradigm of testing theories, allowing substitutions where experience changes but behavior does not.

data.claim: The 'closure paradigm' in consciousness science, which takes a neuroscientific account of the brain as input without amendment, conflicts with the testability of theories of consciousness and needs revision.
data.support: (Kleiner & Hartmann, 2023) argues that if theories don't amend the neuroscientific model, they cannot account for how experimental data supports one theory over another.

data.claim: There is currently no substantive theory of measurement for consciousness science, unlike in psychology or quantum physics where such theories were crucial for progress.
data.support: Historical examples from psychology (Stevens, Krantz et al.) and quantum physics (von Neumann) are used to illustrate the importance and impact of measurement theories.

data.claim: A measurement theory for consciousness science will likely be as consequential as in psychology and quantum physics, and mathematics might offer the tools to develop it.
data.support: Measurement theories in other sciences are based on mathematical representations of the measurement process.

data.claim: The introduction of mathematical spaces and structures to describe conscious experiences constitutes early signs of a 'structural turn' in consciousness science, promising to improve theories, experiments, measures, and concepts.
data.support: Pioneering work (Clark, Rosenthal) and diverse applications (quality spaces, qualia spaces, experience spaces, etc.) are cited as evidence of this development.

data.claim: The most exciting promise of a structural turn is the creation of new methodologies for consciousness science, including novel conceptual engineering avenues like mathematical phenomenology.
data.support: Structural approaches could address aspects of phenomenal experience difficult to express in common language (e.g., nondual awareness) and provide empirically grounded ways of representing properties.

data.claim: Computational phenomenology, which models phenomenology using computational tools (e.g., Predictive Processing Theory), is a part of mathematical phenomenology and requires foundational work on mathematical representation.
data.support: Models of computation are inherently mathematical models, thus foundational work for mathematical phenomenology applies.

data.claim: No-go theorems are an important methodological tool in consciousness science, capable of establishing unintuitive conclusions from uncontested mathematical assumptions.
data.support: Analogies to John Bell's proof in physics and examples from (Kleiner & Ludwig, 2023) and (Kleiner & Hoel, 2021) are provided.

data.claim: Contemporary AI systems cannot be conscious if general chip design details and the dynamical relevance of consciousness are assumed.
data.support: (Kleiner & Ludwig, 2023) showed that the exact adherence of a Processing Unit (PU) to a pre-set formal system prevents consciousness from making a difference in its substrate.

data.claim: Computational functionalism implies that consciousness is a 'mortal computation' (cannot be separated from its hardware), which suggests contemporary and near-future AI systems (immortal computations) could not be conscious.
data.support: Hinton (2022) introduced the concept of mortal computation. (Kleiner, 2024a) provides a first indication that functionalism implies mortality, aligning with Putnam (1967) but contradicting some contemporary AI analyses.

data.claim: Mathematical philosophy of mind, as the application of mathematical methods to philosophical questions of the mind, is a worthwhile enterprise that facilitates interaction between philosophy and consciousness science.
data.support: Leitgeb (2013) defines mathematical philosophy and emphasizes its role in reforming mind sciences, working with scientists, and addressing philosophical questions with formal methods.

data.claim: Consciousness is a natural phenomenon amenable to scientific study.
The goal of consciousness science is to achieve progress and a deeper understanding of conscious experience.
Mathematical rigor and formal methods are valuable tools for scientific inquiry.
The existence of conscious experiences and their properties as a subject matter for investigation.
The possibility of developing a 'paradigm' for consciousness science analogous to those in other natural sciences.
The general understanding of 'measures of consciousness' and 'C-tests' as methodologies to infer states of consciousness from experimental data.
The relevance of philosophical insights and conceptual clarity for scientific progress.
Non-collatability is a necessary operational consequence of characteristic features of conscious experience such as ineffability, privateness, and inaccessibility.
data.support: Argument that these features destroy the possibility of identifying an aspect over several subjects (Section 2, Phenomenological Axiom 3.6).

data.claim: Qualia are defined as all non-collatable aspects of experience of an experiencing subject within a given class C.
data.support: Axiomatic definition (Definition 3.9) warranted by including paradigmatic examples (color experiences, Nagel's 'what it is like') and replacing Chalmers' concept of phenomenal consciousness.

data.claim: Non-collatability induces a fundamental difficulty in any scientific approach, implying that qualia cannot be referenced intersubjectively in scientific models or empirical analysis, leading to a fundamental explanatory gap.
data.support: Argument that intersubjective referencing is impossible for non-collatable aspects, which is a prerequisite for scientific explanation (Section 4).

data.claim: Conscious experience can be formally represented as an 'experience space E', whose elements are labels for aspects of experience and whose mathematical structure is induced by collatable relations between these aspects.
data.support: Derived from Phenomenological Axiom 3.12 (recognizability of qualia) and Phenomenological Axiom 3.14 (collatable relations of qualia), leading to Definition 3.1 and the construction of E (Section 3.2).

data.claim: The ambiguity of any reference to aspects of experience, due to non-collatability, can be precisely quantified in terms of the automorphism group Aut(E) of the experience space E.
data.support: Mathematical derivation showing that relabellings that preserve the structure of E are elements of Aut(E), and these define equivalence classes of labels (Section 3.3).

data.claim: Empirically well-defined references to experience are given by the equivalence classes of labels with respect to the automorphism group Aut(E).
data.support: Argument that these equivalence classes describe what is intersubjectively accessible and empirically well-defined (Section 2, Section 3.3).

data.claim: A necessary condition for a pre-model of consciousness to be empirically well-defined is that there is an Aut(E)n action (6.5) on kinematically possible trajectories K which maps solutions to solutions, meaning Aut(E)n is a symmetry group of the model.
data.support: Definition 6.2 and Lemma 6.3, derived from the requirement that relabelling choices should not make a difference to the model's solutions.

data.claim: The need for an Aut(E)n symmetry in a model of consciousness is a direct mathematical consequence of non-collatability.
data.support: Lemma 6.3 directly states this, linking the symmetry requirement to the non-trivial nature of Aut(E) when non-collatable aspects exist (Section 6.1).

data.claim: The proposed mathematical framework allows formal models of consciousness to go beyond what the standard methodology can do by relating individual elements of E and P prior to imposing the symmetry that ensures well-definedness.
data.support: Argument that the non-trivial action ỡ (6.6) on physical states, allowed by the framework, enables models to address individual qualia, unlike direct descriptions which only deal with equivalence classes (Section 6.3).

data.claim: The phenomenological grounding, incorporating the formal-mathematical methodology, provides a suitable framework for the scientific study of consciousness, including qualia proper.
data.support: Summary of how the framework addresses non-collatability and the explanatory gap, integrating philosophical concepts with mathematical tools (Definition 3.19, Section 6.3).

data.claim: Integrated Information Theory (IIT) can be formalized within this framework as a pre-model of consciousness, and to account for non-collatability, it requires an Aut(Es) symmetry.
data.support: Analysis of IIT's 'qualia space Es' and its relation to the experience space E, and the argument for implementing the symmetry (Section 8.1).

data.claim: The Expected Float Entropy (EFE) model specifies relations whose automorphism group has non-trivial orbits, implying that the theory only determines minimizers up to transformations.
data.support: Mathematical analysis of EFE's invariance under state transformations, leading to the conclusion about U(.,.) and R(.,.) (Section 8.4).

data.claim: Assuming the closure of the physical is incompatible with the possibility of a scientific study of consciousness itself.
data.support: A transcendental argument (Remark B.1) based on the necessity of communication about Q and the physical mediation of communication channels.

data.claim: A preliminary choice of a class C of experiencing subjects is made for experimental investigations.
'Conscious experience' denotes the totality of impressions, feelings, thoughts, perceptions, etc. an experiencing subject lives through at a particular instant of time (Definition 3.1).
'Aspects of experience' denote specific or general features, parts, properties or elements of a particular experience or set of experiences (Definition 3.2).
Phenomenological Axiom 3.4: A statement about aspects of experience holds for all experiencing subjects in a class C (Definition 3.4).
Phenomenological Axiom 3.6: Aspects of experience can be divided into two classes: non-collatable and collatable (Phenomenological Axiom 3.6).
Phenomenological Axiom 3.12: Qualia can be recognized to a certain extent; experiencing subjects can identify qualia they have previously experienced (Phenomenological Axiom 3.12).
Phenomenological Axiom 3.14: Qualia have relations that can be collated within the class C (Phenomenological Axiom 3.14).

Convention 3.17: For every collatable aspect of experience, the mathematical structure of E contains a unary collatable relation X which allows one to select this aspect of experience uniquely (Convention 3.17).

For the Hilbert space example (Example 3.24): (A1) With respect to any two qualia of one experiencing subject, the experiencing subject might have an experience which has exactly these qualia as ineffable aspects. (A2) There is a unique neutral quale '0' and for every quale 'e', a quale '-e' such that an experience including both 'e' and '-e' is not distinguishable from the neutral quale.
A generalized definition of Integrated Information Theory (IIT) is provided that captures its inherent mathematical structure.
data.support: Formal definitions of system classes, experience spaces, repertoires, integration levels, and the overall IIT algorithm (Definitions 1-11).

data.claim: Classical IIT 3.0 fits precisely within the generalized IIT framework.
data.support: Detailed mapping of classical IIT components (systems, proto-experiences, repertoires, decompositions, cuts) to the generalized definitions in Section 9 and Appendix A.

data.claim: Quantum IIT, as defined by Zanardi et al., fits precisely within the generalized IIT framework.
data.support: Detailed mapping of Quantum IIT components (systems, proto-experiences, repertoires, decompositions, cuts) to the generalized definitions in Section 10.

data.claim: The generalized framework allows for the extension of classical IIT to systems with continuous time and non-Markovian dynamics.
data.support: Redefinition of cause-effect repertoires using trajectories and limits (Section 11.1).

data.claim: The generalized framework can resolve the problem of uniform probability distributions not existing for non-compact continuous state spaces.
data.support: Suggestion to replace uniform distributions with canonical uniform measures (e.g., Lebesgue, Haar) and redefine proto-experiences using the space of all measures (Section 11.2).

data.claim: The problem of arbitrary metric choices in IIT is fundamentally conceptual/philosophical and can be resolved by tying metrics to the phenomenological structure of conscious experience.
data.support: Argument that the distance function in experience spaces should mirror the similarity of conscious experiences (Section 11.3).

data.claim: The proposed mathematical structure simplifies and clarifies the IIT algorithm.
data.support: The concise presentation of core ingredients (integration levels, scalings, cores) and the overall definition in a few lines (Section 12).

data.claim: The generalized definition allows overcoming most identified mathematical problems of contemporary IIT.
data.support: Discussion of how the framework addresses limitations like discrete time, Markovian dynamics, and discrete state spaces (Section 12).

data.claim: Integrated Information Theory (IIT) aims to specify the conscious experience (quality and quantity) of a physical system in a particular state.
The number of subsystems remains the same under cuts or changes of states.
Each set of subsystems for a given system is finite (with a note on future extension).

There is a natural embedding of the experience space of a subsystem into the experience space of the larger system, allowing the experience of a major complex to be viewed as an element of the system's experience space.
In physics, state spaces are defined such that dynamical laws allow determining the trajectory of each state.
Existing approaches to representing conscious experience mathematically lack an explicit definition of 'mathematical structure of conscious experience'.
data.support: Analysis of the current state of the field, noting various names and fragmented approaches across psycho-physics, philosophy, phenomenology, neuroscience, and consciousness theories.

data.claim: The condition (MDC), which states that a mathematical structure describes conscious experience if its domains correspond to aspects of conscious experiences and its axioms are satisfied, is insufficient as a definition for a mathematical structure of conscious experience.
data.support: Demonstrates three problems: (1) it allows for incompatible structures (e.g., discrete and non-discrete topologies) to pertain to the same conscious experience; (2) it permits arbitrary re-definitions of structures (e.g., rescaling a metric function) without meaningful constraint; and (3) it is indifferent to the specific details of conscious experience, requiring minimal input beyond a set of aspects.

data.claim: The proposed definition of 'mathematical structure of conscious experience' (MSC), which requires that the domains of the structure are subsets of all aspects (A) and that for every function or relation (Sj) in the structure, there is a corresponding Sj-aspect in A, resolves the three problems identified with (MDC).
data.support: Explains that (1) incompatible structures cannot share an S-aspect, preventing both from being MSCs; (2) re-definitions alter the relata, necessitating a new, non-automatic check for the existence of a corresponding S-aspect; and (3) the requirement of S-aspects forces engagement with the specific details of conscious experience, preventing indifference.

data.claim: Relative similarity, when formalized as a strict partial order (C, <) where C represents color qualities and < signifies 'less similar to a reference', is a mathematical structure of conscious experience (MSC).
data.support: Demonstrates that the axioms of a strict partial order (irreflexivity, asymmetry, and assumed transitivity) are satisfied by the interpretation of relative similarity. It is shown that the relative similarity aspect 'a' satisfies the definition of a '<-aspect', meaning variations change 'a' if and only if they do not preserve '<'.

data.claim: Standard metric structures (M, d) that use real numbers as a domain are not mathematical structures of conscious experience (MSCs).
data.support: Argues that the complex construction of real numbers (e.g., as equivalence classes of Cauchy sequences) does not correspond to any identifiable aspects of conscious experience, thus failing condition (S1) of MSC.

data.claim: Even a modified metric structure (M, d) that uses natural numbers (derived from a strict partial order) is not a mathematical structure of conscious experience (MSC).
data.support: Argues that there is no identifiable 'd-aspect' in conscious experience corresponding to 'being a specific number of degrees of similarity apart', thus failing condition (S2) of MSC.

data.claim: Topological structures, specifically a topology of visual content, are mathematical structures of conscious experience (MSCs) when linked to phenomenal unity via the subsumptive unity thesis.
data.support: Assumes the 'subsumptive unity thesis' (that for any set of phenomenal states, there is an additional phenomenal state that subsumes them). It is demonstrated that the 'phenomenal unity aspect' (ax) satisfies the definition of an 'X-aspect' for any set X in the topology T. Furthermore, the axioms of a topology are shown to be satisfied by 'regions in visual experience' as members of T.

data.claim: Conscious experiences can be represented as a set E of experiences.
Every conscious experience e exhibits a set of aspects A(e).
Aspects can be instantiated relative to other aspects.
Variations are partial mappings v: A(e) → A(e').
For the relative similarity example, transitivity of 'less similar than' holds.
For the topological structure example, the 'subsumptive unity thesis' holds true for all sets X in T.
For the topological structure example, 'any set' in the subsumptive unity thesis is understood as 'any set of aspects that are experienced as being unified'.
For the topological structure example, positions are aspects of visual experiences.
AI systems running on contemporary computer chips (CPUs, GPUs, TPUs, etc.) cannot be conscious if consciousness is dynamically relevant.
data.support: A formal no-go theorem (Theorem 4) is proven using definitions of dynamical relevance (Definitions 1 & 2), functional and postsilicon verification (Equations 1 & 2), and AI consciousness (Definition 3). The proof demonstrates that assuming an AI system is conscious under the condition of dynamical relevance leads to a contradiction with the verified dynamics of the hardware.

data.claim: Dynamical relevance is a formal condition describing whether a property (e.g., consciousness) is relevant for the temporal evolution of a system's states as described by a theory.
data.support: Conceptual explanation with intuitive examples (moving car, electrical circuit) and formal definitions (Definitions 1 & 2) are provided to clarify the concept.

data.claim: Dynamical relevance is implied by concepts such as strong emergence, some forms of weak emergence (downward causation), intrinsic/functional value of consciousness, and violation of causal closure of the physical.
data.support: Arguments are presented linking these concepts to the idea that consciousness would make a difference to the time evolution of physical states.

data.claim: Empirical investigation of consciousness plausibly relies on consciousness being dynamically relevant.
data.support: The argument is made that for experiments (e.g., EEG, verbal reports) to work as intended and for data to corroborate or falsify theories, consciousness must make a difference to the physical dynamics being measured.

data.claim: Current theories of consciousness (e.g., IIT, GNW) imply dynamical relevance in their metaphysical interpretations, but IIT's mathematical formulation does not instantiate it.
data.support: Analysis of the metaphysical foundations of IIT and GNW, and an examination of IIT's mathematical mapping from physical description to conscious experience, which does not alter system dynamics.

data.claim: Functional and postsilicon verification processes ensure that processor dynamics (and thus AI system dynamics) adhere precisely to their computational specifications, precluding or suppressing deviations.
data.support: Description of industry-standard verification steps (simulation, formal verification, in-circuit testing) and their purpose, formalized by Equations 1 and 2.

data.claim: The no-go theorem does not apply to biological substrates or other systems not subject to the same rigorous verification processes as AI chips.
data.support: Clarification of the theorem's scope, stating it is limited to systems running on 'designed and verified' substrates, which biological systems are not.

data.claim: The no-go theorem does not imply that deterministic systems cannot be conscious, but rather that *verified* systems cannot deviate from their specified dynamics.
data.support: Clarification of the distinction between determinism and adherence to a formal system by design, addressing a common objection.

data.claim: If consciousness is dynamically relevant, and an AI system states it is conscious, the cause of this statement cannot be that the AI system is actually conscious.
data.support: This is a direct logical consequence of the no-go theorem: if consciousness is dynamically relevant, AI systems cannot be conscious, therefore any self-report of consciousness by an AI cannot be due to actual consciousness.

data.claim: Consciousness is dynamically relevant (DR), meaning it makes a difference to the temporal evolution of a system's states.
Processing units (CPUs, GPUs, TPUs) are designed and verified to ensure their dynamics evolve precisely as described by a computational theory, precluding or suppressing deviations.
AI systems operate on these verified processing units.
There exists a 'true' theory of consciousness (M*) that describes the actual facts about consciousness, even if it is unknown.
There exists a 'fundamental reference theory' (TF, e.g., quantum theory) to which states of any other relevant reference theory can be mapped.
Formulating theories of consciousness that target binary classification (e.g., conscious/unconscious) is relatively straightforward.
data.support: It only requires identifying a property, function, or dynamical mode and mapping configurations to 0 or 1.

data.claim: Formulating theories that relate to a mathematical space or structure is much more difficult than binary classification theories.
data.support: It requires specifying domains, functions/relations, and satisfying axioms, demanding more information and constraints.

data.claim: Structural theories of consciousness are likely to be more predictive and have a broader explanatory scope than non-structural theories.
data.support: They meet more constraints and account for phenomenal structure as an integral aspect of phenomenal character.

data.claim: Structural methodologies might inspire and be inspired by novel theoretical ideas, potentially combining features of existing theories.
data.support: Mentions proposals like the Conscious Turing Machine or Integrated World Modelling Theory as examples.

data.claim: Structural methodologies could lead to more testable theories and new avenues for experimental investigation.
data.support: If structural theories are more predictive, they are easier to test, and new predictions about structural facts offer new experimental avenues.

data.claim: Structural thinking could yield new experimental tools and methodologies for measuring Neural Correlates of Consciousness (NCCs).
data.support: Mentions a methodology by Fink et al. (2021) that could address foundational challenges in existing NCC measures.

data.claim: Structural approaches raise the possibility of constructing new, more powerful measures of consciousness that focus on phenomenal character more comprehensively.
data.support: Analogies to geographic maps and quantum tomography illustrate how structural knowledge can decode rich information from limited data.

data.claim: Structural approaches can be essential in conceptualizing consciousness and its potential problems, shaping pre-theoretic intuitions.
data.support: They are relevant for epistemic arguments (Mary's room) and modal arguments (colour inversion), potentially forcing a reconsideration of intuitions built on these arguments.

data.claim: It is currently unclear how much of phenomenal character (e.g., self, ego, other minds, pre-reflective awareness) can be grasped by structural tools.
data.support: Poses questions about the amenability of subtle or remote facets of phenomenal character to structural analysis.

data.claim: Even if amenable to structural tools, measuring structural facets of phenomenal character might be difficult, costly, or impossible in experimental practice.
data.support: Questions the feasibility of constructing a full quality space for a single modality experimentally.

data.claim: It is unclear if structural approaches can model the intrinsic nature of qualia or qualities, or get closer to understanding the 'core' problem of consciousness.
data.support: Questions whether structural approaches have any handle on modeling intrinsic properties or merely circumscribe their structure.

data.claim: Structural approaches are not metaphysically presuming and are not inherently tied to physicalist or reductionist metaphysics.
data.support: Distinguishes 'structural approaches' (applying mathematical structure) from 'structuralist approaches' (assuming individuals are individuated by structure, i.e., trivial automorphism group). Most mathematical spaces used in science have non-trivial automorphism groups.

data.claim: Structural approaches offer versatile descriptive tools applicable independently of specific metaphysical assumptions, across various research programs.
data.support: They can be used and might be beneficial in any type of metaphysical program, from reductive physicalism to property dualism or idealism.

data.claim: There is a crucial difference between structural and structuralist agendas, and clarity is needed about which agenda one is pursuing.
data.support: This distinction arises from the two senses of the term 'structure' (general mathematical vs. narrow structuralist sense).

data.claim: Structural approaches are compatible with the existence of intrinsic or private properties of consciousness.
data.support: If such properties exist, the automorphism group of the structure is not trivial, meaning points cannot be individuated by structure alone.

data.claim: The assumption that the physical and the phenomenal are related by a structure-preserving mapping (ISO) is not justified.
data.support: Isomorphisms presuppose structures on both ends and do not explain, predict, or define phenomenal structure; they do not provide 'what if things had been different' information.

data.claim: Homomorphisms and isomorphisms are not the appropriate mathematical objects to define, explain, predict, or control phenomenal structure.
data.support: They are mappings between domains that preserve relations, but do not pick out or define structure, nor do they provide counterfactual information needed for explanation/prediction.

data.claim: Using the assumption of a structure-preserving mapping (ISO) without proper justification is not a viable option.
data.support: (ISO) is a very consequential assumption for theoretical and experimental work.

data.claim: There is no general mathematical principle to relate the physical and phenomenal in a structuralist turn; structural theories must be built one-by-one.
data.support: The challenge lies in finding the right mathematics to explicate specific ideas, concepts, and metaphysical underpinnings in each case.

data.claim: Conscious experience does not inherently 'come with' mathematical structure; mathematical spaces are tools requiring definitions and conventions (methodologies) for their application.
data.support: Analogous to English language terms needing definitions, claims about structural facts are relative to the methodology defining phenomenal structure.

data.claim: Existing methodologies for defining quality spaces (Clark, Rosenthal, IIT 2.0) have significant shortcomings.
data.support: IIT lacks a phenomenal interpretation (Rosetta Stone Problem); Clark and Rosenthal conflate mathematical convenience, laboratory operations, and conscious experience as sources of structure.

data.claim: The metric function introduced in Clark's methodology is unwarranted from the perspective of phenomenal character.
data.support: It is introduced for mathematical convenience, not grounded in conscious experience, and leads to an infinity of additional points not derived from tasks/stimuli.

data.claim: The metric function in Rosenthal's methodology might be due to mathematical convenience, and the resulting space depends on the chosen stimulus space topology (a laboratory operation).
data.support: The metric is not experientially derived, and the topology choice for stimulus variation is a lab operation, not inherent to experience.

data.claim: Existing proposals for defining phenomenal structure (based on conditions on domains and mathematical axioms) are insufficient.
data.support: They are prone to admitting incompatible structures, allowing arbitrary re-definitions, and are indifferent to structural facts of conscious experience (referencing Kleiner & Ludwig, 2023).

data.claim: A new methodology for phenomenal spaces is needed, which takes previous ones into account but avoids their identified issues.
data.support: Proposes a methodology where phenomenal structure's automorphisms are identical to variations of conscious experiences (Kleiner & Ludwig, 2023).

data.claim: Consciousness can be scientifically studied.
Phenomenal character possesses structure.
Mathematical tools can be effectively used to describe or model conscious experiences.
The ultimate goal of consciousness science is to explain, predict, or control phenomenological properties in terms of physical properties.
In any scientific experiment, the measurement results must be stored or transmitted, and these stored data are determined by the physical properties of the storage device or transmission channel.
data.support: Argument based on the physical nature of data storage (e.g., magnetization vectors on a hard disk, ink molecules on paper) and formalized using functions dD and dM.

data.claim: A theory of consciousness obeys the closure of the physical if and only if it does not posit any changes to the physical events explained, predicted, or otherwise determined by natural science, which is formally represented by an injective function i: PT → PP.
data.support: Definition provided in Section 2, with formalization.

data.claim: An assumption is unscientific if it implies that any two different theories obeying that assumption are empirically indistinguishable.
data.support: Argument that such an implication is incompatible with empirically based scientific practice and undermines scientific progress.

data.claim: The closure of the physical (as defined in the paper) implies that all theories obeying it are empirically indistinguishable.
data.support: Formal proof (Theorem 1) demonstrating that for any two theories T1 and T2 obeying the closure of the physical, their predicted measurement results OT1 and OT2 must be identical.

data.claim: The causal closure of the physical (an ontological assumption) implies the epistemic closure of the physical (the paper's definition).
data.support: Analysis of common interpretations of causal closure (e.g., Kim, Jackson) showing that they necessitate the existence of the injective function i: PT → PP.

data.claim: The closure of the physical (both its epistemic and causal versions) is unscientific.
data.support: Derived directly from the claims that causal closure implies epistemic closure, and epistemic closure leads to empirical indistinguishability, which is defined as unscientific.

data.claim: The closure of the physical is a central and widely accepted assumption in the philosophy of mind and the scientific study of consciousness.
Scientific theories of consciousness must make testable statements about possible measurement results to be considered scientific.
Measurement results, whether first-person or third-person, must be stored or transmitted in a physical data repository to be analyzed and shared in a scientific context.

The Newman problem is a fundamental problem for structural theories and assumptions across science, arising from the traditional understanding of structural claims (D1 and D2) which allows any structure to be trivially satisfied given enough elements.
data.support: Explanation of conditions (D1) and (D2) and presentation of Theorem 1 (Newman's Theorem) from existing literature (Newman, 1928; Frigg & Votsis, 2011; Ketland, 2004).

data.claim: The Newman problem applies directly to consciousness science, undermining structural research programs (epistemic and ontic phenomenal structural realism) and theories of consciousness that address phenomenal structure, especially for non-human systems where ostensive definitions fail.
data.support: Formulation of analogous conditions (C1) and (C2) for consciousness science, discussion of implications for structuralist research and theories like Integrated Information Theory (IIT), and the argument that ostensive definitions are insufficient for non-human systems.

data.claim: A suitable definition of phenomenal spaces and mathematical structures of conscious experience, incorporating 'higher-order R-properties' and 'variations', resolves the Newman problem by requiring a specific 'sort' of phenomenal property whose satisfaction does not follow from Theorem 1.
data.support: Introduction of the concepts of 'variations' and 'R-properties' (Def 5 in Appendix A), and the proposed new condition (C2''') which demands the existence of a corresponding higher-order phenomenal R-property.

data.claim: The proposed solution, based on 'higher-order R-properties' and 'variations', can be generalized to resolve the Newman problem for structural claims about the world in general.
data.support: Argument that the concepts of higher-order properties and variations can be applied in a general setting, and demonstration of how the new conditions (D1') and (D2') break down Theorem 2 (Cardinality Theorem) in the Ramsey sentence formulation.

data.claim: Relations that induce trivial automorphism groups cannot satisfy the proposed conditions for a structural claim, thus the problem of trivial automorphism groups does not undermine the solution.
data.support: Formal proof in Lemma 2 (Appendix B) demonstrating that if no variation preserves a structure S, then no S-property can exist, which contradicts the requirement for an R-property.

data.claim: The proposed solution is preferable to the 'naturalness' solution for the Newman problem, especially in the context of phenomenal character, due to issues with defining 'natural kinds' and the presumption that the world is mathematical in a way that phenomenal character is not.
data.support: Critique of the 'naturalness' solution's reliance on non-structural language, its problematic definition of 'natural kinds', and its assumption that conscious experiences have a naturally given mathematical structure.

data.claim: Mathematical structures are a suitable means to investigate, model, or measure conscious experience.
'Phenomenal properties' are a valid conceptual choice for discussing conscious experience.
Variations of experiences can be described by functions mapping phenomenal properties to phenomenal properties.
The world (or conscious experience) can be meaningfully described in terms of properties and relations, and that these properties can be higher-order.
Second-order logic (quantification over predicates) is a valid framework for expressing structural claims.

the class of all computations.

A novel concept of general purpose computing where the parameter values defining the learned computation are only useful for that specific hardware instance, meaning the computation dies with the hardware. It can also be understood as a computation that fundamentally transcends some of the constraints of Turing computation.
the class of immortal computations
the class of all systems.
all computations that a system S∈ Sys can realize or implement.
the class of computations that can be coded with any existing programming language
