A computation is a Turing computation iff it can be realized by (the abstract mathematical model of) a Turing machine.
All organisms capable of feeling pain are Probabilistic Automata.
Every organism capable of feeling pain possesses at least one Description of a certain kind (i.e., being capable of feeling pain is possessing an appropriate kind of Functional Organization).
No organism capable of feeling pain possesses a decomposition into parts which separately possess Descriptions of the kind referred to in 2.

For every Description of the kind referred to in 2, there exists a subset of the sensory inputs such that an organism with that Description is in pain when and only when some of its sensory inputs are in that subset.
There is a system S & Syso that is capable of conscious experience e.
Concerns the nature of computations, specifically what the computation is that implements a function, rather than merely whether a function is Turing-computable.
The application and study of formal and mathematical methods as applied in, or relevant to, the scientific study of consciousness.
data.section: Mathematical Approaches in the Scientific Study of Consciousness

data.definition: Hypotheses about how conscious experiences and the subject matter of the natural sciences, most notably the brain, relate.

The desideratum that theories should be formulated in such a way that they can determine whether a given dynamical system is conscious, irrespective of its origin or composition (e.g. whether it is a biological brain, hurricane or computer).
data.section: 1.1.1 The Role of Mathematics in Constructing Theories of Consciousness

data.definition: A theory of consciousness must explain why measures measure what they measure.
The model or theory from natural science that a theory of consciousness T is built on, or makes use of.
Consciousness detection procedures that can be used to determine whether a subject in an experimental trial has experienced a stimulus consciously or not.
Means to infer whether a system is conscious at all, meaning: whether it has conscious experience at all, or not.
A formal mapping where O denotes a set of experimental data sets, and E denotes an abstract notion of states of consciousness.
Variations of the part of the brain that is responsible for conscious experiences, according to the theories, without changing the report.

data.term: Theory of measurement (or measurement theory) for consciousness science
data.definition: A substantive theory that provides a foundation for measurements of the various forms.
data.section: 2.3 What is Measurement in Consciousness Science?

data.definition: Theories that employ a different way to handle, describe or represent conscious experience, based on mathematical spaces and mathematical structure.
A set of assumptions that are taken to characterise the essential properties of conscious experiences in full.

data.term: Predictive Processing Theory (PP) and its Active Inference doctrine
data.definition: Also known as 'Free Energy Principle', arguably a first comprehensive theory of brain function.
Concepts that allude or refer to formal notions, but are not presented in a formal form.
data.section: 1.2.3 The Important Case of Non-Formal Theories

data.definition: The idea that the structure of conscious experiences fully determine all non-structural experiential facts, including which phenomenal properties are instantiated in an experience.

data.term: Isomorphism between the physical structure of the brain and the phenomenal structure of experience (assumption)
data.definition: An assumption that there is an isomorphism between the physical structure of the brain and the phenomenal structure of experience.
A 'body of methods used in a particular field of study or activity'.
Denotes various concepts in consciousness science, including the object of investigation (conscious experiences) and a way of engaging with consciousness scientifically and philosophically.
Aims to apply mathematical concepts and techniques in phenomenological investigations, most notably in the form of mathematical presentations of the results of such investigations.

The modelling of phenomenology in terms of computational tools from computer science, or in terms of the computational framework provided by Predictive Processing Theory and its Active Inference doctrine.
Theorems, in the mathematical sense of the term, that establish a conclusion about a subject matter of interest based on mathematical assumptions and a proof.
A computation is mortal if it cannot be separated from the hardware on which it runs; if 'it dies with the hardware'.
The application of mathematical methods to philosophical questions and problems of the mind.

data.term: Analysis of the target phenomenon (role of philosophy of mind)
data.definition: The study of concepts that refer to the target phenomenon, so as to make the phenomenon, or properties thereof, accessible to scientific investigations.

data.term: Analysis of methods (role of philosophy of mind)
data.definition: The critical analysis of existing methods, constructive analyses of existing methods, and the proposal of new methods.

data.term: Analysis of results (role of philosophy of mind)
data.definition: The analysis of results of investigations of the mind sciences, including empirical and theoretical investigations, to improve understanding.
The use of scientific results as bottom-up constraints on philosophy of mind, so as to inform philosophical research on philosophical questions, for example metaphysical theories.
The question of whether artificial systems are or can be conscious.
The computation that biological systems like brains implement.
The very idea that consciousness is a computation.
The requirement that a theory of consciousness posits that consciousness makes some difference to the time evolution of the states of its reference theory.
The paradigm that consciousness science is to take a neuroscientific account of the brain as 'input' to explain what consciousness is, without amending or adding to this input.
A development where mathematical spaces and structures are used, in conjunction with existing tools, to improve theories, experiments, measures, and concepts in consciousness science.
In the context of 'Conscious Turing Machine', 'model' is understood in the sense of computer science, which is different from the notion of 'model' in neuroscience and other natural sciences.

In the context of Processing Units (PUs) supporting AI, 'artificial' means not only man-made but also that 'the system is made to behave in an exact pre-specified way', governed by pre-set mathematical rules.

data.term: A grounding of the scientific study of consciousness
data.definition: Contains at least an explicit definition of what is to be studied and an explicit outline of the methodology.
The totality of impressions, feelings, thoughts, perceptions, etc. which an experiencing subject lives through at a particular instant of time.
Specific or general features, parts, properties or elements of a particular experience or of a set of experiences.

data.term: An aspect of experience is non-collatable
data.definition: There does not exist a reasonable method to establish its identity over different experiencing subjects in the class C.
All non-collatable aspects of experience of an experiencing subject within the class C.

data.term: The mathematical structure of a scientific theory T
data.definition: Comprises at least: A set of dynamical variables d; Some background structure b; A set of kinematically possible trajectories K; Some laws L; A set of dynamically possible trajectories D which are also called solutions of T.

data.term: A group G is a symmetry group of a theory T
data.definition: If and only if the following conditions are satisfied: (a) There is an effective action G × K → K of G on K. (b) This action leaves the solutions D of T invariant.

A theory as in Definition 5.1, where: (i) The dynamical variables are a Cartesian product of the physical state space P of Tp together with one copy of the experience space E for each experiencing subject, d=E×E× ... ×E×P. (ii) Kinematically possible trajectories K are a subset of families of dynamical variables, K⊂{(e^1_t, e^2_t,...,e^n_t, p_t)_{t∈I}}, where e^i_t ∈ E, p_t ∈ P, n is the number of experience spaces in (5.1) and I is some parameter space.

data.term: A necessary condition for a pre-model of consciousness M to be empirically well-defined
data.definition: There is an Aut(E)^n action (6.5) on K which maps solutions to solutions, i.e. which satisfies σ_s(D) = D for all s∈ Aut(E)^n.
data.section: 6.2. The Mathematical Structure of Models of Consciousness

data.definition: A pre-model of consciousness M as defined in Definition 5.3 which additionally carries an Aut(E)^n symmetry of the form (6.5).
data.section: 6.2. The Mathematical Structure of Models of Consciousness

data.term: A model of consciousness M describes the physical as closed
data.definition: If and only if D|p = Dp, where D|p is defined in (5.4) and where Dp has been introduced in Section 5.1 to denote the solutions of the physical theory Tp which underlies the model M.
Those aspects of conscious experience which do not have a function or structure, where 'function' and 'structure' are as defined in Chalmers' grounding.
data.section: Appendix A. Chalmers' Grounding of the Scientific Study of Consciousness

data.definition: A statement about aspects of experience which holds for all experiencing subjects in a class C.
Aspects of experience can be divided into two classes: a) Aspects of experience which are non-collatable. b) Aspects of experience which are collatable.
Qualia can be recognised to a certain extent: Experiencing subjects can identify qualia which they have previously experienced.
Qualia have relations that can be collated within the class C.
For every collatable aspect of experience, the mathematical structure of E contains a unary collatable relation X which allows one to select this aspect of experience uniquely.
"The physical domain is causally closed." (and "For every physical event, there is a physical sufficient cause.")
An explanation specifies the function and structure of an explanandum in terms of the the function and structure of accepted theoretical notions.

In both Chalmers' grounding (CG) and the phenomenological grounding (PG), the assumption of the closure of the physical (ACoP) implies that the states c of communication channels cannot be functionally dependent on q.

data.term: grounding of the scientific study of consciousness
data.definition: A conception of the phenomenon to be studied and a conception of a methodology suitable to do so, including an explicit definition of what is to be studied and an explicit outline of the methodology.
An aspect of experience is non-collatable if there is no reasonable method to identify whether two or more experiencing subjects in an experiment experience this very aspect of experience.

A mathematical space representing conscious experience, where elements are labels for aspects of experience, and its mathematical structure is induced by collatable relations between aspects of experience.

The grounding of the scientific study of consciousness derived in this paper, based on phenomenological axioms, which specifies that experience (Definition 3.1) and its relation to the physical domain are to be studied, including intersubjectively well-defined aspects via quotient space (3.8) and qualia proper via experience space (3.1) and the formal-mathematical methodology from Section 6.

A scientific theory (as per Definition 5.1) where dynamical variables are a Cartesian product of a physical state space P and 'n' copies of the experience space E (for 'n' experiencing subjects), and kinematically possible trajectories are a subset of families of these dynamical variables.
A pre-model of consciousness M (as defined in Definition 5.3) which additionally carries an Aut(E)^n symmetry of the form (6.5).

Refers to 'a collection of methods, practices, procedures and rules used by those who work in some field' [Wik18b], 'a system of methods used in a particular area of study or activity' [Oxf18], specifically including the specification of what constitutes an experiment.
One of several translations of the German word "Grundlegung", referring to a comprehensive framework for the scientific study of consciousness.
Specifically denotes 'the totality of impressions, feelings, thoughts, perceptions, etc. which an experiencing subject lives through at a particular instant of time' (Definition 3.1).

A placeholder for 'specific or general features, parts, properties or elements of a particular experience or of a set of experiences' (Definition 3.2), emphasizing that these may not be strictly separable.

Specifically defined as 'all non-collatable aspects of experience of an experiencing subject within the class C' (Definition 3.9), focusing on the operational consequence of non-collatability rather than intrinsic nature.

Means 'anything that occurs or manifests itself in a general sense, including both scientifically observable “empirical phenomena” (such as data of an experiment) as well as what is directly or indirectly perceived (experiences)' (Footnote 24).
Used in a general sense: 'A variable may represent something as simple as a natural number just as well as an operator-valued field on some manifold' (Footnote 26).
Refers to 'all those phenomena which are currently considered to be the subject of a natural science (physics, chemistry, earth science, biology, etc. [Wik18a])' (Appendix A).
Used in the broader sense of 'any causal role in the production of behaviour that a system might perform' [Cha10, p. 6], not in the narrow teleological sense (Appendix A).
Used in a 'spatiotemporal sense' (Appendix A).
Specifically refers to a notion where 'an explanation specifies the function and structure of an explanandum in terms of the the function and structure of accepted theoretical notions' (Appendix A).

Applicable to 'any “putative fact regarding some difference or lack of uniformity within some context” [Flo17]', potentially including non-physical quantities, but typically transformed into physical data for scientific analysis (Section B.2).

A quantity 'a' is functionally dependent on 'b' according to some model of the MTCp setup if, according to this model, 'a' is a non-constant function of 'b' (Footnote 39 clarifies this is defined by the respective grounding, having a nomological flavor).

A class each of whose elements S, called systems, come with the following data: 1. a set St(S) of states; 2. for every s∈ St(S), a set Subs(S) ⊂ Sys of subsystems and for each M∈ Subs(S) an induced state s|M ∈ St(M); 3. a set Ds of decompositions, with a given trivial decomposition 1 ∈ Ds; 4. for each z ∈ Ds a corresponding cut system S² ∈ Sys and for each state s∈ St(S) a corresponding cut state sẽ ∈ St(S).

A set E with: 1. an intensity function || . ||: E → R+; 2. a distance function d: E × E → R+; 3. a scalar multiplication R+ × E → E, denoted (r, e) → r · e, satisfying || r · e || = r · || e ||, r · (s · e) = (rs) · e, 1 · e = e for all e ∈ E and r, s ∈ R+.

For experience spaces E and F, we define the product to be the space E × F with distance d((e, f), (e', f')) = d(e, e') + d(f, f'), intensity ||(e, f) || = max{|| e ||, || f ||} and scalar multiplication r· (e, f) = (r·e,r·f).

data.term: A decomposition of e over D
data.definition: A mapping ē: D → E with ē(1) = e.

Given by a choice of experience space PE(S), called the space of proto-experiences, and for each s ∈ St(S) and M, P∈ Subs (S), a pair of elements causs (M, P), effs (M,P) ∈ PE(S) and for each of them a decomposition over DM,P.
A specification of a cause-effect repertoire for every S∈ Sys such that PE(S) = PE(S²) for all z∈ Ds.

The subsystem C∈ Sub(S) for which φ(eC) is maximal. If the maximum does not exist, we define the core to be the empty system I.

(QM,s|M) M∈Subs(S)

data.definition: Core integration scaling of Q(S, s).

Determined as follows. The data of the theory is a system class Sys along with a cause-effect structure. The theory then gives a mapping Sys → Exp into the class Exp of all experience spaces, sending each system S to its space of experiences E(S) defined in (12), and a mapping St(S) → E(S) s ↦ E(S, s) which determines the experience of the system when in a state s, defined in (14). The quantity of the system's experience is given by Φ(S, s) := || E(S, s) ||, and the quality of the system's experience is given by the normalized experience E(S, s). The experience is located in the core of the collection Q(S, s), called major complex, which is a subsystem of S.

data.definition: Consists of all partitions of the set N of elements of S into two disjoint sets M and M⊥. We denote such a partition by z = (M, M⊥). The trivial decomposition 1 is the pair (N, ∅).
The same as S but with a new time evolution T(M,M⊥) defined for each i = 1, ..., n as T(M,M⊥) := { Ti if i∈ M⊥; TiωM⊥ if i∈ M } where ωM⊥ ∈ P(M) denotes the uniform distribution on St(M).

P(S), where P(S) is defined in Example 3. Thus elements of PE(S) are of the form (p, r) for some p ∈ P(S) and r∈ R+, with distance function, intensity and scalar multiplication as defined in the example.

S(Hs) with Hs = ⊗_{i=1}^{n} Hi, where S(Hs) ⊂ L(Hs) describes the positive semidefinite Hermitian operators of unit trace on Hs, aka density matrices.

The space of probability measures whose first moment is finite.

data.term: space of proto-experiences PE(S) (continuous state spaces)
data.definition: M(S), where M(S) denotes all measures on St(S).
T(p) = Π_{i=1}^{n} T_i(p) for all p∈ P(S)
A formal, axiomatic definition of IIT that encompasses classical IIT 3.0 and Quantum IIT as special cases.

The expression do(mt, mc) denotes a variant of the so-called “do-operator”. It indicates that the state of the system, here at time t, is to be set to the term in brackets. This is called perturbing the system into the state (mt, mc).
The pair of maximally irreducible repertoires scaled by φmax(M). This is equivalent to what is called a concept, or sometimes quale sensu stricto, in classcial IIT [Ton15], and denoted as q(yt).
The Q-shape Qs (S) is the collection of all concepts specified by the mechanisms of a system... this makes Qs (S) what is usually called the conceptual structure or cause-effect structure.
The factor φmax(M) ensures that the distance used here corresponds precisely to the distance used in [OAT14], there called the extended Earth Mover's Distance.
The subsystems of S are what is called candidate systems in [OAT14], and which describe that 'part' of the system that is going to be conscious according to the theory.

The core integration scaling finally picks out that candidate system with the largest integrated information value. This candidate system is the major complex M of S, the part of S which is conscious according to the theory as part of the exclusion postulate of IIT.

data.term: maximally irreducible conceptual structure (MICS) or quale sensu lato
data.definition: Its Q-shape is the maximally irreducible conceptual structure (MICS), also called quale sensu lato.

data.term: constellation of concepts in qualia space
data.definition: Thus E(S, s) is the constellation of concepts in qualia space E(M) of [OAT14].

data.term: A mathematical structure describes conscious experience (MDC)
data.definition: A mathematical structure describes conscious experience (MDC) if and only if the following two conditions are satisfied: (D1) The domains of the structure are sets whose elements correspond to aspects of conscious experiences. (D2) The axioms of the structure are satisfied.
A set E of conscious experiences of an experiencing subject. Individual conscious experiences in that set are denoted by symbols like e and e'. Formally e, e' ∈ E.

A placeholder for concepts such as qualia, qualities, or (instantiated) phenomenal properties. For every experience e ∈ E, A(e) denotes the set of aspects instantiated in this experience. A is the union of all A(e). Individual aspects are denoted by small letters such as a, b, c.
An aspect a is instantiated relative to aspects b1,..., bm, or simply that a is relative to b1,..., bm, if it requires other aspects for its instantiation.
A change of one experience e into another experience e'. Formally, a variation is a partial mapping v : A(e) → A(e').
A tuple S = ((Ai)iel, (Sj)jeJ) of domains Ai and functions or relations Sj.

Those elements that are related by a structure. For a relation R on a domain A with arity m, these are the elements of the m-tuples (b1,..., bm) ∈ R. For a function f: A1 × ... X Am-1 → Am, the relata are the elements of the m-tuples (b1, ..., bm-1, bm) where bm = f(b1,..., bm−1).
A mathematical structure S where its domains are subsets of A (the set of all aspects of experiences) and for every relation or function Sj, there is a corresponding Sj-aspect in A.

A variation v : A(e) → A(e') changes an aspect a ∈ A(e) relative to b1, ..., bm ∈ A(e) if and only if a is instantiated relative to b1, ..., bm in A(e), but a is not instantiated relative to v(b1), ..., v(bm) in A(e').
data.section: 2.3. What is a Mathematical Structure of Conscious Experience?

data.definition: A variation v : A(e) → A(e') preserves a structure S with respect to relata b1, ..., bm ∈ A(e) if and only if we have (P1) R(b1,..., bm) = R(v(b1), ..., v(bm)) if S is a relation R, or (P2) v (f(b1,..., bm−1)) = f (v(b1), ..., v(bm−1)) if S is a function f.
data.section: 2.3. What is a Mathematical Structure of Conscious Experience?

data.definition: An aspect 'a' that, under any variation, behaves exactly as the structure S does: whenever S is preserved, the S-aspect does not change; whenever the S-aspect changes, the structure S is not preserved.
Roughly speaking, a sequence of rational numbers that get arbitrarily close to each other. Two Cauchy sequences are defined to be equivalent if the difference between their elements tends to zero.

d(x, y) = length<(x, y), where length<(x, y) is formally defined as: 0 if x = y, min |{x → y}| if x < y, min |{y → x}| if y < x, ∞ otherwise, where x → y denotes a path along the strict partial order from x to y, {x → y} denotes the number of elements in the path (with x counted but y not counted), and where the minimum selects the shortest path.

An instantiation of a phenomenal property, or quale, by a subject at a given time. This instantiation constitutes part of the experience of the subject at the time. An experience e, in our terminology, is an experience of a subject at a given time. Hence, a phenomenal state is an instantiation of a phenomenal property, or quale, in an experience e.

For any set X ⊆ A(e) of aspects of an experience, there is an additional aspect in A(e) that subsumes the aspects in X. This aspect is the experience of what it is like to experience the aspects in X as part of one experience e together, the experience that they are unified. It is instantiated relative to the elements of X.

Structure-preserving mappings from a structure to itself. Automorphisms are mappings v that map the domains of a structure to themselves. These mappings have to be bijective, and they have to preserve the structure, meaning that they have to satisfy (P1) for all elements of the domain in case of relations, and (P2) for elements of the domains in the case of functions.
For all points x, y, z ∈ M: Positive definiteness (d(x, y) > 0 and d(x, y) = 0 if and only if x = y), Symmetry (d(x, y) = d(y, x)), and Triangle inequality (d(x, y) ≤ d(x,z) + d(z,y)).
The collection T must include the empty set and the whole domain, be closed under finite intersections, and be closed under arbitrary unions.
For all x, y, z ∈ C: Irreflexivity (no x ∈ C with x < x), Asymmetry (if x < y, then not y < x), and Transitivity (if x < y and y < z, then also x < z).
For any set of phenomenal states of a subject at a time, the subject has a phenomenal state that subsumes each of the states in that set.
Something in conscious experience that corresponds to a mathematical structure S.
Used as a placeholder for concepts such as qualia, qualities, (instantiated) phenomenal properties or similar concepts, which are the building blocks of conscious experience.
Refers specifically to the relations or functions defined on the domains of a mathematical structure, distinct from the domains themselves.
Given a scientific theory T and a system S within the scope of the theory, k_T(S,s) denotes how the state s evolves in time according to T.

For every theory of consciousness (ToC) M, there is at least one reference theory TR in Y such that the physical part of any state s of M, and therefore also any dynamical evolution k_M, can be expressed in TR. k_M|TR is what M says about the evolution of reference states on TR's level of description.

data.term: Consciousness is dynamically relevant according to M with respect to TR
data.definition: S is conscious in k_M → k_M|TR ≠ k_TR. This means that if S is conscious according to a ToC M, then the dynamical evolution as specified by M differs from the dynamical evolution as specified by the underlying neuroscientific theory alone.
Consciousness is dynamically relevant only if it is dynamically relevant according to the 'true' ToC M* with respect to some reference theory TR ∈ Y.

data.term: AI system S is conscious according to a theory of consciousness M
data.definition: Only if there is at least one dynamical evolution k_Tcomp in which the system is conscious according to M.
Verification of processing units ensures that any dynamical effects that change the computational dynamics of a processing unit are precluded or suppressed.
If consciousness is dynamically relevant, and AI systems are conscious, then there are dynamical effects that change the computational dynamics of an AI system.
AI systems run on processing units.

Consciousness is 'relevant' to a system's time evolution if the time evolution with consciousness differs from the time evolution without consciousness. More generally, it describes the relation between a theory of consciousness and a reference theory on which the theory of consciousness is built, where being conscious makes a difference for the time evolution of a system.
Consists of two things: domains (the sets on which the structure is built) and functions or relations (that express connections between the points).
The sets on which the structure is built, comprising the points, or elements, in a space.

data.term: Functions and/or relations (of a mathematical structure)
data.definition: The second ingredient of a mathematical structure, which map some of the domains to other domains or relate points to each other.
A one-to-one mapping from the domains of the structure to themselves which preserves the functions or relations (structure in the narrow sense of the term).
Make use of mathematical spaces or mathematical structures to represent or describe conscious experiences.
Assume that all points of the space can be individuated by their relational structure, meaning that no two points have the same relational structure.
A bijective mapping between the domains of two structures that preserves the relations or functions of these structures.
A map that is one-to-one and onto, meaning that every element in the target space gets mapped to by exactly one element in the source space.

Defined exactly like isomorphisms, except that they do not have to be one-to-one or onto, so that some elements in the target space might not get mapped to, and/or several elements in the source space might map to the same element in the target space.
Denotes homomorphisms or isomorphisms, with the understanding that the domains and structures of the source and target have been adapted appropriately to avoid technical problems.

Constructed by fixing a class of stimuli S, defining two tasks (discrimination and relative similarity), using discrimination to define global indiscriminability and qualities, and then introducing a metric via multidimensional scaling.
Each set in a partition of stimuli (based on global indiscriminability) contains stimuli which are globally indiscriminable from each other.

Constructed by building Just Noticeable Differences (JNDs) from variations of stimuli and a discrimination task, where regions reachable by varying a stimulus without creating a JND constitute qualities, and a metric function is introduced by counting minimal JND steps.
Defines what it means to "draw a line without lifting a pen" on an abstract space, providing the notion of continuous curves.
Structuralism about a domain is true iff the automorphism group of that domain is trivial.

data.term: (ISO) The physical and the phenomenal are related by a structure-preserving mapping
data.definition: The physical and the phenomenal are related by a structure-preserving mapping from the phenomenal domain to the physical domain.
That mathematical structure whose automorphisms are identical to the variations of the qualities as experiences change.
A simpler term for "mathematical structure of conscious experience" in the context of their new methodology.

data.term: Structure (in the context of structuralist ideas)
data.definition: In the context of structuralist ideas, it refers *only* to the functions and relations that a mathematical structure contains, not including the domains (points/elements). The author clarifies this as "structure in the narrow sense of the term".
The author clarifies that 'domain' has two meanings: the mathematical structure sense (sets on which the structure is built) and the general language sense. The paper uses both.

The author notes that the mathematical concept of homomorphism is "too strong to express the underlying idea" when the physical has much more structure than the phenomenal. The author admits using "structure-preserving mapping" to denote homomorphisms or isomorphisms with adapted domains/structures to avoid technical problems.
the theories that are tested, compared, or derived in experiments in the scientific study of consciousness, regardless of what metaphysical status of consciousness they presuppose.

the physical events which T is committed to, for example the firing of some neurons or the instantiation of some functional property. Every element in P_T is a description of an event that occurs, according to T, in the actual world.
the physical events which natural science explains, predicts or determines. Whatever it is that natural science says or implies about the physical events in the actual world is part of the class P_P.

an injective (one-to-one) function i of the form i: P_T → P_P, which specifies for every physical event and description that the theory of consciousness is committed to the corresponding event and description explained, predicted, or determined by natural science.
an experiment
all data sets which could result from this experiment according to some assumption or theory. So O_M denotes the possible measurement results of M in some context.
the data sets which can occur in M according to T (pre- or retrodictions of T).
Two theories T and T' are empirically indistinguishable if there is no single experiment M such that O_T ≠ O_T' in M.
the set or class of all physical events (and descriptions) that can possibly occur in the real world
all records that can possibly be stored on a storage device D

a function where P(P) is the set of all subsets of P, called the power set of P, and where P(O_D) is the power set of O_D. The function d_D provides for every logically possible set of physical events P ⊂ P of the actual world a class of data sets O_D ⊂ O_D that could be stored on D at a particular time.

It selects from all physical events which, according to P, are part of the real world those which are relevant for data storage on the device D, e.g. the magnetization vectors in the case of a hard disk.

data.question: What precisely does it mean to realize or implement a mortal computation?

data.question: Developing a more detailed and constructive notion of mortal computation.
data.context: The paper relies on a differential definition of mortal computation, and a more comprehensive understanding is needed for further research and application of the concept.

data.question: Develop a more detailed and constructive notion of mortal computation.
Further explore the implications of mortal computation for AI consciousness.
Investigate mortal computation as a concept of interest with respect to questions of the mind.

The paper strongly implies that 'Only artificial systems that employ mortal computations can instantiate consciousness,' but immediately qualifies this by stating that the results 'do not, however, prove this to be the case' because consciousness (a mortal computation) 'might be the case that... can be realized by immortal computations.'
data.context: The strong claim about the necessity of mortal computation for consciousness instantiation and the explicit acknowledgment that this claim is not definitively proven, with a significant counter-possibility (realization by immortal computations) that weakens the direct implication for AI consciousness.

data.question: This chapter is not a review or comprehensive assessment of mathematical consciousness science. The selection of topics is highly biased around the research of the author, and it only mentions a small part of the research that 200+ researchers, who have joined the mathematical consciousness science community as represented by the Association for Mathematical Consciousness Science, have produced.
data.context: The chapter provides only a limited and biased perspective on mathematical consciousness science.

data.question: It is impossible to foresee what mathematical consciousness science might become. The following introduction to some of the contemporary themes of mathematical consciousness science should therefore be understood as outlining a very preliminary picture.
data.context: The introduction is preliminary and cannot fully predict the future of the field.

data.question: The use of mathematical formalism in constructing theories of consciousness is not obviously a good idea. The large majority of theories of consciousness that exist today is not formulated in mathematical terms, and the science is making good progress nevertheless.
data.context: Calls for mathematization need strong justification.

data.question: Any call for mathematization, either in general or in specific cases, needs to introduce good reasons for why a mathematization should be applied. Good reasons that justify not only the effort of applying the mathematization, but which also take into account the further scientific progress of theories. The exactness and devotion to detail involved in mathematical methods can easily inhibit a progressive research programme.
data.context: Mathematization can hinder progressive research if not applied carefully.

data.question: The summary of motivations for research on theories of consciousness in mathematical consciousness science might be highly biased by the author's own work, particularly work that is directed at uncovering or reconstructing the mathematical structure of existing theories of consciousness.
data.context: The summary of motivations is biased by the author's specific research focus.

data.question: The assessment of how mathematics might be of help—or, in some cases, even necessary—in constructing theories of consciousness (questions (a) and (b) above) is very initial.
data.context: The assessment is preliminary.

data.question: Regarding question (c)—of how to go about building mathematical theories of consciousness—the present results suggest only one important answer: there is no one-fits-all solution.
data.context: No general recipe for building mathematical theories of consciousness.

data.question: The actual work of explicating ideas in concrete cases remains challenging and requires as innovative research as always.
data.context: Applying mathematical methods remains challenging.

data.question: Virtually all theories of consciousness that have been proposed to date fail to satisfy the requirement that a theory of consciousness must explain why measures measure what they measure, for one of two reasons.
data.context: Existing theories are empirically untestable or false.

data.question: Theories that offer a specific hypothesis (e.g., formal IIT) mostly fail because they do not model how subjective report or other behaviour that measures and C-tests rely on, comes to reflect the content of experience.
data.context: Specific theories like IIT lack concrete explanations for how report depends on experience.

data.question: Theories that operate with a less specific hypothesis (e.g., GNWT) fail because their specifications are too general to afford an explanation of why measures measure what they measure.
data.context: Less specific theories like GNWT are too general to explain how measures work.

data.question: To provide an explanation that features enough details to preclude substitutions (where brain parts responsible for consciousness can be varied without changing report) is likely no easy feat; a general recipe is probably not available.
data.context: Difficult to provide sufficiently detailed explanations for individual theories.

data.question: The exploration of structural tools for building theories of consciousness has just begun.
data.context: The field is in its early stages.

data.question: Much of the mathematical structure that appears to be essential for IIT's description of conscious experience in terms of formal spaces is actually auxiliary and merely derives from the particular notion of (network-like) classical systems that has been applied in previous expositions of the theory.
data.context: Previous expositions of IIT might have included auxiliary mathematical structure, obscuring the essential parts.

data.question: There is a fundamental issue with testing IIT that derives both from IIT's mathematical formalism and the typical paradigm of testing theories of consciousness. This issue appears for all major theories of consciousness presently proposed.
data.context: A fundamental issue with testing IIT (and other major theories) due to its formalism and testing paradigm.

data.question: A full categorical version of IIT that presents the theory in terms of a functor requires breaking with the formalism of IIT that is published in the literature, and hence is not available to date.
data.context: A complete categorical IIT is not yet available due to the need to break with existing formalism.

data.question: Integrated Information Theory and Predictive Processing are, at the present stage of development, of particular interest to mathematical consciousness science because they are the only formal theories within the Overton window of consciousness science at large.
data.context: Limited number of formal theories currently within the Overton window.

data.question: The task of improving and clarifying theories of consciousness also concerns theories which are not presented in mathematical form at the present time.
data.context: The scope of improvement/clarification extends beyond formal theories, which is a broader challenge.

data.question: The characterisation of Global Neuronal Workspace Theory (GNWT) is good enough for contemporary purposes and experimental investigations, but for the theory to properly handle consciousness in organisms and systems that differ from healthy humans, it must specify precise structures and patterns of connectivity.
data.context: GNWT's characterization is insufficient for non-standard cases (e.g., AI, different organisms) without formal specification.

data.question: Primarily, neither measures of consciousness nor C-Tests are mathematical in nature. They are based on subjective reports, objective performance or behavioural measures.
data.context: Mathematical consciousness science needs to model these formally.

data.question: What there isn't, at present, however, is a substantive theory of measurement (or measurement theory) for consciousness science that provides a foundation for measurements of the various forms.
data.context: Lack of a foundational measurement theory for consciousness science.

data.question: Some progress has already been made in regard to mathematical representation of measures and their integration with theories, albeit in unsystematic form.
data.context: Progress on mathematical representation and integration of measures is unsystematic.

data.question: Current results constitute only very initial steps, and a further exploration of all of the above-mentioned questions (regarding measurement theory) is urgently needed.
data.context: Current progress is very initial, much more work is needed.

data.question: The hallmark of a successful measurement theory, the allocation of new measurement procedures to a field, as for example the case with additive conjoint measurement (Luce & Tukey, 1964) in psychology, is still nowhere in sight.
data.context: A truly successful measurement theory for consciousness, with new procedures, is still far off.

data.question: The review of the promises of a structural turn is very limited.
data.context: The description of structural turn promises is not comprehensive.

data.question: Current structural theories (IIT, Higher Order Thought Theories, Expected Float Entropy Theory) do not yet account for the actual structure as found in psychophysical approaches and mathematical phenomenology.
data.context: Current structural theories do not yet fully account for actual psychophysical and phenomenological structures, limiting their advantages.

data.question: The assumptions presumed in (Fink et al., 2021) for a new paradigm to search for Neural Correlates of Consciousness (NCC) are not justified as general conditions on which an NCC research programme can rely.
data.context: The assumptions underlying a new paradigm for NCC research are not generally justified.

data.question: The assumption of an isomorphism between the physical and phenomenal domains, or of a structure-preserving mapping more generally, does not serve the purpose it is required to serve in this context for NCC research.
data.context: A key assumption for NCC research (isomorphism) is problematic.

data.question: The research programme outlined in (Fink et al., 2021) can only be understood as a research programme that presumes a specific class of structural theories of consciousness.
data.context: The NCC research program is limited to a specific class of structural theories.

data.question: The description of structural research in this chapter has only mentioned a small fraction of the existing work.
data.context: The description of structural research is limited.

data.question: At the present time, there is a division of labour, where philosophers are concerned with the analysis of concepts that structural claims should refer to, and mathematicians are concerned with the analysis of what structural claims mean.
data.context: Division of labor between philosophers and mathematicians on structural claims.

data.question: Knowledge about the mathematical structures of conscious experience is too limited at the present point of development to draw any thorough metaphysical conclusions.
data.context: Limited knowledge of mathematical structures of conscious experience hinders drawing thorough metaphysical conclusions.

data.question: Simple examples, like direct interpretation of what Large Language Models (LLMs) state about their own experiences, are not suitable for rigorous tests for AI consciousness.
data.context: Direct interpretation of LLM reports is not a rigorous test for AI consciousness.

data.question: The nature of Processing Units (PUs) has not received any attention in investigations of whether AIs have minds, including questions of AI consciousness, prior to the work carried out in (Kleiner & Ludwig, 2023).
data.context: Lack of attention to the nature of processing units (PUs) in AI consciousness research.

data.question: Neither of the results presented in (Kleiner & Ludwig, 2023) or (Kleiner, 2024a) attempt to provide a final answer to the question of artificial consciousness, as they both only target contemporary and near future systems.
data.context: The results do not provide a final answer to AI consciousness, as they are limited to contemporary/near-future systems.

data.question: The introduction, if it has met its goal, has done so in a hopelessly bias way. There is a host of valuable work in mathematical consciousness science that this introduction hasn't even begun to mention.

data.question: What constitutes a measurement, and what not? For example, does simple verbal report constitute a measurement? And how far can no-report paradigms be pushed while still constituting measures of consciousness?

data.question: If consciousness inference procedures are independent from a theory's prediction (which prima facie seems ideal), then for every correct inference of an experience, one can modify the part of the system that matters for consciousness to obtain a different, non-overlapping prediction while keeping the inferred state constant, making the theory false or untestable.
data.context: The ideal of independent inference procedures and the counter-intuitive result that this makes theories untestable or false.

data.question: The no-go theorem establishes that contemporary AI systems cannot be conscious, which runs counter to many intuitions but aligns with the original definition of computational functionalism by Putnam (1967).
data.context: The no-go theorem's conclusion about AI consciousness and common intuitions, while aligning with an older definition of computational functionalism.

data.question: The result that if computational functionalism were true, then contemporary and near-future AI systems (immortal computations) could not be conscious, contrary to thinking in several contemporary analyses.
data.context: The result that contemporary AI systems could not be conscious (if computational functionalism is true) and current thinking in AI consciousness analyses.

data.question: The framework provides a foundation only for specific characteristic features of consciousness: ineffability, privateness, and cognitive, linguistic, and communicative unavailability.
data.context: The framework needs to be expanded to account for other key characteristics of conscious experience.

data.question: The formalism developed requires the collatability of relations between aspects of experience.
data.context: Any non-collatable relation between experiences has to be ignored.

data.question: When attempting to ground the axioms of a Hilbert space structure for the experience space, some axioms cannot be motivated based on phenomenological observations, and certain assumptions (e.g., existence of a neutral quale and its cancellation) are beyond empirical justification.
data.context: This particular mathematical structure (Hilbert space) for the experience space may not be fully justified phenomenologically, though it can be used for 'toy models'.

data.question: The precise meaning of 'instant' (in 'conscious experience at a particular instant of time') needs to be fixed.
data.context: This is a detail that needs to be specified during the model-building process for any particular model of consciousness.

data.question: For Integrated Information Theory (IIT), the mathematical structure of its 'qualia space' (Es) needs to be motivated in more detail, specifically why elementary qualia are labeled by elements of Ps x Ps and whether this structure has a phenomenological interpretation.
data.context: This is crucial for the further development of IIT, as its algorithm makes essential use of these elements.

data.question: For the Expected Float Entropy (EFE) model, the existence or uniqueness of minimizers for the efe(R, U, p) function is not discussed in the original work.
data.context: This affects the mathematical rigor and interpretability of the relations R and U determined by the theory.

data.question: For the EFE model, it is unclear whether it is an alternative to, or a complement of, models that aim to describe qualia sensu stricto (e.g., IIT).
data.context: This affects the scope and comparative utility of the EFE model within consciousness studies.

data.question: For the EFE model, whether the relations among aspects of experience are nuanced enough to identify individual qualia (i.e., if all orbits of the automorphism group are trivial) is a phenomenological question.
data.context: This requires a systematic account of relations between qualia found in experience and is a prerequisite for model-building.

data.question: For the EFE model, identifying the weighted relations R and U between neuronal states with the manifold relations between aspects of experience is a significant challenge.
data.context: This identification is central to how the model connects brain states to conscious experience and may depend on the interpretation of probability distributions p(s) when applied to the brain.

data.question: For Conscious Agent Networks, the specific structure of the spaces W, X, and G, and the definitions of the maps P, D, and A are not fixed by the theory and must be chosen according to the application.
data.context: This requires further specification for any concrete application of the model.

data.question: For Conscious Agent Networks, it is an open question whether the model aims to address non-collatable aspects of experience.
data.context: This determines if the model needs to incorporate the symmetry requirements derived in the paper for empirical well-definedness.

data.question: For Conscious Agent Networks, it is an open question whether the theory aims to make predictions with respect to experiments involving reports of conscious agents.
data.context: This determines if the model needs to incorporate the symmetry requirements derived in the paper for empirical well-definedness.

data.question: How scientific explanation is to be defined, including basic questions about which relata a causal relation refers to and how causality is defined.
data.context: This is a fundamental philosophical question that impacts the grounding of scientific studies of consciousness, particularly in Chalmers' framework.

data.question: Expand the general mathematical framework to take other key characteristics of conscious experience (beyond ineffability, privateness, and inaccessibility) into account.

Investigate which mathematical structures are implied by other key characteristics of conscious experience, such as subjectivity and intrinsicality, and determine if mathematical structure can sufficiently account for them.

Improve the preliminary definition of irreducible subgraphs (ISGs) and the overall GNW model substantially to facilitate a full-fledged model.
Combine the GNW model with ideas from IIT or other models to provide an explicit account of how the state of the global workspace relates to experience.

For Conscious Agent Networks, define the mathematical structure of experience spaces (Xi) and disposition spaces (Gi) based on phenomenological analysis to address the objection that the model could apply to unconscious agents.
If the Conscious Agent Networks theory aims to make empirical predictions, further mathematical structure is necessary to ensure the model is empirically well-defined.
For the Expected Float Entropy (EFE) model, depending on phenomenological analysis, the model may need to be extended to address the hard problem of consciousness.

Assuming the closure of the physical (ACoP) in the phenomenological grounding implies that communication channels (physical) cannot functionally depend on conscious experience (Q), which violates a necessary condition for the scientific study of consciousness (that communication about Q can depend on Q).
data.context: The assumption of the closure of the physical and the possibility of a scientific study of consciousness.

data.question: Integrated Information Theory (IIT) describes the physical as closed, meaning the dynamical evolution of the physical domain is not changed by the theory. This raises the question of how IIT's mathematical postulates can be evaluated experimentally, as experimental data (being physical) would be determined by physical laws alone, independent of how experience arises.
data.context: IIT's postulate of physical closure and the empirical testability of its claims about consciousness.

data.question: Classical IIT 3.0 is limited to physical systems with discrete time-evolution, Markovian dynamics, and discrete sets of states.
data.context: Prevents IIT from being a fundamental theory of consciousness and requires reconciliation with present theories of physics. Limits applicability to systems like those with continuous state spaces (e.g., neuron membrane potentials) where uniform probability distributions may not exist.

data.question: The maximalization and minimalization operations (unified in the notion of core subsystems) in the IIT algorithm do not guarantee unique results in classical or quantum IIT.
data.context: Leads to ill-definedness of the algorithm's output, including the Φ value, and has a major impact on the overall results.

data.question: The contemporary definition of IIT, as well as the formalization presented in this paper, relies on there being a finite number of subsystems for each system.
data.context: This assumption might not hold true in reality, limiting the applicability of the theory to real-world systems.

data.question: How to fix the freedom in the choice of time parameter for defining cause-effect repertoires in continuous time systems.
data.context: For discrete time, neighboring time-steps are an obvious choice, but for continuous time, several choices exist (e.g., semi-derivatives, arbitrary fixed time scale, or limits), and a definitive choice is needed.

data.question: Justifying the choice of metrics used in the IIT algorithm.
data.context: The metrics are chosen arbitrarily to some extent, and different choices imply different results for the quantity and quality of experience, which is problematic. The resolution is considered a conceptual or philosophical task, requiring a justification for why a particular metric should be used, potentially by linking it to the phenomenological structure of conscious experience.

data.question: Achieving a more proper understanding of how the mathematical structure of experience spaces corresponds to the phenomenology of experience.
data.context: This includes understanding how the general definition and specific definitions (classical/quantum IIT) relate to important notions of qualia, such as ineffability, intrinsicality, non-contextuality, transparency, or homogeneity.

data.question: Extend the formalization to the infinite case by assuming every system has a fixed but potentially infinite indexing set for subsystems.

data.caption: What is an automorphism? This figure illustrates the concept of automorphisms. Automorphisms are somewhat analogous to rotations of a space around some axis (top row). More formally, an automorphism is a function that maps every point of a mathematical space to a different point of the same space, one-to-one, in such a way that all relations of the space are preserved: whenever two points are related before the mapping, they are also related after the mapping. This is illustrated by the bottom row, where individual points of the space are depicted by coloured dots, and relations are depicted by red lines. An automorphism maps every dot to a new dot, represented here by the change in location of the colours, in such a way that when two dots were related before the mapping (red line between two dots) the targets of the mapping are also related (red line between target dots). Automorphisms form a group because automorphisms can be inverted, and because any two automorphisms can be combined to form another automorphism, in this case one from the left-hand space all the way to the right-hand space. (For interpretation of the colours in the figure(s), the reader is referred to the web version of this article. Depiction of CIE colour space gamuts by Wikimedia Commons, Michael Horvath, under CC BY-SA 4.0; this image is shared under the same license.)
data.description: The figure shows two rows of diagrams illustrating automorphisms. The top row depicts two 3D color spaces (CIE color space gamuts) with arrows indicating a rotation, labeled "Automorphism". The bottom row shows two sets of colored dots connected by red lines, representing points and relations in a mathematical space. An arrow points from the left set to the right set, illustrating how an automorphism maps each dot to a new position while preserving the red-line relations between dots. The color spaces have axes labeled 0, 50, 100, 150, 210, 240, 270, 300, 330.
data.significance: This figure visually explains the concept of an automorphism, which is crucial for understanding the formal definition of structuralism and the distinction between structural and structuralist approaches in consciousness science.

data.caption: Structural vs. structuralist approaches. Structural approaches make use of mathematical spaces or mathematical structures to represent or describe conscious experiences. These spaces and structures may, and in general do, admit for automorphisms (cf. Fig. 1). This implies that there are points in the space which have the exact same relational structure. Structuralist approaches, on the other hand, assume that all points of the space can be individuated by their relational structure, meaning that no two points have the same relational structure. This can only hold true if the space does not admit automorphisms, other than the identity mapping that is always an automorphism.
data.description: The figure presents two conceptual diagrams contrasting "Structural" and "Structuralist" approaches. The "Structural" diagram shows a set of colored dots with relations (lines) and an arrow pointing to a similar set, labeled "Automorphisms". Below this, it states "Points with identical relational structure". The "Structuralist" diagram shows a set of colored dots with relations (lines) and two crossed-out arrows, labeled "No automorphisms" and "No points with identical relational structure".
data.significance: This figure clarifies the distinction between structural and structuralist approaches by illustrating how the presence or absence of automorphisms in a mathematical structure determines whether individuals can be uniquely individuated by their relational structure alone.

data.caption: What is an isomorphism? This figure illustrates the concept of isomorphisms as applied in consciousness science to link a phenomenal space or structure (left) with a physical space or structure (right). By definition, isomorphisms operate on the level of points. An isomorphism maps every point of the phenomenal space to a point in the physical space. It does so in such a way that the relations between points (indicated here by red lines) are preserved, meaning that any two points which are related on the left are related in the exact same way on the right. The mapping also needs to be invertible. An isomorphism presupposes that structures on both sides of the mapping are given. It does not define, or pick out, the structure in its target domain, which is why it is not a suitable mathematical object to explain, predict, or define phenomenal structure in terms of physical structure. (Depiction of CIE colour space gamut by Wikimedia Commons, Michael Horvath, under CC BY-SA 4.0; this image, excluding the drawing of the brain, is shared under the same license. Drawing of the human brain from Freepik.)
data.description: The figure illustrates an isomorphism between a "Phenomenal Space/Structure" (left) and a "Physical Space/Structure" (right). The phenomenal space is represented by a 3D CIE color space gamut with axes labeled 0, 50, 100, 150, 200, 270, 300, 330, 340. The physical space is represented by a stylized human brain. An arrow labeled "Isomorphism" connects the two, showing how points and their red-line relations in the phenomenal space are mapped to points and relations in the physical space, preserving the structure.
data.significance: This figure visually defines an isomorphism as a structure-preserving mapping between phenomenal and physical domains, highlighting its role in consciousness science for relating conscious experiences to physical brain states.

data.caption: Different definitions imply different spaces. Mathematical spaces and mathematical structures are tools to describe or represent phenomenal character, much like technical language terms are too. Different definitions or conventions of how to use mathematical terms to describe or represent phenomenal character-different conventions of what terms like 'mathematical structure of conscious experience' or 'phenomenal space' mean-lead to different structural representations of the same set of experiences, here illustrated by three different CIE colour spaces. Black arrows indicate different definitions or conventions, which imply different methodologies for constructing phenomenal spaces in the lab. Different geometrical shapes indicate different types of spaces that result from applying these methodologies. Much like technical language terms might differ in scope, quality, adequacy, and presuppositions, definitions or conventions regarding mathematical structures differ in scope, quality, adequacy and presuppositions. (Depiction of CIE colour space gamuts by Wikimedia Commons, Michael Horvath, under CC BY-SA 4.0; this image is shared under the same license.)
data.description: The figure shows three distinct 3D CIE color space gamuts, each representing a "Phenomenal Character". Each gamut is depicted with different geometrical shapes (sphere, cone, irregular blob) and orientations, implying different structural representations of the same set of experiences. Black arrows point from a central conceptual label "Phenomenal Character" to each of the three distinct color spaces, indicating that different definitions or conventions lead to different structural representations.
data.significance: This figure illustrates that the choice of methodology and definitions for "phenomenal structure" directly impacts the resulting mathematical representation of conscious experience, emphasizing the need for clarity in defining phenomenal structure in structural research.

data.caption: How to define phenomenal spaces? This figure illustrates how to define phenomenal spaces and other mathematical structures of conscious experience. One starts out with a choice of qualities (bottom left), for example colour qualities, sometimes also called qualia or conceptualised as instantiated phenomenal properties. The qualities form a set that constitutes the points of the phenomenal space (bottom right). Every experience comprises a subset of qualities, and as experiences change from one experience to the next, the subset of qualities that is realised varies (top left). These variations can be understood as mappings from the set of qualities to itself, and therefore have the same formal structure as automorphisms (Fig. 1): mappings from the points of a space to other points of the space (top right). This allows for the following simple definition of phenomenal structure: phenomenal structure is that mathematical structure whose automorphisms are identical to the variations of the qualities as experiences change. Put differently, phenomenal structure (indicated here by red lines) is that mathematical structure which renders the statement true: the variations of (qualities of) conscious experiences are the automorphisms of the structure (top centre). For details, cf. (Kleiner & Ludwig, 2023). (Depiction of CIE colour space gamuts by Wikimedia Commons, Michael Horvath, under CC BY-SA 4.0; this image is shared under the same license.)
data.description: The figure presents a flowchart-like diagram explaining how phenomenal spaces are defined. It starts with "Qualities" (bottom left), represented by a set of colored dots. An arrow points to "Mathematical Set" (bottom right), showing the qualities forming a set of points. Another path starts with "Variations" (top left), also a set of colored dots, leading to "Variations of conscious experiences = Automorphisms of structure" (top center), which then points to "Automorphisms" (top right), a set of colored dots with relations. Red lines indicate the structure. The overall diagram illustrates how variations of conscious experiences, understood as automorphisms, define the mathematical structure of phenomenal spaces.
data.significance: This figure outlines a methodology for defining phenomenal spaces by linking the variations of conscious experiences to the automorphisms of a mathematical structure, providing a concrete approach to constructing structural representations of consciousness.

data.caption: An Integrated Information Theory specifies for every system in a particular state its conscious experience, described formally as an element of an experience space. In our formalization, this is a map Sys → Exp from the system class Sys into a class Exp of experience spaces, which, first, sends each system S to its space of possible experiences E(S), and, second, sends each state s ∈ St(S) to the actual experience the system is having when in that space, St(S) → E(S) s ↦ E(S, s). The definition of this map in terms of axiomatic descriptions of physical systems, experience spaces and further structure used in classical IIT is given in the first half of this paper.
data.description: The diagram illustrates the high-level structure of an Integrated Information Theory (IIT). It shows two boxes: 'Physical systems and states' and 'Spaces and states of conscious experience'. An arrow labeled 'E' connects 'Physical systems and states' to 'Spaces and states of conscious experience'. Below the boxes, a mathematical mapping `Sys → Exp` is described, where `Sys` is a class of systems, `Exp` is a class of experience spaces. It further details that each system `S` maps to `E(S)` (space of possible experiences) and each state `s ∈ St(S)` maps to `E(S, s)` (actual experience).
data.significance: This figure provides a high-level conceptual overview of how an Integrated Information Theory maps physical systems and their states to conscious experiences, setting the stage for the formal mathematical definitions presented in the paper.

data.caption: To help explain the example of relative similarity, this figure illustrates experiences with color qualities and variations thereof. Subfigure A illustrates an experience of three color chips as well as the concept of relative similarity: many readers will experience the color of the top-left color chip to be less similar to the reference chip than the color of the top-right color chip. Subfigure B illustrates our notation for the color aspects corresponding to the color chips. Subfigures C and D illustrate variations v of experiences: a swap of two color aspects in C; and a replacement of two color aspects in D.
data.description: The figure consists of four subfigures (A, B, C, D) illustrating color chip experiences and variations. Subfigure A shows three circular color chips: a yellow reference chip at the bottom, a light blue chip (top-left), and a darker blue chip (top-right). Subfigure B labels these chips as 'b0' (reference), 'b1' (top-left), and 'b2' (top-right), establishing notation for color aspects. Subfigure C demonstrates a variation 'v' where the positions of 'b1' and 'b2' are swapped, showing the light blue chip on the right and the darker blue on the left after the variation. Subfigure D illustrates another variation 'v' where 'b1' and 'b2' are replaced by new color aspects, 'b3' (green) and 'b4' (yellow), in their respective positions.
data.significance: This figure provides a visual and conceptual foundation for understanding relative similarity as a structural aspect of conscious experience. It concretely illustrates how 'color qualities' and 'variations' are represented, which is essential for applying the paper's proposed definition of a Mathematical Structure of Conscious Experience (MSC) to the example of a strict partial order.
