Develop approximate, probabilistic, finite-horizon, or coarse-grained versions of the canonical quotient for real-world empirical applications.

data.claim: Current deep learning systems face increasing demands for speed and resources, leading to environmental compromise.
data.support: General statement about the state of the art in deep learning.

data.claim: A future computing paradigm will involve systems that synthesize new deep networks, invent learning protocols without training, and feature novel data structures, software/circuit-free, fully analog, and adaptive reusable hardware.
data.support: Visionary statement for the next revolution in computing.

data.claim: The organic nested deep learning network (ON²) executes an entire self-learning theory step-by-step in a chemical beaker, utilizing the optimization power of supramolecular synthesis.
data.support: The entire paper describes the design, implementation, and operation of the ON² system.

data.claim: The ON² system achieves almost instant optimization, irrespective of complexity, by encoding computational choices into molecules that collide to explore 10^9 options per second.
data.support: Description of molecular self-assembly dynamics and its role in rapid optimization.

data.claim: A novel language encodes problems as geometric shapes for chemical reactions, enabling data regeneration by assembling discrete clocks in a 3D space, inspired by protein and neuron clock-assemblies.
data.support: Introduction of the data structure (R³ : (x, z) → (φ1,φ2,φ3)) and its function in encoding problems.

data.claim: Supramolecular synthesis in the ON² system learns invariants to regenerate input, enabling fully unsupervised learning without explicit training.
data.support: Explanation of how spontaneous self-assembly determines network structure and constructs solution paths.

data.claim: The ON² system operates via a push-pull loop between field-based (CAf) and matter-based (CAm) clock-structures, synthesizing at least four layers of hierarchical architectures that form the network's neurons.
data.support: Detailed description of the CAf/CAm interaction, resonance minimization, and multi-layer synthesis.

data.claim: Three nested deep learning networks (Ø1-Ø2-Ø3) continuously convolute each other's clock-assembly/neuron-nodes, optimizing invariant trees using a common Hamiltonian and higher-dimensional multinions as activation functions.
data.support: Description of the nested network architecture and its operational principles.

data.claim: The gel computer's operation is a version of a classic Turing machine, where a single nanowire acts as a TM and the nanowire assembly functions as a Universal Turing Machine (UTM).
data.support: Reference to Table T1 and Appendix for detailed mapping of system components to TM/UTM criteria.

data.claim: The gel processor can generate complex geometric shapes using a Geometric musical language (GML), which logarithmically reduces resource demand with increasing information complexity, unlike conventional computers.
data.support: Description of GML's capabilities and its efficiency advantage over O^n complexity in digital processing.

data.claim: The ON² system can identify one of 10^7–10^34 possible choices within a four-layer deep learning network for almost all problems.
data.support: Calculations of variations and implied performance from constant processing times.

data.claim: Pre-processing, processing, and post-processing times are constant (~2 ms, ~10-15 min, ~2 ms respectively) for all problems, irrespective of their complexity.
data.support: Reference to movie S1 and Table T1.

data.claim: A 3D printer feeds input data as electromagnetic frequencies into a chemical beaker, creating intertwined isofrequency loops that condense into a gel superstructure, which then emits phase-correlated electromagnetic signals as a 3D clock assembly.
data.support: Description of the 3D printer, antenna array, cavity, and the self-assembly process (figure 2(A), movie S2, online text A).

data.claim: The gelator molecules absorb energy to optimize nanowire and seed structures, encoding recurring events as angular momentums and polarity on optical vortices, which condense into an integrated hologram for data retrieval and analysis.
data.support: Description of the energy absorption, structure optimization, and information encoding via optical vortices (figure S1, figures S2, S3).

data.claim: The ON² system demonstrates the detection of various invariances (position, rotation, size, count, environment) as part of general-purpose computing.
data.support: Demonstrations using Cheetah video (movie S5) and other general-purpose computing tasks (movie S6).

data.claim: The gel computer operates with thermal energy (~13 Cal) but requires continuous 10–15 nW electromagnetic signals for input data.
data.support: Stated energy requirements for computation.

data.claim: The gel encodes vast temporal and spatial ranges by tuning nanowire geometry and seeds, rendering traditional concepts of scalability, resources, and speed redundant for gel computing.
data.support: Explanation of how spatio-temporal density determines computing strength (figure 2(C)).

data.claim: The gel emulates complex spatio-temporal relations using a coupling factor and fractal growth, which shrinks real-world space and time by a power law.
data.support: Description of the coupling factor and power law for fractal growth (figure 2(D)).

data.claim: The system performs three transitions (filter, memorize point, line, plane, and 3D shapes) of clocks, which are abstract geometric manifolds of resonance frequencies and invariants, equivalent to orthogonal transformations of two tensors.
data.support: Description of the transitions and their nature as invariants (movies S7-S12, figures S6-S16, Table T1).

data.claim: The ON² system is a geometric deep network that extracts differential clocks in orthogonal space, analogous to finding a common sphere between overlapping clocks, with the number of self-assembly layers depending on input clock-assembly symmetries.
data.support: Analogy to geometric deep networks and explanation of layer dependence on symmetry.

data.claim: The system can amplify electromagnetic beating signals and orthogonally project holograms (4D, 5D, 6D) to isolate and retain only the invariant parts as static structures.
data.support: Description of using antennas, ac signals, and orthogonal projection (figures 3(C), 3(D)).

data.claim: Gel superstructures resonantly activate geometrically similar peaks, enabling the creation of new invariants and classifiers for unknown problems, a capability distinct from existing AIs that select from predefined databases.
data.support: Comparison with existing AIs and reference to figures 2(D), 1(C).

data.claim: A gel, once trained by a single-shot video, can classify unknown events naturally for different inputs, or allow user-chosen classifiers, by synthesizing new invariants or clock assemblies from memorized ones.
data.support: Demonstration with Cheetah video and other animal videos (figure 4(A), movie S6, figure 4(B)).

data.claim: The gel naturally labels objects, classes, and invariants, stores information for decades without refreshing, and is reusable (can be melted and reused for all problems).
data.support: Reference to online tables T2-T8 and direct statements about storage and reusability.

data.claim: Multiple problems can be solved simultaneously in one gel with a single-shot training due to its fractal deep learning architecture where neural net layers grow within and above, enabling parallelism.
data.support: Description of fractal deep learning and its implications for concurrent problem-solving.

data.claim: The gel system satisfies the criteria for a Universal Turing Machine (UTM) by mapping its components and operations to TM tape, cell states, read/write functions, memory, instruction sequences, loop counting, and Boolean algorithms.
data.support: Detailed explanation in the Appendix, including how vortex polarization encodes Boolean codes and phase singularity points count loops (figure S13).

data.claim: The fundamental principles of molecular self-assembly and resonance can be reliably controlled and harnessed for complex computational tasks.
The proposed mapping between molecular structures/dynamics and abstract computational concepts (e.g., clocks, neurons, Turing machine components) is valid and functionally equivalent.
The 'Geometric musical language' (GML) provides a robust and efficient means of encoding and processing information in a chemical system.
The ability to remotely control and read out the chemical processes via microwave input and optical holograms is effective and accurate.

data.caption: Survey respondents vs. thin/heavy tailed simulations – three scenarios.
data.description: Three rank-ordered line charts, each comparing the distribution of the ratio of most to second most pleasurable experience from survey respondents (red dots) against simulations derived from a normal distribution (blue dots) and a lognormal distribution (green dots). The three scenarios represent different numbers of experiences sampled per simulated individual: 1000, 100, and 10. The x-axis represents rank-ordered extrema ratios [1-77 individuals], and the y-axis represents the ratio of most to second most pleasurable experience (normalized 0-1).
data.key_data: For 1000 experiences sampled, the lognormal-derived simulations (green) closely track the survey respondents (red) data points, especially at higher extrema ratios.; For 100 experiences sampled, the lognormal-derived simulations (green) show a better fit to survey respondents (red) than normal-derived simulations (blue).; For 10 experiences sampled, the lognormal-derived simulations (green) still provide a better fit to survey respondents (red) than normal-derived simulations (blue).
data.significance: This figure provides indirect evidence for the HTV hypothesis by demonstrating that the observed distribution of intensity ratios from survey respondents aligns better with a heavy-tailed (lognormal) underlying distribution of experiences than with a narrow-tailed (normal) distribution, suggesting that extreme experiences are more frequent and accessible than typically assumed.

data.caption: Described vs inferred ratios: Pain questions.
data.description: A scatter plot comparing the 'Ratio of most to second most extreme as described' (x-axis, capped at 10 for graph legibility) against the 'Ratio of most to second most extreme as implied by scalar scores on 0-10 scores' (y-axis) for pain questions (n=65). A 'Line of equality' is drawn, and points to the right of this line indicate that respondents described their most extreme experience as more intense than implied by their 0-10 scalar scores if interpreted cardinally.
data.key_data: X-axis (described ratio) ranges from 1 to 10 (capped).; Y-axis (implied ratio) ranges from 1.0 to 3.0.; The majority of data points (blue dots) are located to the right of the 'Line of equality', indicating that described ratios are generally higher than inferred ratios.
data.significance: This figure provides strong evidence that respondents perceive a greater intensity difference between their most and second most extreme pain experiences than a cardinal interpretation of the 0-10 scale would suggest, supporting the idea of a 'kinked' scale and the HTV hypothesis.

data.caption: Described vs. inferred ratios: pleasure questions.
data.description: A scatter plot comparing the 'Ratio of most to second most extreme as described' (x-axis, capped at 10 for graph legibility) against the 'Ratio of most to second most extreme as implied by scalar scores on 0-10 scores' (y-axis) for pleasure questions (n=64). A 'Line of equality' is drawn, and points to the right of this line indicate that respondents described their most extreme experience as more intense than implied by their 0-10 scalar scores if interpreted cardinally.
data.key_data: X-axis (described ratio) ranges from 1 to 10 (capped).; Y-axis (implied ratio) ranges from 1.0 to 3.0.; The majority of data points (blue dots) are located to the right of the 'Line of equality', indicating that described ratios are generally higher than inferred ratios.
data.significance: Similar to Figure 2, this figure provides strong evidence that respondents perceive a greater intensity difference between their most and second most extreme pleasure experiences than a cardinal interpretation of the 0-10 scale would suggest, further supporting the 'kinked' scale and the HTV hypothesis.

data.claim: A specific molecule (PCMS) has been designed and synthesized, wherein input energy transmits in a cycle, functioning as a molecular oscillator.
data.support: Description of the molecular design incorporating a dendrimer matrix, pH sensor, molecular rotor, and electromagnetic switch, along with the detailed synthesis protocol for PCMS (Fig. 1c, Methods section).

data.claim: The synthesized PCMS molecule forms a jelly that acts as a chain of oscillators, exhibiting a fractal-like resonance band with an infinite number of discrete, theoretically predictable energy levels.
data.support: Figure 1d illustrates the fractal resonance band, theoretical calculations (Methods) suggest a fractal distribution of energy levels in linear oscillator chains, CEES plots (Fig. 2a-f) show peaks moving along a line with pH/density changes, and Movie 5 demonstrates the fractal energy level distribution.

data.claim: The PCMS system exhibits a specific triangular energy transmission path (S→C→M) that is universal and blocks other energy transmission routes.
data.support: CEES plots (Fig. 2a-f) show sequential brightening of S, C, and M peaks, Movie 4 demonstrates the triangular energy transmission path, and theoretical tracking of the path mimics pH/density variation (Fig. 2h).

data.claim: The observed regularity in intensity variation of the PCMS system, as a function of pH and density, provides the foundation for designing a logic gate.
data.support: Observation of peaks moving along a line in Fig. 2h, demonstrating non-random and regular changes in intensity variation.

data.claim: By correlating the energy levels of the organic jelly's resonance band with pH and density, a logic gate with an infinite truth table is realized, allowing for indefinite zooming into any part of the truth table to reveal new truth tables.
data.support: Construction of a two-input, three-output logic gate truth table (Fig. 3c), demonstration of detecting 14 movement steps with low-resolution sensors (Fig. 3a,b), and the capability to zoom 10^6 times with high-resolution sensors (Keithley 6430), supported by theoretical explanation of fractal spectrum from nested oscillators (Methods summary).

data.claim: The PCMS molecules exhibit adaptive behavior, where input conditions spontaneously reflect in changed path dynamics, resembling chaotic computing where dynamics are encoded in the input arrangement.
data.support: SEM observations of spontaneous molecular motions (Fig. 4a, Movie 6), adopted paths changing with input arrangement, and random motions following well-defined geometric paths with increasing PCMS (Fig. 4b).

data.claim: The system maintains a constant period or time cycle even under random PCMS motions and restores its energy transmission rhythm under noise, enabling it to sustain a defined geometric path and logical fluorescence output with high resolution.
data.support: Observations of constant rhythm, noise restoration, sustained geometric path, and high resolution withstanding capability.

data.claim: The unprecedented resolution of the system embeds memory and facilitates 'instantaneous decision-making' by allowing zooming into operational matrices to store astronomically large data.
data.support: Conceptual explanation of the zooming capability (e.g., converting a 10x10 pH-density matrix into a 1000x1000 one) and its implications for data storage and decision-making based on the time cycle of the smallest matrix.

data.claim: Current silicon-based logic gates and miniaturization approaches are reaching their fundamental limits, necessitating radical new computing paradigms.
An 'infinite logic' principle, replacing discrete bits with a continuum, is critically demanded for true adaptive logic and chemical computing.
The theoretical understanding of fractal distribution of energy levels in linear oscillators provides a valid basis for designing new materials.
The ability to measure energy levels with increasingly higher resolution is achievable and practical for realizing infinite state accessibility in a logic gate.

data.caption: Examples of hyperbolic space: a saddle surface, a cube in H3, and a dodecahedron tiling H3.
data.description: Three visual examples illustrating hyperbolic geometry, as described in the text. The first is a 2-dimensional 'saddle' surface (left image) with negative curvature. The second is a cube embedded in 3-dimensional hyperbolic space (H3) (middle image) with thin edges and pointy corners. The third is a dodecahedron with right-angled corners, tiling H3 (right image).
data.significance: This figure visually introduces and explains the concept of hyperbolic geometry, which is fundamental to the paper's hypothesis about the geometry of DMT experiences.

data.caption: Examples of psychedelic visuals experienced by researcher A on various substances, illustrating different symmetry groups.
data.description: A set of images showing visual patterns experienced by a psychonaut (researcher A) under the influence of 2C-B, LSD, 4-HO-MET, and DMT. The visuals are described as exhibiting various 2-dimensional wallpaper symmetry groups and spherical symmetry groups. The text mentions 'top left', 'top middle', and 'the rest' implying multiple distinct visual examples.
data.significance: These visuals support the claim that psychedelic experiences, particularly DMT at the Chrysanthemum level, involve complex symmetrical patterns and can instantiate various wallpaper and spherical symmetry groups, linking phenomenology to mathematical structures.

data.caption: Examples of Magic Eye level scenes: a lobster, a cone, and furniture.
data.description: Three visual examples representing scenes experienced at the Magic Eye level of a DMT trip. These include a lobster (left image), a cone (center image), and a collection of furniture (a lamp, a chair, and a table) (right image). The objects are described as being patterned with the 'Chrysanthemum' texture, contorted to accommodate the scene's curvature, similar to autostereograms.
data.significance: These figures illustrate the types of objects and scenes encountered at the Magic Eye level, demonstrating how the Chrysanthemum texture integrates with 3D geometrical shapes in a hyper-curved phenomenal space.

data.caption: Impressionistic replication of a Waiting Room experience, showing a textured world-sheet with an entity and the evolving micro-structure of the texture.
data.description: A set of images providing a visual interpretation of a DMT Waiting Room experience. The left image depicts an enclosed room with shimmering walls and an entity looking at a futuristic contraption. The images on the right illustrate the dynamic evolution of the world-sheet's texture, showing its micro-structure constantly unfolding in new symmetrical ways (bottom right), and propagating changes at high speed (top right).
data.significance: These images provide a visual interpretation of the Waiting Room level of DMT experience, highlighting the complex, dynamic, and textured nature of the perceived environment and entities, and the high degree of curvature.

data.caption: Examples of 'impossible objects' experienced on DMT, sourced from Paul Nylander and Robert Fathauer.
data.description: Visual representations of highly curved, complex, and interlocking geometric objects, referred to as 'DMT Object 1, 2, 3, 5' (from Paul Nylander) and 'DMT Object 8' (from Robert Fathauer). These objects are described as 'truly impossible objects' that are difficult or impossible to represent in normal reality, often having many saddles.
data.significance: These objects exemplify the 'truly impossible objects' that emerge at higher DMT levels (Waiting Room and Breakthrough), demonstrating the extreme curvature and non-Euclidean geometry of these states that challenge Euclidean representation.

data.caption: Example of a 'self-dribbling basketball' as an impossible object.
data.description: A visual representation of a 'self-dribbling basketball,' an object described as becoming more curved the more one tries to 'grasp' it. This illustrates constant 'context switches' resulting from excess curvature being pushed towards the edge of experience and turning into walls and corridors.
data.significance: This figure serves as a concrete example of an 'impossible object' that cannot be stabilized in Euclidean space, further supporting the paper's argument about the hyperbolic geometry of DMT experiences and the difficulty of integrating them due to dynamic curvature.

data.claim: An assembly of DDQ molecular switches can be built to function as a massively parallel cellular automaton, where each molecule communicates with multiple neighbors simultaneously.
data.support: Description of DDQ molecule properties (Fig. 1a, 1c), STM-based writing and reading of four conducting states (Fig. 1b, 1d), and observation of molecular circuits with varying neighborhood sizes (Fig. 1e, 1f, 1g).

data.claim: The molecular assembly can spontaneously reconfigure its hardware (circuit-domains) based on the input pattern's charge density, enabling dynamic adaptation to new problems.
data.support: Observation that excess electron concentration dictates DDQ re-orientation into specific circuit types (Fig. 1f, 1g, Movie 3), and the correlation between input pattern, transformed circuit, and logic state transport rules.

data.claim: The molecular assembly exhibits seven distinct logic-state transport rules that govern the movement and transformation of information (states 1s and 3s).
data.support: Detailed description of Rule 1 (Convergent Universe, Movie 4), Rule 2 (spatial/temporal limits, Fig. 2, SI d), Rule 3 (Divergent Universe), Rule 4 (Life of logic states), Rule 5 (Collapse of space), Rule 6 (Transformation), and Rule 7 (Priority of Rules, Figs. 2, 4, SI h).

data.claim: The molecular CA can perform fundamental computing operations including writing, erasing, retrieving information, directed information propagation, and realizing an AND logic gate.
data.support: Demonstration of sequential writing, static storage, and erasure (Fig. 3a), simulation and experimental transport of information packets (Fig. 3b), and the realization of an AND gate based on Rule 1 and Rule 3 interactions (Fig. 3c, 3d).

data.claim: The molecular CA can perform density classification and Voronoi decomposition, demonstrating its ability to categorize information and segment computational space.
data.support: Categorization into 8 circuit classes based on charge density (Fig. 4a, 4b), spontaneous classification of density distributions into distinct circuit domains (Fig. 4c), and the formation of linear borders between circuit domains resembling Voronoi cells (Fig. 1e, 4d).

data.claim: The molecular CA can mimic complex natural phenomena, specifically electron diffusion and the evolution of cancer cells, by tuning input patterns and CA rules.
data.support: Demonstration of electron transport following diffusion features, with a calculated diffusion coefficient (Fig. 5a, 5b, 5c, Movie 5), and emulation of cancer cell mutation dynamics, showing N3 (cancer cells) dependence on cell population N and distinct kinetic behaviors (Fig. 6a, 6b, 6c, Movie 5).

data.claim: The molecular assembly processes information in parallel at hundreds of sites simultaneously and offers significantly faster computation for certain natural phenomena compared to their biological counterparts.
data.support: Observation of Rules executed at ~300 DDQ sites simultaneously (reference 18), and comparison of mutation/diffusion speeds in the assembly versus natural systems (e.g., ~600 cells mutate in 6 minutes vs. 10^9 cells in 100 years).

data.claim: The four distinct conducting states of the DDQ molecule (0, 1, 2, 3) are stable and reliably represent logical states.
The STM tip's physical manipulation and bias application precisely control the molecular states and interactions as intended for computational encoding and rule execution.
The definition of a 'wire' based on tunneling current between DDQs accurately reflects a functional connection for information transfer.
The observed reconfigurations and pattern evolutions are deterministic and controllable enough to be considered computational processes, not just random physical fluctuations.
The analogies drawn between molecular behavior and biological processes (neurons, cancer cell mutation, diffusion) are valid for demonstrating the system's computational potential.
The simulator used to model the CA rules and patterns accurately reflects the underlying molecular physics and experimental observations.

data.caption: Core takeaways of affective neuroscience on valence
data.description: A two-column table summarizing common views of valence and why these views are not perfect descriptions. The left column, 'Valence is often:', lists five common views: how the brain represents value, a result of getting what we want, involved with reinforcement learning, proximately caused by opioids, and proximately caused by certain brain regions. The right column, 'but this isn't a perfect description, since:', provides counter-arguments for each view, such as 'It's only a correlation, and 'value' is a fuzzy abstraction' or 'Injection of opioids into key regions doesn't always cause pleasure'.
data.key_data: Valence is often: How the brain represents value; but this isn't a perfect description, since: It's only a correlation, and 'value' is a fuzzy abstraction; Valence is often: A result of getting what we want; but this isn't a perfect description, since: 'Liking' and 'wanting' are handled by different brain systems; Valence is often: Involved with reinforcement learning; but this isn't a perfect description, since: 'Liking' and 'learning' are handled by different brain systems; Valence is often: Proximately caused by opioids; but this isn't a perfect description, since: Injection of opioids into key regions doesn't always cause pleasure; Valence is often: Proximately caused by certain brain regions; but this isn't a perfect description, since: Activity in these regions doesn't always cause pleasure
data.significance: This figure critically summarizes the current understanding of valence in affective neuroscience, highlighting the limitations and complexities that necessitate a new theoretical approach like the one proposed in the paper.

data.caption: Factorizing the problem of consciousness
data.description: A flowchart illustrating a three-task process for a rigorous 'theory of consciousness'. It begins with three main tasks: 'Task 1: Abstraction', 'Task 2: Restructuring', and 'Task 3: Interpretation', each with a brief description. Below these tasks, four interconnected boxes represent the stages of formalizing consciousness: 'Physical system' (neurons, synapses, etc.), 'Logical Diagram' (abstracted physical processes), 'Mathematical Object' (reorganized logical system, shown with a small graph and a 3D plot), and 'Meaning' (human-level facts about qualia). Arrows indicate the progression from physical system to meaning through these tasks.
data.significance: This figure provides a conceptual framework for how to approach the 'problem of consciousness' by breaking it down into distinct, manageable tasks, which is essential for developing and interpreting an information geometry of mind.

data.caption: Requirements for an elegant formalism for valence
data.description: A Venn-like diagram with two overlapping circles, representing 'Qualia Formalism' and 'Valence Realism'. Each circle is associated with two descriptive text boxes. 'Qualia Formalism' includes 'Qualia Formalism: For any conscious experience, there exists a mathematical object isomorphic to it.' and 'Qualia Structuralism: The mathematical object isomorphic to a conscious experience has a rich set of mathematical structures.' 'Valence Realism' includes 'Valence Realism: Valence (subjective pleasantness) is a well-defined and ordered property of conscious systems.' and 'Valence Structuralism: Valence has a simple encoding in the mathematical representation of a system's qualia.'
data.significance: This figure visually outlines the foundational assumptions and properties required for an elegant and robust formal theory of valence, establishing the theoretical ground for the Symmetry Theory of Valence.

data.caption: Symmetry Theories
data.description: A three-column table comparing three symmetry theories: Symmetry Theory of Valence (STV), Symmetry Theory of Homeostatic Regulation (STHR), and Symmetry Theory of Aesthetics (STA). Each column lists a core statement for the respective theory and its proposed ontological status (e.g., 'Law of the universe; exactly true in all conscious systems' or 'Contingent fact (aliens or AIs could work differently)').
data.key_data: Symmetry Theory of Valence (STV): Symmetry in the mathematical representation of an experience corresponds to its pleasure; Law of the universe; exactly true in all conscious systems; Symmetry Theory of Homeostatic Regulation (STHR): The brain's primary attractor is symmetry, and symmetry gradients in brain networks are coupled to homeostatic requirements; Contingent fact (aliens or AIs could work differently); Symmetry Theory of Aesthetics (STA): Symmetry is a core factor in what we find beautiful because symmetry in stimuli often translates to symmetry in internal networks; Contingent fact (aliens or AIs could work differently)
data.significance: This table clearly differentiates between the proposed symmetry theories, clarifying their distinct claims and their relationship to fundamental laws versus contingent biological facts, which is crucial for understanding the paper's overall theoretical ecosystem.

data.claim: Controllable ion migration is achieved by dynamically regulating asymmetric electrical double layer formation, leading to the development of triboiontronics.
data.support: The mechanism is illustrated in Fig. 1a-d, showing how asymmetric EDL formation creates an ion concentration gradient and drives ionic current.

data.claim: A direct-current triboiontronic nanogenerator (PDC-TING) is developed by dynamically managing asymmetric EDL formation between dielectric substrates and liquids.
data.support: Comparison of output performance with conventional TENGs (Fig. 1f, g), showing DC output (0.97 µA) for PDC-TING compared to AC or weaker signals for TENGs.

data.claim: The PDC-TING produces a transferred charge density of 412.54 mC/m² and a peak power density of 8.45 W/m², significantly exceeding current hydrovoltaic technology and conventional triboelectric nanogenerators.
data.support: Quantitative measurements presented in Fig. 3f, g, h, and comparison data in Fig. 4f.

data.claim: The extent and direction of asymmetry in electrical double layer (EDL) formation play a crucial role in determining the efficacy and direction of ion migration, thereby influencing the PDC-TING output.
data.support: Experiments with different pre-moistening methods for Au/PET layers, showing varying Isc values (e.g., 0.97 µA for pristine, 8.20 µA for bottom pre-moistened, -2.75 µA for top pre-moistened) in Fig. 1h and Supplementary Fig. 6.

data.claim: Adjusting the metal sputtering time on the dielectric substrate controls the coverage of the charge-collecting layer, affecting its conductivity and the contact electrification (CE) properties, which in turn forms diverse EDLs.
data.support: Experiments showing the effect of Au sputtering time on PDC-TING output (Fig. 1i, j), internal resistance, microscopic crack observations (Supplementary Fig. 11), and surface potential measurements (Fig. 2c, d, e).

data.claim: Specific EDL models can be developed for dielectric, pure metal, and dielectric-sputtered-metal surfaces, with the latter (sputtered metal on dielectric) being crucial for effective ion flux in PDC-TING.
data.support: Conceptual models in Fig. 2f, g, h, supported by experimental CE data (Fig. 2c, d, e) showing different charge densities and polarities for various surfaces.

data.claim: The PDC-TING output can be significantly enhanced by regulating electrostatic fields, increasing surface hydrophilicity via plasma treatment, and increasing ion concentration in the liquid.
data.support: Experiments showing increased Isc with positive electrostatic fields (Fig. 3b), plasma treatment (Fig. 3d), and higher LiCl concentrations (Fig. 3e).

data.claim: Modifying the charge-collecting layer to enable redox reactions, in synergy with dynamically controlled EDL formation, significantly enhances the efficiency of the triboiontronics (SDC-TING).
data.support: Mechanism illustrated in Fig. 4a, verification experiment in Fig. 4b, redox equations (1) and (2), cyclic voltammetry (Supplementary Fig. 31), and theoretical explanation using Gibbs free energy and Nernst equation (Eq. 3-6).

data.claim: The SDC-TING achieves a peak power density of 38.64 W/m² and a transferred charge density of 540.70 mC/m², representing a substantial increase compared to systems relying solely on redox reactions or PDC-TING.
data.support: Quantitative measurements in Fig. 4c, d, e, and comparative analysis in Supplementary Fig. 33, showing 435.35% and 2869.23% increases.

data.claim: The SDC-TING can function as an integrated energy harvesting and storage device and has potential applications in human-computer interaction and neuromorphic computing by mimicking bionic neurologic circuits.
data.support: Demonstration of charging a 1mF capacitor (Fig. 4g), conceptual power management system (Fig. 4h), and ion regulation for bionic neurologic circuits (Fig. 4i).

data.claim: The validity of the two-step electrical double layer (EDL) model for insulating dielectric-liquid interfaces.
The fundamental principles of contact electrification (CE) and electrostatic induction.
The established electrochemical principles governing redox reactions, Gibbs free energy, and the Nernst equation.
The ability of iontronics to enhance charge transport and information flow compared to electronics.

data.caption: Hippocampal neuron membrane potential was measured using a patch clamp on a culture plate, and simultaneously, an atomic sharp needle was inserted deep inside the axon of that neuron. The experimental details and explanation of the study can be found in our previous paper (Figure 4a of Ghosh et al., 2016); we had previously published this plot in a different format. The red plot depicts the nerve impulse measured by a Patch Clamp and black plot is the signal generated by filament assembly, simultaneously.
data.description: A line chart showing Potential (mV) on the y-axis against Time (ms) on the x-axis. Two lines are plotted: 'Patch Clamp-membrane' (red) representing nerve impulse and 'Coaxial probe-axon filament' (black) representing signal generated by filament assembly. Both lines display pulse trains with similar morphology over a 4 ms duration.
data.key_data: Patch Clamp-membrane: Peak potential ~40 mV, pulse width ~0.5 ms, period ~1 ms.; Coaxial probe-axon filament: Peak potential ~20 mV, pulse width ~0.5 ms, period ~1 ms.; Time range: 0-4 ms.; Potential range: -20 to 50 mV.
data.significance: This figure provides experimental evidence of MHz bursts from a single neuron's neurofilament bundle, showing a striking similarity in pulse characteristics to the brain signals observed in anesthetized patients, supporting the hypothesis that microtubules are the source of these MHz signals.

data.caption: We have zoomed in twice on the filamentary bursts observed in Figure 1. Using the SMA probe, which we touched on the forehead of a patient under anesthesia with a BIS value of around 40-50, we found a burst in the spectrum analyzer's range of 6MHz to 26MHz. We have zoomed one pulse to its right. We find that the pulse widths are the same for both cases. More than 20 different culture plates we studied in 5 separate batches, we always observed the 55-60kHz bursts from neurofilaments. For all 40 patients studied, we observed 58-64kHz bursts from the forehead of anesthetic patients.
data.description: Two line charts, (a) and (b), displaying pulse trains. Chart (a) shows 'Potential (mV)' vs 'Time (ms)' for a filament inside a single axon when a neuron fires, with a zoomed-in pulse showing a width of 0.018 ms and labeled 55.5 kHz. Chart (b) shows 'Potential (mV)' vs 'Frequency (MHz)' for a human subject's forehead under anesthesia, with a zoomed-in pulse showing a peak at 15.00 MHz and labeled 61 kHz. The main plot in (b) shows multiple peaks in the 10-25 MHz range.
data.key_data: Chart (a) (axon filament): Peak potential ~10 mV, dominant frequency 55.5 kHz, pulse width 0.018 ms.; Chart (b) (human forehead): Peak potential ~25 mV, dominant frequency 61 kHz (as labeled for zoomed pulse), main peaks in 10-25 MHz range, zoomed pulse peak at 15.00 MHz.; Text claims: 55-60 kHz bursts from neurofilaments, 58-64 kHz bursts from human forehead, pulse widths are the same for both cases.
data.significance: This figure provides a direct visual comparison between the characteristics of bursts from single neurons (microtubules) and those observed from the forehead of anesthetized patients, highlighting their similar frequencies and pulse widths (as stated in the text), which supports the paper's hypothesis that microtubule activity is the source of these MHz signals and a neural correlate of consciousness.

data.caption: In the Computational Science and Technology (CST) simulator, we recreated virtual hardware, as shown above, to simulate various types of signal transmission. We provide three tables Table 1, Table 2 and Table 3, compiled from different works of literature, the structural parameters already published, and we are still fine-tuning to replicate a real physical scenario, when a signal tries to enter inside the brain and when a signal emits from inside.
data.description: A cross-sectional schematic diagram illustrating the 15 layers of the brain structure from the scalp to the cortical columns, as modeled in the CST simulator. It shows a 'Source' and 'Drain' for signal transmission, with labels for each layer including Skin, Dense connectivity tissue, Aponeurosis, Loose conductivity tissue, Periosteum, Outer cortical bone, Middle diploe bone, Inner cortical bone, Dura mater, Pia mater, Arachnoid mater, Bridging veins, Superior Sagittal Sinus, Sub-arachnoid space, and Cortical columns with a Microtubule bundle.
data.significance: This diagram visually represents the multi-layered brain model used in the simulations, providing a clear context for understanding how signals are theorized to transmit through different tissues from the cortex to the scalp.

data.caption: This is a summary of all AC and DC simulations for 15 layers plotted together. Ions of other layers do not absorb low-frequency or ionic transmissions. However, there are significant sharp gradients in low-frequency conductivity among all 15 layers that disrupt the shape of potential; the effective resistance is high, and we have calculated as low-frequency absorption. Around THz, there is thermal absorption. As Hz and GHz signals are compromised for two distinct reasons, only MHz signals with minimal absorption can be partially emitted and largely reflected back (note that absorption, transmission, and reflection add up to 1).
data.description: A line chart showing 'Absorption Potential (mV)' on the y-axis against 'Frequency (Hz)' on a logarithmic x-axis, ranging from 10^0 to 10^15 Hz. Multiple colored lines represent absorption for different components: Blood, proteins minerals (purple), CSF (blue), Three layers of bone (green), Thermal absorption band (orange), and Water (red). The chart highlights a frequency range of '6MHz to 212MHz' with minimal absorption.
data.key_data: Frequency range: 10^0 to 10^15 Hz.; Blood, proteins minerals: Peak absorption ~10 mV around 10^7 Hz.; CSF: Peak absorption ~15 mV around 10^8 Hz.; Three layers of bone: Peak absorption ~10 mV around 10^6 Hz.; Thermal absorption band: Significant absorption from 10^12 Hz upwards.; Water: Peak absorption ~15 mV around 10^10 Hz.; Minimal absorption range: 6 MHz to 212 MHz.
data.significance: This figure is central to the paper's argument, demonstrating through simulation that only MHz signals experience minimal absorption and can be partially transmitted while largely reflected back, making them ideal candidates for brain signals that can reach the scalp without significant disruption. It contrasts this with Hz and GHz signals, which are compromised.

data.caption: Another simulation of transmitted signal from 15th layers helical structure, i.e. microtubule to the skin crossing the 14 layers in between. The black line is the vibrational spectrum of the microtubule in the cortical column's neuron and red line is the average output of the bundle's vibrations, this is also the triplet (earlier triplet was observed in neurons and microtubules, Saxena, K., (2020)) we observe in the awake persons forehead experimentally.
data.description: A line chart showing 'Response Amplitude' on the y-axis against 'Frequency (GHz)' on a logarithmic x-axis, ranging from 10^-5 to 10^1. It displays the 'Combined System Response (MHZ Enhanced)' for signal transmission from microtubules to the skin across 14 layers. Multiple lines represent different noise components (Noise: White, kHz Noise, MHz Noise, GHz Noise) and signal components (kHz Band Signal, MHz Band Signal, GHz Band Signal, Combined Response). The 'Skin Transparency' is also indicated for MHz, GHz, and kHz. The black line represents the vibrational spectrum of the microtubule, and the red line is the average output of the bundle's vibrations, showing a 'triplet' pattern.
data.key_data: Frequency range: 10^-5 to 10^1 GHz (10 kHz to 10 GHz).; Peak response amplitude: ~0.35 at ~10 MHz.; MHz Band Signal peak: ~0.35 at ~10 MHz.; GHz Band Signal peak: ~0.2 at ~2.5 GHz.; kHz Band Signal peak: ~0.1 at ~100 kHz.; Skin Transparency: MHz > GHz > kHz.; Triplet peaks in red line (Combined Response) around 10 MHz.
data.significance: This simulation demonstrates that the combined system response, particularly in the MHz range, allows for significant signal transmission from microtubules to the skin, while other frequencies are attenuated. The observed 'triplet' pattern in the MHz range further supports the hypothesis of microtubule-generated signals as a neural correlate of consciousness.

data.claim: Computational functionalism about consciousness is often criticized for relying on observer-relative interpretations of physical systems.
data.support: Citing existing philosophical literature and objections (e.g., Searle-style arguments, triviality arguments, abstraction fallacy).

data.claim: A state is functionally defined by its complete counterfactual role: how the system would evolve and respond from that state under possible future interactions.
data.support: Conceptual argument using an elevator controller example to illustrate that states are defined by future possibilities and indistinguishable microstates collapse into a single functional state.

data.claim: The canonical functional structure is externally accessible but not externally labeled, as it is fixed by the system's counterfactual organization once the relevant interface of inputs, outputs, and interventions is specified.
data.support: Argument that the structure is produced by quotienting the system's state space by an equivalence relation defined over possible future behaviors, rather than by assigning meanings to states.

data.claim: If two deterministic interactive systems over the same input and output sets have the same complete input-output behavior, then their canonical functional structures are isomorphic.
data.support: Formal proof (Theorem 1, Canonical Realization Theorem) demonstrating the isomorphism between the canonical functional structures of behaviorally equivalent systems and a canonical machine.

data.claim: Consciousness depends on properties defined over the canonical functional structure of a system.
data.support: This is the central philosophical thesis (Definition 1) of canonical functionalism, providing a more rigorous target for functionalist theories of consciousness.

data.claim: The canonical functional structure provides a formal candidate for Chalmers's principle of organizational invariance, suggesting that consciousness-relevant properties should factor through isomorphic canonical functional structures.
data.support: Argument that the framework sharpens Chalmers's principle by providing a precise mathematical object for 'same organization'.

data.claim: Canonical functionalism responds to Block-style worries about overly liberal functionalism by requiring the relevant functional structure to be state-based, counterfactual, transition-sensitive, and canonical.
data.support: Argument that the framework avoids attributing consciousness to every behavioral duplicate or interpreted computation by demanding preservation of the appropriate canonical structure.

data.claim: The unfolding argument, lookup-table objections, and the Chinese Room argument can be understood as test cases for whether a system that differs in implementation nevertheless realizes the same consciousness-relevant functional structure.
data.support: Analysis of each objection, showing how canonical functionalism reframes the debate into a precise question about the preservation of the canonical functional structure.

data.claim: Consciousness-relevant functional properties are not properties of raw physical states, but of their equivalence classes under complete future behavioral role, meaning they are invariant under canonical functional equivalence.
data.support: Formal definition of the supervenience claim (C(S, x) = C(T, y) if b_x^S = b_y^T) and its factorization through the canonical quotient.

data.claim: The canonical functional structure is closely related to the causal-state construction in computational mechanics and e-machines, sharing the insight that states are defined by their future-directed roles.
data.support: Comparison of the framework with computational mechanics, highlighting similarities in defining states by future consequences and differences in application (interactive systems vs. stochastic processes).

data.claim: Functionalism is a central and potentially viable position in the philosophy and science of mind.
Consciousness is a natural phenomenon that can be studied scientifically and potentially realized by artificial systems.
It is possible to specify a relevant interface of inputs, outputs, and interventions for an interactive system.
The concept of 'complete future behavior' under all admissible future input histories is a meaningful idealization, even if empirical applications require approximations.

data.caption: FIG. 1. (a) Tubulin protein dimer structure (left). A schematic showing dimensions of tubulin dimer and how 2D sheet of tubulin dimers fold into a single microtubule (middle). A schematic of cross-section of microtubule, STM measures conductivity across this ring. (b) STM image of a single tubulin dimer, tip bias 2 V, 100 pA, and scale bar is 4.3 nm. Inset shows percentage change in conductivity, as function of bias, from a typical current voltage characteristic measured on a point shown with a circle pointing on the top of the tubulin dimer. (c) STM image of a single microtubule, bias 2.7 V, 30 pA, and scale bar is 50 nm. Inset shows a similar plot like tubulin in panel (b).
data.description: Panel (a) illustrates the tubulin protein dimer structure with dimensions (6.5 nm, 8 nm), its assembly into a 2D sheet and then a microtubule (25 nm diameter), and a cross-section indicating STM measurement. Panel (b) is an STM image of a single tubulin dimer (scale bar 4.3 nm) with an inset line chart showing percentage change in conductivity versus applied tip bias (0 to +2V), peaking around +2V. Panel (c) is an STM image of a single microtubule (scale bar 50 nm) with an inset line chart showing percentage change in conductivity versus applied tip bias (0 to -20mV), exhibiting a sharp peak around -20mV.
data.key_data: Tubulin dimer dimensions: 6.5 nm, 8 nm; Microtubule diameter: 25 nm; Figure 1(b) STM: tip bias 2 V, 100 pA, scale bar 4.3 nm, conductivity peak around +2V; Figure 1(c) STM: bias 2.7 V, 30 pA, scale bar 50 nm, conductivity peak around -20mV
data.significance: This figure introduces the fundamental building blocks (tubulin dimer) and the assembled structure (microtubule), demonstrating their distinct electrical conductivity responses, which are crucial for understanding their memory-switching properties.

data.caption: FIG. 2. (a) Current voltage characteristic along the surface of microtubule measured using AFM tip vibrating at 1 MHz, measurement circuit is shown at the top left panel and the corresponding AFM image is in the top right corner. The ac conductivity measurement circuit is at the right bottom inset. (b) The gold electrode chip on Si/SiO2 substrate, scanning electron micrograph image, scale bar is 100 µm, the 200 nm wide ion trap region is zoomed. (c) Schematic of dc conductivity measurement set up (left), and AFM image of the device constructed, here current source is shown, for voltage source measurement only one pair of electrode was used. Scale bar is 400 nm. L is the actual device length. (d) The ac (red) and dc (green) resistance measurements in two typical devices, one class A (circle-line), another class B (line) as a function of applied bias. (e) Statistical distribution for dc resistances for 100 devices in Mega-Ohm. (f) Statistical distribution of ac resistances for 100 devices, at 1 MHz, in kilo-Ohm.
data.description: Panel (a) presents a linear current-voltage (I-V) characteristic curve for a microtubule surface, measured with an AFM tip at 1 MHz, ranging from -10 µA to 10 µA and -0.3 V to 0.3 V. Insets show the measurement circuit and an AFM image. Panel (b) is an SEM image of a gold electrode chip on Si/SiO2, with a 100 µm scale bar and a zoomed 200 nm ion trap region. Panel (c) shows a schematic of the DC conductivity setup and an AFM image of the device (400 nm scale bar). Panel (d) displays AC (red) and DC (green) resistance measurements for two device classes (A and B) as a function of DC bias, showing quantized resistance levels (DC: 0-600 MΩ, AC: 0-170 kΩ). Panels (e) and (f) are pie charts showing the statistical distribution of DC resistances (in MΩ) and AC resistances (in kΩ at 1 MHz), respectively, for 100 devices.
data.key_data: Figure 2(a) I-V: Current range -10 µA to 10 µA, Voltage range -0.3 V to 0.3 V; Figure 2(b) Scale bar: 100 µm, ion trap width: 200 nm; Figure 2(c) Scale bar: 400 nm; Figure 2(d) DC resistance values: 600, 300, 100, 25 MΩ; AC resistance values: 170, 115, 105, 69, 39 kΩ; Figure 2(e) DC resistance distribution: 25 MΩ (50%), 100 MΩ (16%), 300 MΩ (10%), 12 MΩ (8%), 10 MΩ (12%), 9 MΩ (4%); Figure 2(f) AC resistance distribution: 120 kΩ (50%), 170 kΩ (16%), 105 kΩ (12%), 69 kΩ (10%), 115 kΩ (8%), 39 kΩ (4%)
data.significance: This figure provides comprehensive electrical characterization of single microtubule devices, demonstrating their linear I-V behavior, quantized resistance states under bias, and the statistical consistency of these properties across multiple devices, validating their potential as multi-level memory elements.

data.caption: FIG. 3. (a) Five IV characteristics, using source voltage scan, the scan starts from 0 to +Vmax to -Vmax and then back -Vmax to + Vmax, during scanning, Vmax was varied at a gap of 0.5 V from 0.5 V to 4.5 V bias, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 volt data are shown. (b) (Top) Schematic of "write (W)-read (R)-erase(E)-read (R)" test-sequence for random access memory (RAM) and read only memory (ROM) applications, "1," "2," and "3" denotes writing pulses. (Below) 10 memory states were written varying from 1mV to 90mV and read using 0.1 mV read bias, only "read" currents (shown as A, B, C, D in b) are plotted here, 10 different currents probe 10 bits of memory-storage and processing. Read pulse and current has opposite polarity because "E" is not erase for microtubule, it is writing another state. (c) Using function generator we send stream of rectangular pulses (input, green) to a single microtubule device varying frequency 1 MHz to 20 GHz (repetition rate of the unit stream shown in b), output (red) is measured across 50 Ω resistance as voltage drop.
data.description: Panel (a) displays five current-voltage (I-V) hysteresis loops for a single microtubule, with current ranging from -15 pA to 15 pA and voltage from -6 V to 6 V, showing different Vmax values (0.5 V to 4.5 V). Panel (b) (top) is a schematic of a 'write-read-erase-read' test sequence for memory, and (below) a line chart showing 10 distinct 'read' current levels (pA) corresponding to 10 memory states written with varying biases (1mV to 90mV). Panel (c) shows input (green) and output (red) voltage pulses over time (0 to 15 µs), demonstrating fast switching response with frequencies from 1 MHz to 20 GHz.
data.key_data: Figure 3(a) I-V: Current range -15 pA to 15 pA, Voltage range -6 V to 6 V, Vmax varied from 0.5 V to 4.5 V; Figure 3(b) Read Current: 10 distinct levels, ranging from approximately -10 pA to 10 pA; Writing biases 1mV to 90mV, read bias 0.1 mV; Figure 3(c) Time scale: 0 to 15 µs; Frequencies 1 MHz to 20 GHz; Output measured across 50 Ω resistance
data.significance: This figure experimentally demonstrates the multi-level memory-switching capabilities of a single microtubule, showing distinct memory states, the ability to write and read multiple bits, and a rapid switching speed, which are essential for its application in advanced memory devices.

data.caption: FIG. 4. (a) Schematic of square hysteresis current-voltage (IV) loop (top left), two nearly linear current-output regions depict a pair of memory-states, say top one is +σs then bottom one is -σs, the corresponding conductivity difference between these two states is Δσ. Corresponding potential wells for ±σs are shown schematically (top right above), if +σs is left well, –σs is right well, σε is the dip between two wells, since σε signifies conductivity of microtubule with zero dipole-shift from original structure, and it is same for any memory-state-pair, we suggest it as σ. From Figure 3(a), a scheme is created by plotting Δσ vs σ (top right below). Three STM images with scale bar 6 nm, dipole direction shifts by a very small angle as shown with arrows. The arrows are plotted by scanning the region by changing STM rotation angle 0° to 180° at a gap of 10° and checking the high contrast regions on a single tubulin (bottom). (b) Tubulin structural parameters, gap between two monomers 0.13 nm to 0.3 nm, and we flip the bias to see that tubulin dimension changes in 5 different ways (5 memory bits), tubulins accommodate themselves on the surface as scan-bias changes.
data.description: Panel (a) includes a schematic of a square hysteresis I-V loop (top left) illustrating two memory states (+σs, -σs) and their conductivity difference Δσ. Corresponding potential wells for these states are shown schematically (top right above), with σε representing the energy barrier. A plot of Δσ vs σ is derived from Figure 3(a) (top right below). Three STM images (scale bar 6 nm) at the bottom show dipole direction shifts within a single tubulin, indicated by arrows, observed by varying STM rotation angle. Panel (b) illustrates tubulin structural parameters (80Å, 8.3Å, 8.4nm, 1.3Å, 3Å) and a bar chart titled 'Tubulin length vs bias induced flipping' showing 5 distinct dimension changes (5 memory bits) as a function of bias, with monomer gaps from 0.13 nm to 0.3 nm.
data.key_data: Figure 4(a) STM images scale bar: 6 nm; STM rotation angle: 0° to 180° with 10° gap; Figure 4(b) Tubulin dimensions: 80 Å, 8.3 Å, 8.4 nm, 1.3 Å, 3 Å; Gap between monomers: 0.13 nm to 0.3 nm; 5 different dimension changes (5 memory bits)
data.significance: This figure elucidates the underlying mechanism of multi-level memory switching in microtubules, directly correlating the observed electrical hysteresis with nanoscale dipole reorientations and structural changes within individual tubulin proteins, thereby establishing a physical basis for multi-bit data storage.

data.caption: The planar osmotic power source. a Schematic illustration of GO/rGO junction and its mechanism of K+ conduction in 2D nanofluidic channels within the planar osmotic power source. b SEM image of the GO layer (cross section). c SEM image of the rGO layer (cross section). d Galvanostatic discharge performance of Au/AgNO3/GO/RTIL/rGO/Au at 0.1 µA. Inset picture shows the photograph of the osmotic power source. e I–V characteristics and power density of Au/AgNO3/GO/RTIL/rGO/Au. f Comparison of energy and power density of Au/AgNO3/GO/RTIL/rGO/Au in the Ragone plot (Data for lithium thin-film batteries, supercapacitors and Al electrolyte capacitors are collected from refs. 47, 48). Source data are provided as a Source Data file.
data.description: Figure 1 presents a comprehensive view of the planar osmotic power source. Panel a is a schematic diagram illustrating the GO/rGO junction and the mechanism of K+ ion conduction through 2D nanofluidic channels, with Au electrodes and GO functional groups (COO-, OH-). Panels b and c show SEM images of the cross-sections of the GO layer and rGO layer, respectively, both with a 4 µm scale bar. Panel d is a line chart depicting the galvanostatic discharge performance of the Au/AgNO3/GO/RTIL/rGO/Au power source at 0.1 µA, showing Voltage (V) versus Capacity (µAh), with an inset photograph of the flexible device. Panel e is a line chart illustrating the current-voltage (I-V) characteristics (Current (µA)) and power density (W cm⁻³) of the Au/AgNO3/GO/RTIL/rGO/Au device. Panel f is a Ragone plot comparing the energy density (Wh cm⁻³) and power density (W cm⁻³) of the Au/AgNO3/GO/RTIL/rGO/Au power source against lithium thin-film batteries, supercapacitors, and Al electrolytic capacitors, with time scales indicated.
data.key_data: Discharge voltage starts around 1.5 V and drops to 0 V at approximately 3.8 µAh capacity (d).; Maximum open-circuit voltage (Voc) is around 1.5 V (e).; Short-circuit current (Isc) is around -11 µA (e).; Maximum power density is around 0.028 W cm⁻³ at approximately 0.7 V (e).; The device exhibits an energy density of approximately 6 mWh cm⁻³ and a power density of approximately 28 mW cm⁻³ (f).; Lithium thin-film batteries range from 10⁻³ to 10⁻¹ Wh cm⁻³ and 10⁻³ to 10¹ W cm⁻³ (f).; Supercapacitors range from 10⁻⁶ to 10⁻³ Wh cm⁻³ and 10⁻¹ to 10³ W cm⁻³ (f).; Al electrolytic capacitors range from 10⁻⁷ to 10⁻⁶ Wh cm⁻³ and 10⁻³ to 10¹ W cm⁻³ (f).
data.significance: This figure elucidates the fundamental design, operational principles, and performance metrics of the planar osmotic power source, demonstrating its high voltage output, substantial power and energy densities, and competitive standing relative to established energy storage technologies.

data.caption: Design and characterization of the triboiontronic device. a The integrated energy harvesting (TENG) and storage (osmotic power source) triboion- tronic device is bendable and its thickness is around 200 µm. b Structure of the integrated device. c Current and d Voltage generated by the TENG. e Voltage profile of the integrated self-charging triboiontronic device. The planar osmotic power source (Au/AgNO3/GO/RTIL/rGO/Au) could be charged by TENG at frequency of 3 Hz and discharged at 1 µA. Source data are provided as a Source Data file.
data.description: Figure 2 illustrates the design and performance of the triboiontronic device. Panel a is a photograph showcasing the flexible and bendable nature of the integrated device, with a thickness of approximately 200 µm, shown with a ruler for scale. Panel b provides a schematic diagram of the integrated device, detailing the connection between a TENG (composed of Rabbit Fur, PI, Cu) and an osmotic power source (GO, rGO, Au electrodes) via a rectifier. Panels c and d are line charts showing the current (µA) and voltage (V) generated by the TENG at different frequencies (1 Hz, 2 Hz, 3 Hz) over time (s). Panel e is a line chart displaying the voltage profile (V) of the integrated self-charging triboiontronic device over time (s), demonstrating its charging by the TENG and subsequent discharge.
data.key_data: Device thickness is approximately 0.20 mm (a).; At 3 Hz, the TENG generates a peak current of approximately -0.35 µA (c).; At 2 Hz, the TENG generates a peak current of approximately -0.25 µA (c).; At 1 Hz, the TENG generates a peak current of approximately -0.15 µA (c).; At 3 Hz, the TENG generates a peak voltage of approximately 45 V (d).; At 2 Hz, the TENG generates a peak voltage of approximately 30 V (d).; At 1 Hz, the TENG generates a peak voltage of approximately 15 V (d).; The device charges from approximately 0.7 V to 1.2 V, with charging taking about 200 s to reach 1.2 V (e).
data.significance: This figure effectively demonstrates the successful integration of the osmotic power source with a triboelectric nanogenerator (TENG) to create a flexible, self-charging triboiontronic device capable of harvesting mechanical energy and powering electronic components.

data.caption: GO aerogel preparation process and parameters for optimized osmotic power source in 3D. a Schematic illustration of preparation process. The GO sheets were reduced by LAA at 60 °C forming a GO hydrogel and then dried through a freeze-drying process. For the GO + KOH aerogel, GO hydrogels were soaked in KOH aqueous solutions to introduce ion concentration difference before freezing. b SEM image of the GO aerogel. Inset photo of the obtained GO aerogel. c SEM image of the GO + KOH aerogel. Inset is the EDS element mapping of the GO + KOH aerogel. d–f The Raman spectroscopy (d), BET tests (e), surface area and pore size (f) of GO aerogels with different GO:LAA ratio. g, h I–V characteristics of power sources with GO aerogels that have different GO:LAA ratio (g) and thickness (h). i Power density of the power sources with different GO aerogel thickness. Source data are provided as a Source Data file.
data.description: Figure 3 details the preparation and optimization of 3D GO aerogels for osmotic power sources. Panel a is a schematic illustrating the GO aerogel preparation process, including LAA reduction at 60 °C, hydrogel formation, and freeze-drying, with an additional step for KOH soaking for GO + KOH aerogels. Panels b and c show SEM images of a GO aerogel and a GO + KOH aerogel, respectively, both with a 30 µm scale bar; panel c includes an inset with EDS element mapping showing K+ concentration. Panel d presents Raman spectra for GO aerogels with varying GO:LAA ratios, showing Intensity (a.u.) versus Raman shift (cm⁻¹). Panel e displays N2 adsorption/desorption isotherms, showing Adsorbed volume (cm³g⁻¹) versus Relative pressure (P/P₀) for different GO:LAA ratios. Panel f is a bar chart comparing the surface area (m²g⁻¹) and pore size (nm) of GO aerogels for different GO:LAA ratios. Panels g and h are line charts showing the I-V characteristics (Current (µA) versus Voltage (V)) of power sources with GO aerogels of different GO:LAA ratios (g) and different thicknesses (h). Panel i is a line chart showing the power density (W cm⁻³) as a function of load resistance (Ω) for power sources with different GO aerogel thicknesses.
data.key_data: K+ concentration in GO + KOH aerogel is 17.3% (c).; ID/IG ratios decrease from 2.15 (GO:LAA 1:0) to 1.51 (GO:LAA 1:2) (d).; Surface area decreases from 403.5 m²g⁻¹ (GO:LAA 1:0) to 15.6 m²g⁻¹ (GO:LAA 1:2) (f).; Pore size decreases from 2.15 nm (GO:LAA 1:0) to 1.51 nm (GO:LAA 1:2) (f).; For GO:LAA 1:0.5, Voc is approximately 0.679 V and Isc is approximately -402 µA (g).; For 15 µm thickness, Isc is approximately -613 µA, with Voc around 0.6 V for all thicknesses (h).; Maximum power density for 15 µm thickness is approximately 0.022 W cm⁻³ at around 10³ Ω (i).
data.significance: This figure provides critical insights into the fabrication and characterization of 3D GO aerogels, demonstrating how precise control over material properties, such as pore size and K+ concentration, can significantly optimize the current output and power density of osmotic power sources.

data.caption: Modular design osmotic power source. a Schematic illustration of the modular design device construction. Two GO aerogels with different K+ con- centrations are sandwiched between charge collectors and separated by an ionogel that consists of RTIL (TESTFSI) and PVDF-HFP polymer matrix. b I–V characteristic and power density of the GO aerogel-based power source with ionogel electrolyte at 25 °C. c I–V characteristic of the power source at -10 °C. d The output performance of the power source at different temperatures. e The foldable design of 20 devices in series connection on both sides of the substrate enabled by self- healing ionogels. f, g The foldable power source could power the electrochromic device (f) and the liquid crystal display screen (g). Source data are provided as a Source Data file.
data.description: Figure 4 illustrates the modular design and performance of the osmotic power source. Panel a is a schematic diagram showing the construction of the modular device, featuring GO aerogels with adjustable K+ concentrations, self-healing ionogels with tunable ion conductivity, and their assembly into an antifreeze power source pack, including a foldable design. Panel b is a line chart displaying the I-V characteristics (Current (µA)) and power density (W cm⁻³) of the GO aerogel-based power source with ionogel electrolyte at 25 °C. Panel c is a line chart showing the I-V characteristics (Current (µA) versus Voltage (V)) of the power source at -10 °C. Panel d is a line chart illustrating the output performance, specifically Voc (V) and Isc (µA), of the power source across a temperature range from -40 °C to 60 °C. Panel e is a photograph of a foldable design with 20 devices connected in series on a substrate, enabled by self-healing ionogels, with an inset showing a close-up. Panels f and g are photographs demonstrating the foldable power source powering an electrochromic device (f, transitioning from 'OFF' to 'ON') and a liquid crystal display screen (g, transitioning from 'OFF' to 'ON' and displaying '88').
data.key_data: At 25 °C, Voc is approximately 0.6 V, Isc is approximately -440 µA, and maximum power density is approximately 0.012 W cm⁻³ (b).; At -10 °C, Voc is approximately 0.54 V and Isc is approximately -57 µA (c).; Voc remains relatively stable around 0.5-0.6 V across the temperature range of -40 °C to 60 °C (d).; Isc increases from approximately 10 µA at -40 °C to over 100 µA at 60 °C (d).; The foldable design connects 20 devices in series (e).
data.significance: This figure underscores the modularity, flexibility, and robust performance of the osmotic power source, particularly its ability to function effectively across a wide range of temperatures and power various electronic devices, highlighting its potential for diverse practical applications.

data.caption: Evolution of the electrical double layer model. a Classical EDL models at conductor-liquid interfaces. b The “two-step” EDL model at dielectric-liquid interfaces. c Triboiontronics EDL model for dynamic regulation of interface charge. d–f Verification of the dynamic regulation mechanism of the triboiontronics EDL model. data.description: The figure illustrates the evolution of electrical double layer (EDL) models and verifies the triboiontronics EDL model. Panel a shows classical EDL models (Helmholtz, Gouy-Chapman, Stern) at conductor-liquid interfaces, depicting the distribution of water molecules, anions, cations, electrons, positive/negative charges, diffuse layer, and Stern layer. Panel b presents the “two-step” EDL model for dielectric-liquid interfaces, detailing Step I (electron transfer) and Step II (ion migration) leading to Stern and diffuse layer formation. Panel c introduces the Triboiontronics EDL model, showing how triboelectric-induced polarization from Dielectric II (positive charges) or Dielectric III (negative charges) dynamically regulates interface charge on Dielectric I, influencing ion distribution and EDL structure. Panels d-f are line charts showing collected charge (Qsc) in nanoCoulombs (nC) versus time (s) to verify the dynamic regulation mechanism. Panel d shows Qsc for Stage I (limited charging), Stage II (forward triboelectric-induced polarization), and Stage III (reverse triboelectric-induced polarization). Panel e shows Qsc for Stage II with increasing positive charge density, and panel f shows Qsc for Stage III with intensifying negative surface charge.
data.key_data: Stage I Qsc: ~1.2 nC; Stage II Qsc: ~40 nC; Stage III Qsc: ~-40 nC; Max Qsc (Stage II, Fig. 1e): ~180 nC; Min Qsc (Stage III, Fig. 1f): ~-100 nC
data.significance: This figure provides a historical context for EDL models and introduces the novel triboiontronics EDL model, experimentally validating its capability for dynamic and reversible regulation of interfacial charge, which is fundamental to the paper's proposed energy-autonomous iontronic systems.

data.description: The figure illustrates neuromimetic circuits enabled by dynamic EDL regulation and their potential applications. Panel a shows a diagram of human locomotion control, detailing primary neurons, interneurons, and lower motor neurons activating flexor and extensor muscles via inhibitory and excitatory synapses. Panel b depicts a bioinspired neuromimetic circuit control, illustrating Stage I (contact electrification of PET with positively charged fur, leading to cation enrichment in water) and Stage II (removal of fur, leading to anion enrichment), demonstrating dynamic EDL regulation. Panel c illustrates biological neural communication with ion flow (Na+) along a neuron. Panel d shows a bioinspired underwater wireless information transmission system, where a triboiontronic device (Au/PET) generates electron current pulses (0 or 1) based on ion transmission in water, with a judgment area and electrometer. Panel e diagrams ion channels, showing neurochemicals, ions, and ligand-gated ion channels regulating ion current and transport. Panel f presents a polyelectrolyte-confined fluidic memristor mimicking synaptic behavior, with a PimB layer regulating anion (A-) and cation (n+) flow for ion memory and synaptic emulation. Panel g outlines the full operational logic of the neuromimetic system, defining signal flow from input encoding (triboiontronics circuit) to ion transmission (underwater wireless communication) to synaptic learning/modulation (ion memory), with an actuation trigger and latency/recovery triggers. Panels h-k illustrate potential applications: brain-inspired computing, brain-computer interfaces, human-machine interaction, and neurorestorative medicine.
data.key_data: Digital output (Fig. 2d): 0 or 1
data.significance: This figure demonstrates the practical implementation of dynamic EDL regulation in neuromimetic circuits, showcasing its utility in bioinspired motor control, underwater communication, and synaptic emulation, thereby establishing a framework for advanced computing and bioelectronic applications.

data.description: This figure illustrates the invariant-tree driven synthesis of new classifiers. Panel (A) presents four columns depicting different phases of classification without training: single-shot learning of Cheetah dynamics, spontaneous classifier determination via vortex assembly, synthesis of new classifiers by combining existing ones, and less-than-one-shot (LO) learning for untrained events. It shows how various animal parts (head, tail, body, legs) are identified and classified into animals like Lioness, Dog, Deer, Pig, and Tiger. Panel (B) shows the live growth of the gel superstructure, highlighting the synthesis of combinatorial classes with distinct structural symmetries coupled by electromagnetic resonance. Panel (C) demonstrates invariant matching by superposing trained and test 3D clock assemblies, showing the progression from SL to SP and back to SL, and the generation of differential ∂η/∂Φ signals along orthogonal axes Φ1, Φ2, Φ3.
data.significance: This figure demonstrates the gel computer's ability to perform single-shot and less-than-one-shot learning by synthesizing new classifiers based on invariant trees, showcasing its unsupervised learning capabilities and adaptability to new, untrained data, which is a core claim of the paper.

data.caption: The principle of the triboiontronics and the construction of the PDC-TING. a Triboiontronics with temporal control of electrical double layer formation. Firstly, when DI water contacted the bottom Au/PET layer, it interacted with the PET substrate through microscopic cracks in the sputtered Au layer, forming a stable EDL. b Secondly, as the top Au/PET layer moved downward to contact with water, the initial CE led to form a new EDL, establishing two EDLs with significantly different symmetries. This created an ion concentration gradient, generating an ionic current /i1. c Thirdly, the detachment of the top Au/PET layer halted ion migration. d Through repeated contact and separation cycles, the ion migration persisted until equilibrium was achieved between the two EDLs. e The model display of the PDC-TING. f Comparison of output performance of different generators. g The effect of different liquid types on the PDC-TING output. h The effect of the extent and direction of the ion concentration gradient on the PDC-TING output. i The effect of the Au-layer sputtering time of Au/PET layers on the PDC-TING output. j The effect of the Au-layer sputtering time of Au/PET layers on the internal resistance of the PDC-TING.

data.significance: This diagram visually explains the fundamental mechanism of triboiontronics, detailing the initial formation of an electrical double layer at the solid-liquid interface, which is central to the device's operation.
