data.definition: The locus at which the experience arises, rather than some more sophisticated experience of a particular singular self or self-awareness. It is consistent with phenomenal experiences of no-self, universal oneness, or fractured/multiple selves.
How a unified first person perspective (1PP) can bind experiences across multiple physically distinct activities, whether billions of individual neurons firing or some other underlying phenomenon.

Once a binding mechanism that creates larger, unified, macro 1PPs is proposed, what mechanism puts a stop to that process? What causes ontologically hard boundaries around these 1PPs and why do the boundaries appear where they do?
How microexperiences come together to yield a bounded consciousness, and how consciousness can exist at the middle level of nature.
data.section: 2.1. Rosenberg's formulation of the boundary problem

data.definition: Refers to why our experience does not exist at the subsystem level, i.e., the Russian dolls nested within us.
data.section: 2.1. Rosenberg's formulation of the boundary problem

data.definition: Asks the parallel question of the larger systems within which individual human entities are nested.
data.section: 2.1. Rosenberg's formulation of the boundary problem

data.definition: Equates a system's consciousness to its causal properties, which can be measured mathematically ('phi') via algorithms mapped from five specific properties claimed to capture human phenomenology. Causal integration of a particular type is proposed as the binding mechanism.
data.section: 2.2. Literature review of the boundary problem

data.definition: Starts from panpsychism and explains how shared resonances between micro-consciousness entities can overcome the binding problem. The slowest shared resonance across different systems is taken to define the subsequent scope of macro-consciousness, with electromagnetic field synchrony (resonance) being the primary type of shared resonance relevant to the scale of human life and consciousness.
data.section: 2.2. Literature review of the boundary problem

data.definition: We experience, at least sometimes, an absolute boundary between our 1PP and the outside world, which consists of events that could be experienced by us and are currently being experienced by others. What produces this absolute, i.e., non-fuzzy boundary?
data.section: 3. Precise statement of five specific boundary problems

data.definition: Our 1PP is capable of experiencing diverse and multiple experiences, often simultaneously or co-jointly. To the extent our 1PP is considered to arise out of a complex, multi-part mechanism, there could be boundaries, whether hard or fuzzy, that enclose some of these nested or constitutive sub-experiences. Are there 1PPs also existing at these lower levels? If not, what creates the important boundary at our meso-level but over-rides or renders meaningless any lower level boundaries? If yes, what mechanism ensures our 1PP remains at the meso level of human experience and not also at some of those lower levels, at least at times?
data.section: 3. Precise statement of five specific boundary problems

data.definition: Our 1PP is in turn nested in larger more complex structures. At times, these operate with considerable physical and causal synchrony, such as singing choirs or football teams. Other times, our collective behaviour has resulted in complex systems, often with a degree of persistence through time and emergent properties, such as cities, price setting and goods transfer via marketplaces, and large language models. Are there 1PPs also existing at these higher levels? If not, what makes the meso-level boundary qualitatively different to each higher level boundary? If yes, what mechanism ensures our 1PP remains at the meso level of human experience and not also at some of those higher levels, at least at times?
data.section: 3. Precise statement of five specific boundary problems

data.definition: The boundary we experience, whether hard or fuzzy, demarcates our phenomenal experiences from the external environment, which includes other people's first person perspectives, i.e., other meso entities separate from our own as well as other physical phenomena more generally. What mechanism makes this a private boundary? Why can we not routinely bridge into others' minds?
data.section: 3. Precise statement of five specific boundary problems

data.definition: There are often multiple possible bounded entities in a given system, potentially with many at similar, lower, and higher spatial levels. These entities might persist, for some definition of pattern stability, for different, overlapping periods of time. However, our normal experience is typically of a single bounded entity persisting through time, at least for some non-trivial periods of time. How is a broadly stable sense of self stitched together across a sequence of such entities?
data.section: 3. Precise statement of five specific boundary problems

data.term: Ontological boundary (for hard boundary problem resolution)
data.definition: A mechanism that results in an ontological boundary that is impermeable to the relevant processes, patterns, or substances determined to make up the 1PP.

In this model, electron transfer and ionization reactions occurred almost simultaneously, leading to the simultaneous transfer of electrons and adsorption of ions on the dielectric surface to form the IHP. Then, under the electrostatic forces, ions of opposite polarity were adsorbed onto the charged surface, forming the OHP. According to the two-step model, the EDL represents an excellent ionic-electronic coupling interface, at which the dynamics of ions and electrons could be adjusted.

Compared with electronics that solely relied on electrons as charge carriers, iontronics harnessed a diverse array of multivalent ions for charge transport, which enhanced the capability to transport multiple charge carriers and information at the ionic-electronic coupling interface, presenting significant potential for enhancing energy.

A nanogenerator where the charge density of the diffuse layer on the dielectric surface was supplemented to create an ion concentration gradient to drive ion migration, adjusting the electronic displacement current to generate a DC ionic-electronic coupling current at levels reaching hundreds of milliamperes per square meter.

A DC-TING where controllable ion migration behavior was achieved by dynamically controlling asymmetric electrical double layer formation between dielectric substrates and liquids, forming triboiontronics. By regulating the coverage of the charge-collecting layer on the dielectric substrate, not only could charge be collected, but also the contact electrification (CE) property between the substrate and the liquid could be adjusted to form distinct EDLs. Through dynamically controlling the CE between the liquid and dielectric substrates with identical charge-collecting layers, asymmetric EDL formation was achieved. It created an ion concentration gradient, generating efficient ionic current in the physically adsorptive direct-current triboiontronic nanogenerator (PDC-TING).
A PDC-TING where introducing redox reactions by altering metal charge collectors enhanced performance further, leading to a more efficient synergistic DC-TING (SDC-TING).

For a conscious property C, the canonical functionalist claims that C should be invariant under isomorphism of canonical functional structures. That is, if two systems have the same canonical functional structure, then they cannot differ in consciousness-relevant functional properties. Equivalently, if two states have identical complete future behavior under the relevant interface, then they share the same consciousness-relevant functional property, which factors through the canonical quotient.

Used in a specific anti-interpretivist sense, meaning that functional roles are determined through possible interactions, interventions, and counterfactual transitions, not by an observer's arbitrary semantic mapping, rather than being independent of all environmental relations.

Refers not to actual observed behavior or a finite behavioral sample, but to the complete counterfactual input-output profile under a specified interface, encompassing all possible future interactions and responses.

data.title: Bioinspired iontronic architectures for neuromorphic intelligence
data.abstract: This paper introduces bioinspired iontronic architectures designed for neuromorphic intelligence, addressing the limitations of silicon-based systems by mimicking the brain's embodied ionic operation. These architectures leverage nanoscale ionic transport, chemical reactions, and energy flow to replicate neural functions like neurotransmission, memory, and learning. By integrating sensing, memory, and computation directly into matter and charge, the proposed iontronic systems offer a path toward energy-efficient, self-organizing, brain-inspired intelligence.
data.thesis: Iontronic architectures, inspired by the brain's use of ions as charge carriers, offer a path toward energy-efficient, self-organizing, brain-inspired neuromorphic matter by establishing a physical basis for embodied intelligence through hierarchical integration of neural functions at the channel, interface, and network levels.

data.title: Volumetric bioprinting of VoluHearts: a next-generation cardiac in vitro model
data.abstract: VoluHeart is a novel cardiac in vitro model created using ultra-fast volumetric bioprinting of induced pluripotent stem cell-derived cardiomyocytes and cardiac fibroblasts within dynamic hydrogels. This bi-chambered model recreates anatomically relevant heart structures, exhibits spontaneous contractions and calcium waves, and demonstrates responsiveness to injury. Its scalability and compatibility with experimental readouts highlight its potential as a high-throughput platform for disease modeling and drug screening.
data.thesis: VoluHeart, a novel cardiac in vitro model combining volumetric bioprinting, dynamic biomaterials, and iPSC-CMs, recreates anatomically relevant heart structures and demonstrates potential as a scalable, high-throughput platform for disease modeling and drug screening, compatible with experimental and clinical readouts, and responsive to injury.

data.claim: The biological brain operates as an embodied ionic system, fundamentally distinct from silicon-based neuromorphic approaches, achieving orders of magnitude greater energy efficiency (~20 W vs. megawatts) due to coupled nanoscale ionic transport, chemical reactions, and energy flow, unlike von Neumann architectures.
data.support: Comparison of the brain's power budget and operational principles (ionic, coupled processes) with silicon-based AI's limitations (von Neumann separation, electron-based, high power consumption).

data.claim: Current electronic neuromorphic devices, while reproducing some synaptic plasticity and in-memory learning, remain limited by their electron-based information carriers, centralized energy supply, and functional mimicry without true physical embodiment.
data.support: Discussion of ferroelectric and two-dimensional material devices' partial success and inherent limitations compared to biological systems.

data.claim: Iontronic systems, by using ions as charge carriers and integrating nanoscale ionic transport, chemical reactions, and energy flow, can replicate neural functions such as Ca2+-gated neurotransmission, memory encoding via asymmetric electrical double layers, and plasticity through memristive ionic networks.
data.support: Proposal of iontronic mechanisms at different scales (channels, EDLs, networks) as direct analogues to biological neural functions.

data.claim: Ionic-electronic hybrid platforms have partially addressed limitations by using external bias to regulate interfacial redox reactions and electrical double layer (EDL) dynamics, enabling ionic processes to modulate electronic transport and co-localize sensing, memory, and computation.
data.support: Cites reference [1] for an ion-electronic hybrid artificial neuron.

data.claim: Realizing embodied intelligence requires a shift towards self-powered ionically coupled systems driven by intrinsic interfacial electrochemical dynamics, where matter, energy, and information are intrinsically linked.
data.support: Logical extension from the identified limitations of current systems and the proposed advantages of iontronics.

data.claim: Artificial nanofluidic channels, with dimensions comparable to the Debye length, can replicate the coupling of ionic migration, field modulation, and interfacial chemistry, converting ionic motion into electrical energy via interfacial redox coupling.
data.support: Cites reference [2] for vertical iontronic energy storage and reference [3] for photoresponsive halide channels.

data.claim: Asymmetric or gated nanochannels can function as ionic rectifiers and transistors for logical operations by modulating ion flow polarity and magnitude.
data.support: Cites reference [4] for bioinspired carbon nanotube-based nanofluidic ionic transistor.

data.claim: Triboelectric-induced polarization in triboiontronic systems can generate transient interfacial electric fields that drive ion redistribution, establishing concentration gradients and directional interfacial potentials, thereby converting mechanical stimuli into interfacial electrostatic modulation without continuous power input.
data.support: Cites reference [5] for harnessing triboiontronic Maxwell's demon and reference [6] for unlocking interfacial charge.

data.claim: Asymmetric electrical double layers (EDLs) in triboiontronic systems exhibit ionic memristive behavior, analogous to synaptic plasticity, supporting excitation-response coupling, temporal integration, and memory effects through hysteretic EDL states.
data.support: Cites reference [7] for neuromorphic functions with a polyelectrolyte-confined fluidic memristor.

data.claim: Iontronic systems can realize the brain's principles of bidirectional signaling, synaptic plasticity, and spatiotemporal integration through devices like Janus MXene membranes (for excitation/inhibition balance) and single-pore nanofluidic memristors (for reconfigurable conductance and potentiation/depression).
data.support: Cites reference [8] for iontronic logic control and reference [9] for single-pore nanofluidic logic memristor.

data.claim: Geometrically asymmetric hydrogel-based iontronics can integrate mechanical and chemical stimuli, linking deformation-induced ion redistribution with logic gating, enabling real-time tactile sensing and feedback.
data.support: Cites reference [10] for mechano-driven neuromimetic logic gates.

data.claim: Future iontronic systems should achieve adaptive temporal dynamics, merge material dynamics with computation, and integrate energy consumption as a cognitive feature to realize true energy-cognition integration.
data.support: Outlines the 'FUTURE DIRECTIONS' for the field, emphasizing challenges like precise control, reliable mappings, and stability.

data.claim: The biological brain's operational principles (ionic transport, energy efficiency, embodied intelligence) represent the ideal model for next-generation AI.
The fundamental mechanisms of neural function (e.g., neurotransmission, memory, plasticity) can be effectively mimicked and scaled using iontronic materials and architectures.
The intrinsic coupling of matter, energy, and information in iontronic systems will lead to emergent cognitive abilities beyond current electron-based AI.
Volumetric bioprinting allows for the rapid creation of complex, multi-chambered cardiac structures like bi-chambered VoluHearts and 4-chambered heart replicas.
data.support: The printing of a bi-chambered VoluHeart (~165 mm³) and a 4-chambered heart replica was achieved within 21 seconds, as shown in Figure 1A.

data.claim: The dynamic HybriGel biomaterial promotes superior iPSC-CM network formation compared to conventional GelMA hydrogels.
data.support: Quantitative analysis of average network length and number of intercellular junctions, and fluorescent images of iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes stained with cardiac troponin T after 14 days of culture, showed enhanced network formation in HybriGel compared to GelMA (Figure 1B).

data.claim: VoluHearts exhibit spontaneous contractions and directional calcium waves, indicating functional activity.
data.support: Within one week of culture, VoluHearts were observed to exhibit spontaneous contractions and directional calcium waves, supported by calcium handling analysis.

data.claim: iPSC-CMs within VoluHearts align along the septum and chamber walls, demonstrating organized tissue architecture.
data.support: Immunofluorescence imaging confirmed the alignment of iPSC-CMs along the septum and chamber walls (Figure 1C).

data.claim: VoluHearts can be used to model myocardial injury, as demonstrated by localized disruption of electromechanical coupling following an apical cryoinjury.
data.support: An apical cryoinjury was applied to the apex, resulting in localized disruption of electromechanical coupling, which was assessed using calcium imaging (Figure 1D).

data.claim: Current in vitro cardiac models struggle to capture the native architecture of the heart and consequently limit the assessment of cardiac functional outputs.
iPSC-CMs are a suitable and representative cell source for modeling human cardiac tissue in vitro.
The chosen readouts (cell viability, network formation, beating rate, immunofluorescence, calcium handling) are sufficient indicators of cardiac function and disease modeling.
The apical cryoinjury adequately simulates a myocardial infarction for validating disease modeling capabilities.

data.title: At the Cutting Edge of the Impossible: A Tribute to Vladimir P. Demikhov
data.abstract: Vladimir P. Demikhov (1916–1998) pioneered experimental intrathoracic transplantations and coronary artery bypass surgery, laying the groundwork for modern heart and lung transplantation and coronary artery disease treatment. Despite his significant contributions, his work was often met with international isolation, speculation, and criticism, particularly regarding his controversial dog head transplantation. This paper provides an account of Demikhov's life and work, highlighting his role as one of the 20th century's greatest experimental surgeons.
data.thesis: Vladimir P. Demikhov (1916–1998) was a pioneering experimental surgeon who performed the world's first experimental intrathoracic transplantations and coronary artery bypass operations, heralding the modern era of heart and lung transplantation and surgical treatment of coronary artery disease, despite international isolation and controversy, particularly regarding his head transplantation experiments.

data.claim: Demikhov designed the first mechanical cardiac-assist device in 1937, capable of maintaining circulation for approximately 5 hours in an animal whose heart had been excised.
data.support: Description of the device's function and its historical context as the 'first ever'.

data.claim: Demikhov performed intrathoracic transplantations of a heart, a lung, and the heart and lungs together in dogs in early 1946, marking the first successful procedures of this kind in any mammal.
data.support: Specific date (June 30, 1946) of a dog surviving 9.5 hours after heterotopic heart-lung transplantation, and Cooper's credit for his 'ingenious' technique.

data.claim: Demikhov's experimental animals lived as long as 30 days after undergoing transplantation of both lungs, attributed to his preservation of the nerves of the diaphragm and normal function of abdominal organs.
data.support: Stated outcome of his transplantation experiments.

data.claim: Demikhov performed the world's first successful coronary bypass operation on a dog on July 29, 1953, with four dogs surviving longer than 2 years and proven anastomotic patency.
data.support: Specific date, survival rates, and confirmation of patency, with acknowledgment of his pioneering contributions by V.I. Kolesov.

data.claim: Demikhov's canine head transplantation in 1954, with a maximal survival of 29 days, was arguably the most controversial experimental operation of the 20th century, leading to widespread ethical debate and accusations of charlatanism.
data.support: Description of the experiment, its maximal survival, and historical accounts of its reception, including Christiaan Barnard's reaction and media coverage.

data.claim: Demikhov received belated international recognition, including membership in the Royal Scientific Society of Uppsala (1960), publication of his monograph (1960), and the first Pioneer Award from the International Society for Heart and Lung Transplantation (1989).
data.support: Historical records of awards, publications, and direct quotes from Christiaan Barnard acknowledging Demikhov as the 'father of heart and lung transplantation'.

data.claim: Demikhov's work, initially considered too new and unconventional, ultimately led to ideas that became routine parts of clinical practice by the time of his death in 1998.
data.support: Summary of the changing attitudes towards his work over time and the concluding statement about his legacy.

data.claim: The inherent value and importance of experimental surgical research, particularly in the field of organ transplantation.
The reliability of historical accounts, including personal recollections from Demikhov's daughter and cited publications, in reconstructing his life and work.
The significance of 'firsts' in scientific and medical history as indicators of pioneering contributions.

data.question: The author states that head transplantation 'will never find its clinical application' and is 'simply impossible,' but then immediately follows with the rhetorical question 'Or . . . or will it?', creating an unresolved ambiguity about its ultimate theoretical possibility or utility.
data.context: The definitive statement of impossibility for clinical application of head transplantation and the author's subsequent rhetorical question challenging that certainty.

data.title: Activity-dependent extracellular potassium changes in unmyelinated versus myelinated areas in olfactory regions of the isolated female guinea-pig brain
data.abstract: This study investigates activity-dependent extracellular potassium ([K+]o) changes in the piriform cortex (PC) of isolated guinea-pig brains, a region with distinct myelinated and unmyelinated fiber bundles. We found that [K+]o rises were larger and faster in unmyelinated layers compared to myelinated areas during seizure-like events and high-frequency stimulations. The results suggest that the larger [K+]o shifts in unmyelinated structures may contribute to seizure generation.
data.thesis: Activity-dependent extracellular potassium ([K+]o) changes are intrinsically different in myelinated versus unmyelinated cortical regions, with larger [K+]o shifts generated in unmyelinated structures potentially serving as a vehicle for seizure generation.

data.title: The in vitro isolated whole guinea pig brain as a model to study epileptiform activity patterns
data.abstract: This paper introduces the in vitro isolated guinea pig brain as a model for studying epileptiform activity patterns. This preparation maintains functional connectivity between brain structures and preserves neuro-glio-vascular interactions, offering advantages over traditional in vivo experiments or in vitro slices. It allows for the study of cellular and network determinants of interictal and ictal discharges, as well as associated changes in extracellular ion and blood-brain permeability, under conditions closely resembling in vivo states.
data.thesis: The in vitro isolated whole guinea pig brain (IWB) is a unique and valuable experimental model that overcomes limitations of in vitro slices by preserving functional connectivity, neuro-glio-vascular interactions, and the blood-brain barrier, allowing for the study of systemic and neurovascular changes during ictogenesis and region-specific epileptiform activity patterns relevant to human focal epilepsies.

data.title: Peripheral blood mononuclear cell secretome from patients with autoimmune encephalitis promotes seizures in vitro
data.abstract: This study demonstrates that the secretome from peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) of autoimmune encephalitis (AE) patients induces seizure-like events and microglial activation in an in vitro guinea pig brain model, independently of neuronal surface antibodies. The secretome from AE patients showed altered levels of various inflammatory cytokines compared to healthy controls. These findings suggest that peripheral inflammatory mediators contribute to seizure generation in AE, highlighting a potential non-antibody-mediated pathogenic mechanism.
data.thesis: The secretome released by peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) from autoimmune encephalitis (AE) patients contributes to seizure generation and microglial activation, suggesting that peripheral inflammatory mediators play a pathogenic role in AE seizures beyond possible antibody-mediated mechanisms.

data.claim: During 4-aminopyridine (4AP)-induced seizure-like events (SLEs), [K+]o increases are larger and faster in the unmyelinated superficial piriform cortex (PCsup) layer I compared to the myelinated lateral olfactory tract (LOT).
data.support: Simultaneous [K+]o measurements in PCsup and LOT during 4AP perfusion (n=16 brains), showing significantly higher [K+]o at SLE onset (Wilcoxon Signed Rank test, Z = 2.197, p = 0.0245) and at K+ peak (Wilcoxon Signed Rank test, Z = 2.922, p = 0.00168). (Fig. 2)

data.claim: High-frequency electrical stimulation (hfST) of the LOT, mimicking pre-seizure discharges, generates statistically larger [K+]o shifts in the unmyelinated PCsup layer I compared to the myelinated LOT and deeper PC layers (PCdeep).
data.support: Simultaneous [K+]o monitoring in PCsup, LOT, and PCdeep during hfST (n=19 in 10 brains for PCsup vs LOT; n=17 in 11 brains for PCsup vs PCdeep), showing significantly larger peaks in PCsup (Wilcoxon Signed Ranks Test, p = 0.000248 vs LOT; p < 0.0001 vs PC500; p = 0.00781 vs PC750). (Fig. 3, 5)

data.claim: During hfST, the dynamics of [K+]o increase differ between PCsup and LOT/PCdeep: PCsup shows a rapid rise to a plateau within the first few trains, while LOT and PCdeep exhibit a slower, more progressive accumulation.
data.support: Analysis of [K+]o velocity vs [K+]o values (Fig. 4A, 5A) and polynomial/linear curve fitting of peak [K+]o amplitudes across consecutive hfST trains (Fig. 4B, 5D).

data.claim: The decay of [K+]o after hfST is significantly faster in the unmyelinated PCsup layer I compared to the myelinated PCdeep layers.
data.support: Measurement of [K+]o levels at the end and 7 seconds after hfST, showing a significantly faster K+ decay ratio in PCsup (paired sample t-test, t(18) = -3.42, p = 0.00302). (Fig. 6B)

data.claim: Hyperexcitability associated with afterdischarges (induced by hfST or SLEs) leads to a prolongation of [K+]o increase and further augmentation, predominantly in the deep PC sites.
data.support: Comparison of K+ decay in PCsup and PCdeep during afterdischarges, showing a statistically different and increased [K+]o in PCdeep (paired sample t-test, t(6) = -2.925, p = 0.0265). (Fig. 6B, 7A/B)

data.claim: Pharmacological blockade of Kir4.1 potassium channels with BaCl2 significantly enhances hfST-induced [K+]o shifts in both superficial (PCsup) and deep (PCdeep) PC layers and decreases the threshold for afterdischarge generation.
data.support: [K+]o measurements before and after BaCl2 perfusion (n=11 in 7 brains), showing significant increases in maximal [K+]o in both PCsup (paired sample t-test, t(10) = -6.3024, p < 0.0001) and PCdeep (Wilcoxon signed rank test, Z = -2.891, p = 9.766 E-4). (Fig. 7C)

data.claim: BaCl2 administration slows the return of [K+]o to baseline in both PCsup and PCdeep after hfST, with a more pronounced slowing in PCdeep.
data.support: [K+]o decay measurements before and after BaCl2 (n=5 brains), showing significant effects of 'site of recording' and 'treatment with BaCl2' on decay, and significant pairwise differences in PCdeep (Tukey post hoc test, p = 0.0417). (Fig. 7D)

data.claim: The isolated guinea-pig brain preparation is a valid model for studying in vivo [K+]o dynamics and excitability in olfactory regions.
K+-sensitive electrodes accurately measure extracellular K+ concentrations.
4-aminopyridine (4AP) and high-frequency electrical stimulation (hfST) reliably induce seizure-like activity and mimic preictal phases, respectively.

BaCl2, at the concentration used (100 μM), primarily and selectively blocks Kir4.1 potassium channels, and any non-selective effects (e.g., on Ca2+ channels) do not invalidate the interpretation regarding K+ buffering.
The histological identification of myelinated and unmyelinated regions (LOT, PCsup, PCdeep) is accurate.

The laminar organization of the piriform cortex, including the distribution of neurons and myelinated/unmyelinated fibers, is consistent with previous literature and the observed functional differences.
The in vitro isolated guinea pig brain (IWB) retains functional connectivity between brain structures and maintains interactions between neuronal, glial, and vascular compartments.
data.support: Demonstrated by the preservation of intrinsic connectivity within and between diencephalic and telencephalic structures, and the functional preservation of the vascular system, blood-brain barrier, and their interaction with brain parenchyma. Electron microscopy showed cerebral capillaries and BBB specializations retain structural integrity after 5h in vitro.

data.claim: The IWB preparation offers experimental advantages over in vivo conditions and in vitro slices for studying brain activity.
data.support: Facilitated access to ventral cortical structures, direct visual control for electrode placement, mechanical stability of recordings (absence of respiration and pulsation artifacts), ability to perform simultaneous field potential recordings from different regions/hemispheres, and preservation of larger neuronal networks compared to slices.

data.claim: Acute epileptiform activities, including interictal and ictal discharges that reproduce abnormal patterns observed in human focal epilepsies, can be induced and analyzed in the IWB.
data.support: Pharmacological manipulations (e.g., arterial perfusion of bicuculline methiodide (BMI), 4-aminopyridine (4AP), kainic acid) induce seizure-like events and periodic interictal spiking. These patterns include low-voltage fast activity (FA) and hypersynchronous activity (HSA) similar to chronic models of temporal lobe epilepsy and human mesial temporal lobe epilepsy.

data.claim: Cellular and network determinants of interictal and ictal discharges can be identified in the IWB.
data.support: Simultaneous extracellular and intracellular recordings, current-source-density (CSD) analysis, and voltage-sensitive dye (VSD) imaging have been used to demonstrate local generation of fast activity, involvement of inhibitory networks in pre-ictal spikes and seizure onset, and specific neuronal populations (e.g., layer II cells in piriform cortex for 4AP-induced seizures).

data.claim: Changes in extracellular ion concentrations (K+, pH) and blood-brain barrier (BBB) permeability associated with epileptiform activity can be identified and analyzed in the IWB.
data.support: Ion-sensitive microelectrodes demonstrated rapid increases in extracellular K+ and biphasic pH changes during interictal spikes and focal seizures. BBB permeability was evaluated by FITC-albumin extravasation and ZO-1 down-regulation after seizures, and by testing the effect of high K+ solutions and BBB-impermeable substances.

data.claim: Epileptiform patterns in the IWB are region-specific and can be independent from neighboring areas.
data.support: BMI induces ictal events in the limbic region but periodic interictal spiking in the olfactory cortex, with PC spikes preventing seizure invasion. 4AP induces different patterns in olfactory and limbic regions. Kainic acid induces seizures restricted to hippocampus/mEC, with PC and neocortex not directly involved.

data.claim: The IWB is a valuable model for studying the induction of non-constitutive adhesion factors, BBB tight junction molecules, and pro-inflammatory molecules during seizures.
data.support: The IWB has been utilized to test the induction of ICAM, selectins, ZO-1, and IL-1beta after seizures induced by BMI, 4AP, kainic acid, and pilocarpine.

data.claim: The physiological and pathological mechanisms observed in the isolated guinea pig brain are sufficiently homologous to those in the human brain to provide relevant insights into human epilepsy.
Acute induction of epileptiform activity with pro-convulsive drugs in a naive brain can model aspects of ictogenesis relevant to chronic epileptic conditions.

The experimental manipulations (e.g., arterial perfusion, electrode insertion) do not fundamentally alter the underlying brain networks and cellular processes in a way that invalidates the findings regarding epileptiform activity.
The secretome from PBMCs derived from AE patients induces seizure-like events (SLEs) in an in vitro whole guinea pig brain preparation.
data.support: Extracellular recordings in the medial entorhinal cortex (mEC) and hippocampal dentate gyrus (DG) showed SLEs after arterial perfusion with AE patient-derived hPBMC secretome, co-perfused with lipopolysaccharide (LPS) and human recombinant albumin (hALB) (Figure 2B,C).

data.claim: The secretome from PBMCs derived from AE patients induces microglial activation, characterized by a shift from resting ramified morphology to an activated amoeboid shape, in an in vitro whole guinea pig brain preparation.
data.support: Morphological analysis of ionized calcium-binding adapter molecule 1 (Iba1)-positive glial cells showed ramification index (RI) values closer to 1 (amoeboid shape) in brains treated with AE patient-derived hPBMC secretome, compared to values closer to 0 (ramified shape) in controls (Figure 3).

data.claim: The secretome from PBMCs derived from AE patients exhibits significantly lower concentrations of anti-inflammatory cytokines (interleukin (IL)-10, IL-1Ra, tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α), IL-2, and IL-6) compared to healthy subjects.
data.support: Multiplex ELLA immunoassay analysis of PBMC secretome showed statistically significant lower levels of IL-10, IL-1Ra, TNF-α, IL-2, and IL-6 in AE patients compared to healthy controls (Figure 4).

data.claim: Treatment with lipopolysaccharide (LPS) and human recombinant albumin (hALB) alone does not induce electrophysiological alterations in the in vitro brain preparation.
data.support: Previous laboratory findings and current observations (n=3) confirmed no electrophysiological alterations with LPS and hALB treatment.

data.claim: Arterial perfusion with LPS, hALB, and hPBMC secretome derived from healthy subjects does not evoke any epileptiform activity.
data.support: Experimental protocol using healthy subject-derived hPBMC secretome (n=13) did not induce epileptiform activity.

data.claim: Peripheral inflammatory mediators from AE PBMCs contribute to seizure generation in AE patients, suggesting a mechanism independent of neuronal surface antibodies (NSAbs).
data.support: This claim is an overarching interpretation derived from the empirical findings that AE patient-derived secretome induces seizures and microglial activation, in contrast to healthy controls, and the observed cytokine profile, supporting the initial hypothesis of NSAbs-independent mechanisms.

data.claim: Autoimmune encephalitis (AE) is characterized by inflammatory processes in the central nervous system and frequently presents with seizures.
Mechanisms independent of neuronal surface antibodies (NSAbs) are likely to contribute to seizures in AE patients.

The in vitro whole guinea pig brain preparation is an ideal model to study the specific direct effects of blood-derived molecules on brain inflammation and excitability in an intact, undamaged brain, especially given the absence of peripheral immune cells or blood-borne molecules.

The co-perfusion of endotoxin lipopolysaccharide (LPS) and human recombinant serum albumin (hALB) effectively induces and mimics a mild functional blood-brain barrier impairment in the in vitro brain preparation.
PBMC secretome represents an intact and stable source of immune biomarkers, reflecting the intrinsic functionality of the patient's immune cells more reliably than serum cytokine levels.

data.question: Lack of direct access to measure K+ increases between the axonal membrane and myelin.
data.context: Cannot directly measure K+ variations in that specific space, only with extracellular electrodes.

data.question: Unavailability of Kir4.1 channel blockers more selective than BaCl2.
data.context: The specific contribution of oligodendrocytes to K+ buffering could not be assessed in more detail.

data.question: The scope of the current study did not include evaluating the impact of [K+]o fluctuations on neuronal membrane excitability through correlation with simultaneously recorded extracellular and intracellular activities.
data.context: This specific aspect of K+ dynamics and neuronal excitability was not addressed in the current work.

data.question: Understanding the complex interactions between synaptic and non-synaptic events/processes that sustain focal seizure activity.
data.context: This is the broader context for understanding seizure generation and progression, which the paper contributes to by studying K+ dynamics.

data.question: Correlate extracellular K+ changes with simultaneously recorded extracellular and intracellular activities to evaluate the impact of [K+]o fluctuations on neuronal membrane excitability.

The abstract claims that K+ containment is more efficient in myelinated regions, but the results indicate that K+ decay (a measure of buffering efficiency) is faster in the unmyelinated superficial piriform cortex (PCsup) compared to the myelinated deep piriform cortex (PCdeep).
data.context: The claim in the abstract ('K+ containment in the extracellular space is more efficient in brain tissue that contains myelinated fibers compared to unmyelinated regions.') and the experimental results ('The [K] decay is faster in superficial PC than in deep PC.' - Section 3, and 'slower [K+]o decay in PCdeep compared to the PCsup' - Section 4).

data.question: Inability to generate spontaneous seizures.
data.context: Pro-epileptic drugs and high-frequency stimulations must be employed to obtain seizure activity.

data.question: Not suitable for detailed experiments on cellular mechanisms of seizure generation/progression.
data.context: Detailed cellular mechanism studies, feasible in less complex preparations like brain slices, are not allowed in the IWB preparation.

data.question: Limited possibility to perform effective local application of blocking drugs when the whole limbic region is massively activated during an ictal event.
data.context: Restricts the ability to apply targeted pharmacological interventions during widespread seizure activity.

data.question: Animal species constraint.
data.context: The model is limited to guinea pigs, proechymis, and rabbits, and attempts to isolate brains from rats and mice have failed due to differences in vascular features.

data.question: Lack of commercial antibodies specifically acting against guinea-pig antigens.
data.context: This can hinder certain molecular and immunohistochemical studies.

data.question: Limited duration of recording.
data.context: The preparation is viable only for 5-7 hours, restricting long-term experimental observations.

data.question: Isolate brains from chronically epileptic guinea pigs to study network changes induced by the epileptogenic process.
Data were collected from a limited number of subjects with heterogeneous subtypes of AE.
data.context: In seronegative cases, the possibility that patients possess unidentified NSAbs cannot be excluded, especially when a full second-level testing was not performed.

data.question: Only a limited subset of inflammatory modulators was analyzed.
data.context: Other cytokines or their combinations may also contribute to ictogenesis, which were not investigated in this study.

data.question: The study is preliminary.
data.context: The results are insufficient to elucidate the precise effect of each individual immune mediator.

data.question: Whether acute microgliosis represents a consequence or a cause of seizure activity.
data.context: The study observed microglial activation in response to AE patient-derived PBMC secretome and associated SLEs, but the acute experimental conditions do not allow for ascertaining causality.

data.question: Conduct further research involving larger cohorts of patients with AE without seizures, patients with epilepsy of nonimmunological origin, and those with systemic autoimmune diseases without seizures.
Achieve a better understanding of peripheral immunological mediators, particularly PBMC secretome components like cytokines, as a potential common fingerprint of immune-mediated seizures.
Translate findings into clinical practice to guide the management of seizures in patients with AE by considering additional mechanisms that go beyond the traditional antibody-mediated mechanisms.

data.significance: This figure demonstrates the correlation between seizure activity, extracellular potassium dynamics, and blood-brain barrier (BBB) disruption, as evidenced by FITC-albumin extravasation, highlighting the model's utility for studying neurovascular changes during ictogenesis.

data.caption: Experimental design. Healthy volunteers and selected autoimmune encephalitis (AE) or suspected AE patients were recruited and whole blood samples were collected. Then, peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) were isolated from whole blood and put in culture. After 6h, PBMC secretome was collected, and it was infused in the in vitro brain preparation. At the end of each experiment, brains were processed for immunofluorescence analysis. PBMC secretome was analyzed by Multiplex immunoassay ELLA. Created in https://BioRender.com. DG, dentate gyrus; FP, Field Potential; IFI, Indirect Immunoflurescence; mEC, medial entorhinal cortex; PC, piriform cortex; RFU, relative fluorescence units.

Then, "PBMCs isolation" is shown, followed by "PBMCs culture" at 37°C for 6h to obtain "PBMCs' secretome". This secretome is then used in two parallel experimental branches: "FP recordings in in vitro brain preparation" (showing a guinea pig brain with DG, mEC, PC regions highlighted) and "IFI assay". Finally, "Multiplex immunoassay (ELLA™)" is shown with a generic signal curve (Signal (RFU) vs [Cytokines] (pg/ml)).
data.significance: This figure clearly outlines the entire experimental methodology, from sample collection to in vitro brain perfusion and subsequent analyses, providing a comprehensive overview of how the study was conducted.

Each experimental protocol lasted 4h. (B) Seizurelike events (SLEs) simultaneously recorded in medial entorhinal cortex (mEC) and in hippocampal dentate gyrus (DG) after arterial perfusion with PBMC secretome of patients positive for anti-N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptor, anti-leucine-rich glioma-inactivated 1 protein (LGI1), and anti-contactin-associated protein 2 (CASPR2) and (C) AE patients without detectable antibodies against neuronal antigens. data.caption: Cytokine concentration in healthy controls (CTR) and autoimmune encephalitis (AE) or suspected AE patients in peripheral blood mononuclear cell (PBMC) secretome at time 6 (t6). data.title: Non-materialist physicalism: an experimentally testable conjecture
data.abstract: This paper introduces Non-Materialist Physicalism to address the unexplained existence of consciousness and the phenomenal binding problem within natural science. It proposes that consciousness arises from quantum-coherent neuronal superpositions at sub-femtosecond timescales, enabling unitary experiential objects. The conjecture yields an experimentally testable prediction of a structural match between phenomenology and physical states, which can be confirmed or falsified using molecular matter-wave interferometry on in vitro neuronal networks.
data.thesis: This paper argues that if physicalism and the ontological unity of science are to be saved, then we will need to revise our notions of both 1) the intrinsic nature of the physical and 2) the quasi-classicality of neurons. In conjunction, these two hypotheses yield a novel, bizarre but experimentally testable prediction of quantum superpositions ('Schrödinger's cat states') of neuronal feature-processors in the CNS at sub-femtosecond timescales.

data.claim: Mankind's most successful story of the world, natural science, leaves the existence of consciousness wholly unexplained.
data.support: Widely acknowledged philosophical problem (explanatory gap, Hard Problem).

data.claim: The phenomenal binding problem deepens the mystery of consciousness.
data.support: Observation that distributively processed neuronal micro-experiences are bound into unitary experiential objects, which neither classical nor quantum physics seem to allow.

data.claim: If physicalism and the ontological unity of science are to be saved, then we must revise our notions of the intrinsic nature of the physical and the quasi-classicality of neurons.
data.support: Argument that current materialist ontology and classical neuroscience cannot explain consciousness or binding.

data.claim: Our minds consist of ultra-rapidly decohering neuronal superpositions in strict accordance with unmodified quantum physics.
data.support: Conjecture based on the completeness of quantum mechanics and the need to explain phenomenal binding.

data.claim: Natural selection has harnessed the properties of these neuronal superpositions so our minds run phenomenally bound world-simulations.
data.support: Evolutionary argument for the adaptive advantage of quantum-coherent binding.

data.claim: The non-classical interference signature of conscious neuronal superpositions will be independently experimentally detectable.
data.support: Proposed experimental protocol using molecular matter-wave interferometry on in vitro neuronal networks.

data.claim: The phenomenology of one's mind reveals the intrinsic nature of the physical.
data.support: Argument following 'new idealists' (Schopenhauer, Russell, et al.) that physics describes relational properties, but not intrinsic nature.

data.claim: The Hard Problem of consciousness is an artifact of materialist metaphysics.
data.support: Reinterpretation of the problem based on the 'new idealist' view of the physical's intrinsic nature.

data.claim: If our ordinary understanding of the fundamental nature of matter and energy as described by physics is correct, and if our neurons are effectively decohered classical objects, then we all ought to be zombies.
data.support: Logical deduction from the premises of classical materialism and neuroscience, leading to the Hard Problem.

data.claim: The argument from microphysical simplicity (Chalmers' challenge a) is addressed by quantum field theory, where diverse values of fundamental fields yield a vast palette of micro-qualia.
data.support: Shift from particle-based ontology to quantum field-theoretic ontology, where fields take a vast range of values.

data.claim: The argument from structural mismatch (Chalmers' challenge b) is an artifact of the coarse-grained temporal resolution of our investigative tools.
data.support: Hypothesis that apparent mismatch disappears at sub-femtosecond timescales, where synchronous firings are actually successive quantum-coherent superpositions.

data.claim: The conjecture will be falsified if the subtle non-classical neuronal interference effects typically detected are irrelevant 'noise'.
data.support: Explicit statement of a falsification condition for the central hypothesis.

data.claim: Phenomenal binding is impossible for discrete, membrane-bound, quasi-classical neurons or 'mind-dust'.
data.support: Argument that mere synchronous activation cannot bind experiences, drawing an analogy to separate minds not forming a mega-mind.

data.claim: Decoherence can be viewed as a progressive phenomenal unbinding, or effective dephasing is a solution to the phenomenal unbinding problem.
data.support: Reinterpretation of decoherence as a mechanism for the loss of phenomenal unity.

data.claim: Our world-simulations must run at anything from around 10^13 to 10^20+ quantum-coherent neuronal 'frames' per second.
data.support: Reinterpretation of Max Tegmark's calculations regarding brain activity timescales.

data.claim: If the physicalistic idealist conjecture is correct, then our everyday classical world-simulations are underpinned at sub-femtosecond timescales by macroscopic quantum-coherent physical states of the CNS.
data.support: Central prediction derived from the combination of physicalistic idealism and the need for quantum coherence to explain binding.

data.claim: The proposed experimental protocol involves training in vitro neuronal networks and then using molecular matter-wave interferometry to detect interference signatures of neuronal superpositions.
data.support: Detailed description of a multi-step experimental procedure.

data.claim: The experiment will confirm the conjecture if it detects non-classical interference signatures that robustly implicate the same neuronal feature-processors identified by classical neuroscience as synchronously activated during object recognition.
data.support: Specific criteria for experimental confirmation, contrasting with 'psychotic noise' or 'collapse-like deviation'.

data.claim: On any classical account of mind, such a perfect structural match between detected quantum superpositions and classical neuronal activity is either physically impossible or vanishingly improbable.
data.support: Contrast with the expectations of orthodox neuroscience and materialist philosophy.

data.claim: Zurek's 'quantum Darwinism' must be applied to the CNS to understand how non-psychotic phenomenal binding of distributed neuronal feature-processors could have evolved.
data.support: Argument that selection pressure can act on proliferating, decohering world-simulations, leading to fitter superpositions.

data.claim: Non-classical phenomenal binding is a necessary precondition for full-spectrum general intelligence.
data.support: Argument that without unitary agents, there is no intelligence or problem-solving capacity.

data.claim: Sentient organic minds are biological devices that can answer questions beyond those a classical Turing machine can answer or even pose.
data.support: Claim that the investigation of qualia requires direct experience, which classical computers lack.

data.claim: Natural science promises a complete story of the universe, where no 'element of reality' should be missing.
Every gross property of the natural world must be theoretically reducible to fundamental physics.
Our presupposition that the intrinsic character of the physical lacks phenomenal properties is an additional metaphysical assumption, not a scientific discovery.

data.title: Olfactory input to the parahippocampal region of the isolated guinea pig brain reveals weak entorhinal-to-perirhinal interactions
data.abstract: This study investigated the propagation of olfactory input from the lateral olfactory tract (LOT) into the parahippocampal region of isolated guinea pig brains using electrophysiological and optical imaging techniques. Findings indicate that olfactory input primarily activates the entorhinal cortex (EC) but does not massively propagate to the perirhinal cortex (PRC). This suggests that strong inhibitory control within the EC hinders EC-to-PRC activity.
data.thesis: The olfactory input to the parahippocampal region is primarily confined to the entorhinal cortex, with limited or no direct or indirect synchronous activation of the perirhinal cortex, suggesting a powerful inhibitory control mechanism hinders activity propagation from the entorhinal to the perirhinal cortex.

data.question: Technical limitations in resolving low synaptic activity with a widespread laminar distribution.
data.context: May exist when field potential laminar analysis is utilized or when the amount of excitation is below the threshold detection of the optical system.

data.question: The signal generated by the narrow cortical strip of cortex formed by area 35 located at the fundus of the rhinal fissure could not be resolved with the imaging technique.
data.context: The presence of a large-capacity vessel enfolded in the pia mater attenuated the intensity of the signal detected by the system, preventing full characterization of area 35 activity with optical imaging.

data.question: The mechanisms which control the propagation of activity from the EC to the PRC (and vice versa).
data.context: Understanding these mechanisms is crucial for clarifying the functional connectivity within the parahippocampal region, especially given the discrepancy between anatomical projections and observed physiological activity.

data.question: Perform further combined morphological and electrophysiological studies at the cellular level to clarify the mechanisms controlling the propagation of activity from the EC to the PRC (and vice versa).

Anatomical data support the view that the olfactory input reaches the most rostral portion of the l-EC and that EC projects to PRC. However, the present electrophysiological and optical imaging study found no direct synchronous population response or massive activation of PRC (area 36) following LOT stimulation or EC activation.
data.context: Anatomical evidence of direct/indirect olfactory input and EC projections to the perirhinal cortex (PRC) and the lack of observed physiological activity in the PRC in response to lateral olfactory tract (LOT) or entorhinal cortex (EC) stimulation.

data.caption: FIG. 1. LOT-evoked field potential profiles in piriform, entorhinal, perirhinal and insular cortices. (A) Ventral view of the right hemisphere of the isolated whole brain. The 16-channel silicon probe was inserted in 10 different positions (black dots), each identified by a corresponding number. The recording sites were arranged in five pairs distributed along the rhinal sulcus at different rostro-caudal levels. (B) Electrode placements in PRC and insular cortex have been verified by the identification of the lesioned tissue (black arrow) on coronal slices stained with thionin. Overlapped LOT-evoked field potential profiles recorded in the 10 positions indicated in A and B. Phase reversal responses were detected only in PC and in EC (6-10). The traces recorded in the superficial and in the deep layers are indicated by the letters s and d, respectively. Only far fields were detected in the corresponding recording sites located in PRC and insular cortex (1–5). IC, insular cortex; 1-EC' lateral entorhinal cortex; m-EC, medial entorhinal cortex; PC, piriform cortex; PRC, perirhinal cortex.
data.description: This figure displays a ventral view of the right hemisphere of an isolated guinea pig brain (A) with 10 black dots indicating 16-channel silicon probe insertion sites. It also shows coronal slices stained with thionin (B) with black arrows pointing to lesioned tissue for electrode placement verification. Overlapped field potential profiles are presented for 10 different recording positions (1-10) in insular cortex (IC), piriform cortex (PC), perirhinal cortex (PRC), lateral entorhinal cortex (l-EC), and medial entorhinal cortex (m-EC) following LOT stimulation. Traces are labeled 's' for superficial and 'd' for deep layers. Phase reversal responses are visible in PC and EC (6-10), while only far fields are detected in IC and PRC (1-5). The y-axis scale is 1 mV and the x-axis scale is 25 ms.
data.key_data: 1 mV (amplitude scale); 25 ms (time scale)
data.significance: This figure demonstrates the distinct field potential responses to LOT stimulation across different parahippocampal regions, highlighting the presence of local synaptic activity (phase reversal) in PC and EC, but only far fields in IC and PRC, suggesting a lack of direct local activation in the latter.

data.caption: FIG. 2. Extracellular field potentials recorded from five adjacent subregions of PRC and EC located at the same rostro-caudal level. (A) Photomicrograph of the ventral view of the guinea pig brain. The aligned recording sites are represented by the black dots. (B) Portion of the coronal slice stained with thionin. The black lines indicate the five positions of the probe during the different recordings. (C) Overlapped field potential profiles recorded in 1-EC (1 and 2) show a clear phase-reversal component. The traces recorded in the superficial and in the deep layers are indicated by the letters s and d, respectively. Field potential profiles recorded in area 35 of the PRC (3) show a small-amplitude potential reversal at ≈30 ms delay. In area 36 (4-5) no laminar reversal was observed, suggesting that the responses represent a volume-conducted far field.
data.description: This figure presents extracellular field potentials recorded from five adjacent subregions of the perirhinal cortex (PRC) and entorhinal cortex (EC) at the same rostro-caudal level. Panel (A) shows a photomicrograph of the ventral view of the guinea pig brain with black dots indicating recording sites. Panel (B) displays a thionin-stained coronal slice with black lines marking probe positions. Panel (C) shows overlapped field potential profiles. Traces 1 and 2 from l-EC exhibit clear phase reversal, with superficial (s) and deep (d) layer recordings. Trace 3 from PRC area 35 shows a small-amplitude potential reversal at approximately 30 ms delay. Traces 4 and 5 from PRC area 36 show no laminar reversal. The y-axis scale is 0.5 mV and the x-axis scale is 25 ms.
data.key_data: 0.5 mV (amplitude scale); 25 ms (time scale); ~30 ms delay (potential reversal in PRC area 35)
data.significance: This figure further characterizes the neural circuits activated by LOT stimulation, confirming local synaptic activity in l-EC and inconsistently in PRC area 35, but consistently absent in PRC area 36, reinforcing the idea of limited direct olfactory input to the PRC.

data.caption: FIG. 3. (A) Schematic drawing of the recording positions in m-EC and area 36 in PRC. Laminar profiles in B1 and B1*, and B2 and B2* were recorded simultaneously in the m-EC and in the PRC, respectively, following LOT stimulation. By changing the intensity of the stimulus, responses with (B1*) or without (B1) a delayed activity in m-EC were evoked. The late m-EC activation was shown to be mediated by the activation of the hippocampus (see Biella & de Curtis, 2000). No local responses were observed in the PRC (B2 and B2*) in the two different conditions of stimulation. As positive control, field potential profiles were recorded in the same positions after stimulation of the nucleus lateralis of the amygdala (AD in the insets in B). The letters s (superficial) and d (deep) on the field potential profiles indicate the position where the traces have been recorded.
data.description: This figure illustrates recording positions and field potential profiles in the medial entorhinal cortex (m-EC) and perirhinal cortex (PRC) area 36. Panel (A) is a schematic drawing of recording positions. Panel (B) shows laminar profiles from m-EC (1, 1*) and PRC (2, 2*) following LOT stimulation. Traces 1 and 1* from m-EC show associative potentials, with 1* indicating a delayed response evoked by adjusted LOT stimulation. Traces 2 and 2* from PRC area 36 show no local responses under either stimulation condition. Insets in B show positive control responses in PRC after stimulation of the nucleus lateralis of the amygdala (AD), which exhibit a clear phase reversal. Superficial (s) and deep (d) layers are indicated. The y-axis scale is 0.5 mV and the x-axis scale is 50 ms.
data.key_data: 0.5 mV (amplitude scale); 50 ms (time scale)
data.significance: This figure investigates the propagation of olfactory information to the m-EC and PRC, demonstrating that while m-EC can be activated (including delayed responses), PRC area 36 consistently shows no local responses, even when m-EC is active, further supporting the lack of massive EC-to-PRC propagation of olfactory-induced activity.

data.caption: FIG. 4. Optical imaging of the LOT-evoked activity in the EC and the PC. Stimulus intensity was set to induce a late response in the m-EC (see text). A photomicrograph of the ventral view of the isolated whole brain preparation is illustrated in the upper left panel. The optical recording with voltage-sensitive dye was performed in the area indicated by the dotted rectangle. The time-course of the optical activity reported in the right panel was measured as fractional changes in fluorescence intensity of the LOT-evoked optical signals at the 10 pixels illustrated in the left panel (1-10). The electrical stimulation to the LOT occurred at time 0. In the middle left panel a scheme of the borders between different limbic structures under examination is shown. In the bottom panels, LOT-evoked optical changes in the EC are illustrated for the time points marked by the vertical lines of the upper right panel. Fractional fluorescence changes encoded in 'pseudocolour', as indicated in the scale, are superimposed on a bright-field image of the preparation. The sequential activation of the 1-EC (panels a-c) and m-EC (panel d) was recorded.
data.description: This figure presents optical imaging data of LOT-evoked activity in the entorhinal cortex (EC) and piriform cortex (PC). The upper left panel shows a photomicrograph of the ventral view of an isolated guinea pig brain with a dotted rectangle indicating the imaged area. The right panel displays time-courses of optical activity (fractional changes in fluorescence intensity) from 10 pixels (1-10) marked on a schematic of the brain in the middle left panel, which outlines limbic structures (m-EC, l-EC, PRC, PC). Electrical stimulation to the LOT occurs at time 0. The bottom panels (a-d) show pseudocolor-encoded fractional fluorescence changes superimposed on bright-field images at different time points (marked by vertical lines in the upper right panel), illustrating sequential activation of l-EC (a-c) and m-EC (d). A color scale indicates fractional fluorescence changes from 0% to 0.06% (for a-d) and 0% to 0.03% (for time-course plots).
data.key_data: 0.03% (max fractional fluorescence change for time-course plots); 0.06% (max fractional fluorescence change for heatmap panels)
data.significance: This figure provides optical imaging evidence that olfactory-induced activity spreads into the l-EC and subsequently to the m-EC, but not to the PRC, further substantiating the electrophysiological findings and confirming the limited propagation of olfactory input to the perirhinal cortex.
