data.claim: Lateral olfactory tract (LOT) stimulation evokes a typical mono-disynaptic response in the piriform cortex and a pure associative polysynaptic response in the lateral entorhinal cortex (l-EC).
data.support: Field potential laminar profiles recorded with 16-channel silicon probes at different rostro-caudal positions in piriform and entorhinal cortices.

data.claim: LOT stimulation does not induce local responses in the insular cortex or area 36 of the perirhinal cortex (PRC); observed potentials in these areas are volume-conducted far fields.
data.support: Absence of depth reversal in field potential laminar profiles and lack of local sinks/sources in current source density (CSD) analysis for insular cortex and PRC area 36.

data.claim: A small amplitude field potential depth reversal was inconsistently observed in PRC area 35 following LOT stimulation, with latencies similar to the l-EC response.
data.support: Field potential laminar profiles in two out of five experiments for PRC area 35.

data.claim: Activity generated in the l-EC does not propagate massively to the PRC.
data.support: Absence of a detectable population response in the PRC after the LOT-evoked potential in the l-EC, and confirmed by high-resolution optical imaging showing no activity in PRC.

data.claim: The medial entorhinal cortex (m-EC) is activated by LOT stimulation with a delayed associative potential, which is mediated via the hippocampal loop.
data.support: Field potential laminar profiles in m-EC following LOT stimulation, and consistency with previous findings demonstrating hippocampal mediation.

data.claim: Even with hippocampus-mediated activation of the m-EC, no local responses are observed in PRC area 36.
data.support: Field potential laminar profiles and CSD analysis in PRC area 36 during m-EC activation.

data.claim: The perirhinal cortex (PRC) in the experimental setup is viable and capable of generating local responses, as demonstrated by a clear phase reversal evoked by amygdala stimulation.
data.support: Field potential profiles in PRC following nucleus lateralis of the amygdala stimulation (positive control).

data.claim: The propagation of neuronal activity from the entorhinal cortex (EC) to the perirhinal cortex (PRC) is hindered, possibly by a powerful inhibitory control generated within the EC.
data.support: The consistent absence of EC-to-PRC activity propagation despite anatomical connections, and consistency with previous findings where hyperexcitability or GABA antagonist application facilitated such propagation.

data.claim: The isolated guinea pig brain preparation is a suitable model for studying olfactory input propagation and parahippocampal circuit function.
Electrical stimulation of the lateral olfactory tract (LOT) accurately mimics the relevant aspects of natural olfactory input.
Field potential recordings and voltage-sensitive dye optical imaging are reliable methods for detecting and localizing synchronous neuronal activity.
Anatomical connections and functional properties observed in other species (rat, cat, monkey) provide a relevant context for interpreting findings in the guinea pig.

data.title: Intrinsic Computational Functionalism: From Observer-Relative Maps to Observer-Independent Structures
data.abstract: This paper develops intrinsic computational functionalism, arguing that consciousness, if computationally constituted, depends on physically realized computational structures inherent to a system, not external interpretations. It introduces two criteria -- system-intrinsic instantiation and causal-dynamical organization under intervention -- to operationalize this view, ensuring observer-independence. The authors propose a three-tier decomposition of identification work, asserting that intrinsic computational functionalism survives anti-computational objections by focusing on dynamics-internal grain selection rather than interpreter-relative label selection.
data.thesis: This paper develops 'intrinsic computational functionalism' (ICF), arguing that if consciousness is computationally constituted, it depends on physically realized computational structures inherent to a system, rather than on external interpretations. ICF is operationalized by two criteria (C1: System-intrinsic instantiation, C2: Causal-dynamical organisation under intervention) and a three-tier decomposition of identification work, which together demonstrate that anti-computational arguments primarily target observer-relative labels (tier i) and do not invalidate intrinsic computational properties identified through dynamics-internal grain selection (tier iii).

data.claim: Anti-computational arguments (e.g., syntax-is-not-semantics, triviality, mapmaker) correctly establish that externally imposed computational interpretations are observer-relative.
data.support: Analysis of existing philosophical arguments by Searle, Putnam, Lerchner, and Piccinini.

data.claim: The observer-relativity of semantic labels (computational interpretation) does not imply the observer-relativity of causal structure (computational implementation).
data.support: Distinction between labelling work an observer performs and facts about a system's own physical organization and causal state transitions, illustrated by a transistor example.

data.claim: Naive computational functionalism, which equates computational identity with formal transition structure alone, is insufficient to ground consciousness because it neglects internal mechanisms, temporal/dynamical properties, and causal grain.
data.support: Argument that lookup tables or recorded traces, despite matching surface behavior, lack the internal organization and counterfactual responsiveness required for consciousness.

data.claim: Chalmers's principle of organizational invariance is a stronger form of functionalism but still requires further constraints, specifically dynamics-internal criteria and intervention testing, to identify the relevant organization.
data.support: Argument that organizational invariance needs to be identified through dynamics-internal criteria and tested under intervention, rather than merely postulated at an abstract level.

data.claim: Criterion (C1) System-intrinsic instantiation: A consciousness-relevant computational property must be specifiable without an external interpreter's vocabulary and invariant under structure-preserving relabellings of the system's variables.
data.support: Definition and operationalization of intrinsicness based on invariance under relabellings that preserve causal topology, analogous to mathematical properties of a triangle.

data.claim: Criterion (C2) Causal-dynamical organisation under intervention: A consciousness-relevant computational property must be grounded in an organized state-space structure where variables mutually constrain one another, and its organization must be exhibited in counterfactual response under intervention.
data.support: Definition and operationalization of causal-dynamical organization, drawing on concepts from mechanistic individuation, effective information, and integrated information theory, emphasizing internal organization and counterfactual structure.

data.claim: C1 and C2 are necessary, but not jointly sufficient, conditions for a computational organization to be a candidate for consciousness-relevance.
data.support: Explicit statement that these criteria identify the minimum form required, but further substantive conditions are needed to select the consciousness-relevant subset.

data.claim: Several research programs (mechanistic functionalism, Integrated Information Theory, universal theories of consciousness) converge on the requirement for intrinsic, observer-independent computational structure.
data.support: Discussion of shared commitments in Piccinini's mechanistic account, IIT's intrinsic existence orientation, and Kanai & Fujisawa's universality requirement.

data.claim: Computational identification work can be decomposed into three tiers: (i) interpreter-relative label selection, (ii) theoretically constrained partition and intervention-space selection, and (iii) dynamics-internal grain selection.
data.support: Detailed explanation of each tier, distinguishing arbitrary symbol assignment (tier i), theory-driven choices (tier ii), and system-determined grain (tier iii).

data.claim: Anti-computational arguments succeed against properties located at tier (i) (arbitrary labels) but do not generalize to properties identified through dynamics-internal causal organization (tier iii).
data.support: Argument that relabelling (tier i) preserves dynamics, while different intervention spaces or grain choices (tier ii/iii) yield distinguishable empirical predictions, thus refuting the generalization.

data.claim: Tier (iii) dynamics-internal grain selection is determined by the system's own intervention-conditional transition structure, not by semantic labels, modelling convenience, or the theorist's vocabulary.
data.support: Reference to dynamics-internal measures like effective information and IIT's exclusion postulate that select the grain based on the system's intrinsic cause-effect structure.

data.claim: Tier (ii) partition and intervention-space choices, while theory-driven and observer-involving, are empirically disciplined and revisable, unlike arbitrary labels.
data.support: Argument that partition choices are answerable to predictions, fit with observed phenomena, and causal organization under intervention, making them empirically testable and falsifiable.

data.claim: A Hopfield attractor network minimally satisfies (C1) and (C2), exhibiting system-intrinsic properties and organized counterfactual structure.
data.support: Analysis of how relabelling nodes preserves attractor landscape (C1) and how single-node perturbations produce distinguishable output distributions (C2).

data.claim: A lookup-table system fails (C2) because it lacks organized state-space structure and counterfactual responsiveness, even if it reproduces surface input-output behavior.
data.support: Contrast with Hopfield network, showing that perturbing intermediate states of a lookup table does not reveal underlying dynamics or characteristic effect distributions.

data.claim: Standard autoregressive transformers often fail (C2)'s internal-organization requirement due to transient hidden activations and reinitialization at session boundaries, preventing persistent, mutually constraining variables.
data.support: Analysis of transformer inference dynamics, noting the reliance on external context buffers rather than endogenous recurrent state dynamics.

data.claim: Whether active-inference models like Beautiful Loop satisfy (C1) and (C2) at the belief-variable level is an open empirical question.
data.support: Discussion of the challenges in showing that belief-variable descriptions track system facts independently of the modeller's choice, and that inferential competition emerges from coupled belief dynamics.

data.claim: Intrinsic computational functionalism does not decide between biological naturalism and substrate-general functionalism but specifies the structural burden that either side must meet.
data.support: Argument that C1 and C2 constrain the kind of physical organization a realizer must have, without committing to a specific level (e.g., molecular-biochemical vs. coarse-grained dynamical).

data.claim: Behavioural and linguistic criteria are insufficient for attributing consciousness to AI systems; internal functional organization is key.
data.support: Argument that current AI systems should not be assumed conscious merely based on sophisticated language or self-description, emphasizing the need to connect reports to internal functional organization.

data.claim: The explanatory gap and the hard problem are bracketed throughout the argument.
Computational structure is assumed to be a candidate for consciousness-relevance.
The argument does not claim that any particular system is conscious.

The 'consciousness-relevant' qualifier is theory-conditional, meaning it asks whether a property could be picked out by a substantive consciousness theory, without committing to which theory is correct.

data.question: The argument assumes only that computational structure is a candidate for consciousness-relevance, without claiming that any particular system is conscious.
data.context: The paper does not assert the consciousness of any specific system, but rather provides a framework for evaluating computational properties relevant to consciousness.

data.question: The criteria (C1) and (C2) are necessary but not sufficient for consciousness.
data.context: Further substantive conditions (e.g., recurrent self-modelling, global availability, non-trivial information closure, temporal continuity) must be defended on their own terms to narrow down consciousness-relevant candidates.

data.question: The present argument concerns only whether observer-imposed labelling is necessary for computational individuation; it does not settle whether environmental or teleological relations also play a role.
data.context: The scope of the argument is limited to addressing observer-imposed labelling and does not provide a comprehensive account of all potential external dependencies for computational individuation.

data.question: Criterion (C1) is not intended as a sufficient metaphysical account of intrinsicness.
data.context: C1 serves as a filter against label-dependent properties, conditional on empirically disciplined tier (ii) partitioning, but does not by itself fix what kinds of intrinsic property bear on consciousness.

data.question: Criterion (C2) does not by itself demonstrate that the property does physical-causal work in the demanding metaphysical sense.
data.context: A simulation can satisfy structural-conditional counterfactuals without having the metaphysical causal efficacy of the simulated kind, meaning C2 does not settle the substrate-based challenge raised by biological naturalism.

data.question: The criteria do not decide between biological naturalism and substrate-general functionalism.
data.context: They only state the structural burden that either side must meet, without committing to a specific theory of consciousness.

data.question: The paper has not settled which intrinsic structures are consciousness-relevant.
data.context: The criteria provide a framework for identifying intrinsic computational organization but do not specify which specific structures are constitutive of consciousness.

data.question: The paper has not settled whether digital substrates can realize the relevant organization at the consciousness-relevant grain.
data.context: The question of substrate suitability for consciousness-relevant computational organization remains open.

data.question: The claim that the consciousness-relevant level is individuable by intervention-conditional internal structure alone remains a substantive commitment rather than a demonstrated conclusion.
data.context: This core tenet of the proposed functionalism is presented as a theoretical commitment, not a fully proven fact within the paper.

data.question: Whether the criteria yield decisive verdicts in practice depends on the empirical and theoretical resources available.
data.context: Practical application of the framework may be constrained by the current state of scientific knowledge and tools.

data.question: What are the further substantive conditions (beyond C1 and C2) required for a computational organization to be consciousness-relevant?
data.context: C1 and C2 are necessary but not sufficient. Conditions like recurrent self-modelling, global availability, non-trivial information closure, and temporal continuity are mentioned as needing defense.

data.question: How to resolve disagreements between different dynamics-internal grain criteria (e.g., IIT, effective information) that can select different grains in the same system?
data.context: The paper acknowledges that these criteria exist and share a commitment to intrinsic structure but do not adjudicate between them, leaving the choice of privileged grain open.

data.question: Is tier (iii) observer-independence parasitic on the choice of partition at tier (ii)?
data.context: While dynamics-internal grain selection (tier iii) is argued to be observer-independent given a partition, a 'residual observer-relativity' enters at the level of selecting the theoretical criterion for tier (iii), and the choice of partition (tier ii) is theory-driven.

data.question: Whether any active-inference implementation satisfies the stronger requirement for C1 (i.e., belief-variable description fixed by system's intrinsic dynamics, not modeller's choice).
data.context: This is an empirical question that cannot be settled from the architecture's vocabulary alone, particularly for belief-variable level descriptions.

data.question: Whether Beautiful Loop (a recent active-inference theory of consciousness) satisfies C1 and C2.
data.context: The paper uses Beautiful Loop as a test case to illustrate the criteria's demands, but its satisfaction of C1 and C2 is stated to be empirically open.

data.question: The simulation-instantiation distinction remains unsettled.
data.context: While the criteria sharpen this distinction, they do not fully resolve it, particularly regarding whether a simulation can have the metaphysical causal efficacy of the simulated kind.

data.question: Which intrinsic structures make a system a subject of experience?
data.context: This is the ultimate question consciousness science needs to answer, and the paper's framework provides necessary conditions but does not specify the sufficient ones.

data.question: Whether register-level physical dynamics under intervention satisfy (C2) for digital chips.
data.context: This is an unsettled question in the context of no-go theorems for consciousness on a chip, treated as a general substrate matter.

data.question: Whether any current theory has fixed the consciousness-relevant features correctly.
data.context: The paper acknowledges that this remains an open question, implying that current theories may not yet accurately identify the features that matter for consciousness.

data.question: AI consciousness research should attend to recurrence, integration, counterfactual response under intervention, self-modelling, and embodiment.
AI welfare debates should treat verbal reports as insufficient by themselves and ask whether such reports are connected to internal functional organisation of the relevant kind.

A 'residual observer-relativity' enters at the level of selecting which theoretical criterion to apply for dynamics-internal grain selection (tier iii), as the choice depends on what one takes consciousness to be.
data.context: The paper's aim to establish observer-independent computational functionalism and the acknowledged theoretical-explanatory dependence in selecting the criterion for tier (iii) grain selection.

data.question: The claim that the consciousness-relevant level is individuable by intervention-conditional internal structure alone is presented as a 'substantive commitment' rather than a 'demonstrated conclusion'.
data.context: The foundational assertion of intrinsic computational functionalism and its status as an unproven commitment within the paper's scope.

data.definition: The labelling work an observer performs, where a voltage may be interpreted as '1', a neural response as 'red', a hidden vector as 'cat', or a dynamical trajectory as 'decision formation', depending on explanatory aims, measurement conventions, and semantic practices.

A fact about the system's own organisation, where a system's physical organisation realises a pattern of causal state transitions in which its mechanisms make systematic differences to later states under relevant interventions and perturbations, rather than merely passing through a sequence that can be retrospectively mapped onto a computation.

The claim that sharing the same formal transition structure is sufficient for sharing the same mental properties, typically in the form of early machine-state functionalism where psychological states are individuated by their position in a Turing-machine table independently of physical realization.

A property is system-intrinsic when its specification does not require an external interpreter's vocabulary, so that its holding or not holding is a fact about the system characterisable without reference to anyone's labelling, and its truth value is invariant under structure-preserving relabellings of the system's variables.
data.section: 5 Two criteria for intrinsic computational organisation

data.definition: An operation that reassigns names to the system's variables without altering the dynamics; it permutes indices, renames states, or changes descriptive vocabulary, but leaves the transition structure and intervention-conditional behaviour intact.
data.section: 5 Two criteria for intrinsic computational organisation

data.definition: The system's own intervention-conditional state-space structure, where its variables mutually constrain one another, so that changing one variable alters the future evolution of others, and whose organisation is exhibited in counterfactual response under intervention.
data.section: 5 Two criteria for intrinsic computational organisation

data.definition: A dynamics-changing operation that sets a variable's value (or perturbs it within an admissible range) and the system evolves from that new initial condition under its own dynamics, distinct from label-changing.
data.section: 5 Two criteria for intrinsic computational organisation

data.definition: The level of identification work where a physical trajectory is read under a particular, arbitrary labelling, such that the system's behaviour is invariant under relabellings that preserve the causal topology, and no fact about the trajectory privileges one labelling over another.

data.term: Tier (ii): theoretically constrained partition and intervention-space selection
data.definition: The level of identification work involving three theory-driven choices for a physical system: a system boundary, a state-space partition, and an intervention space, which are answerable to predictions, fit with observed phenomena, and the system's causal organisation under intervention.

The level of identification work where the grain at which the consciousness-relevant property is specified is selected from the system's own intervention-conditional transition structure, rather than from semantic labels, modelling convenience, or the theorist's vocabulary.
A measure that quantifies how informatively a system's intervention-conditional transitions distinguish successor states.
data.section: 2 The anti-computational challenge, 5 Two criteria for intrinsic computational organisation, 7 Three tiers of identification work

data.definition: A process that selects components by their stable causal contributions under perturbation.
Selects the single grain at which cause-effect structure is maximal.
Any two systems with the same fine-grained functional organisation will have qualitatively identical experiences.

The view that, if consciousness is computationally constituted, it depends on physically realised computational structures the system has in virtue of itself rather than on labels imposed by an external interpreter.
A framework separating identification work into: (i) interpreter-relative label selection, (ii) theoretically constrained partition selection, and (iii) dynamics-internal grain selection.

data.term: Computation (as defined by Horsman et al.)
data.definition: The paper refers to Horsman et al.'s definition ('the use of a physical system to model a target abstract entity, mediated by an encoding-decoding loop relative to a computational entity') as a 'broader' view that 'treat[s] any encoding-decoding loop as constitutively interpretive,' which the authors disagree with for their intrinsic computational functionalism. This definition is presented as a 'further worry' that the paper aims to address or distinguish from its own view.
